articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot gold prices were near steady and spot silver prices were modestly higher in early U.S. trading Friday, as a softer dollar and lower Treasury yields on the week continued to support precious metals following Thursday's rebound. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling an October rate increase during overnight remarks at the International Monetary Fund meetings, reducing immediate tightening expectations despite persistent inflation pressure. At the time of writing, spot gold was trading near $4,172.10 an ounce, up $2.30, or 0.06%, while spot silver was trading near $57.630, up $0.330, or 0.57%.
Market positioning remains divided between stubborn inflation and growing concerns about economic resilience. September CPI rose 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while Thursday's producer-price report showed a 1.3% monthly increase and a 6.3% annual gain, the largest monthly rise since March 2022. Producer energy prices jumped 10.8%, adding to concerns that elevated crude and fuel costs could prolong inflation. September retail sales increased 0.8%, suggesting consumer demand remains resilient, while initial jobless claims rose slightly to 199,000.
The inflation data have kept December Federal Reserve tightening expectations elevated, but near-term rate pricing has shifted considerably. Following Warsh's remarks in Bangkok, traders reduced the probability of an October rate hike to roughly 15%, while the probability of a December increase remained near 89%. The 10-year Treasury yield was trading near 5.11%, down approximately 14 basis points on the week, as concerns about debt-financed artificial intelligence investment helped fuel demand for government bonds. The dollar index retreated toward 101.9, easing another source of pressure on bullion.
Friday's September import and export prices, industrial production report and the approach of the Fed's pre-meeting communications blackout are the next immediate considerations. Softer economic data would reinforce the October-pause trade and support gold, while persistent inflation keeps the prospect of additional tightening and renewed yield pressure in place ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a major source of geopolitical and energy-market uncertainty despite another modest decline in crude prices Friday. Attacks on commercial vessels near the strait have intensified in October, with two cargo ships sinking after separate incidents and other vessels reporting projectile strikes. The absence of a durable U.S.-Iran agreement continues to threaten the stability of Middle Eastern exports, even as some regional crude flows have recovered. The International Energy Agency's decision to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks is helping offset immediate supply concerns. However, U.S. crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels last week, while hurricane-related production disruptions and lower distillate stocks have added to physical-market tightness. Brent crude traded near $105.26 a barrel and WTI near $97.11.
For gold, the transmission remains mixed: geopolitical insecurity supports safe-haven demand, but elevated oil prices sustain inflation expectations and the risk of higher interest rates. Silver remains more vulnerable to shifts in industrial sentiment, although the weaker dollar is supporting its recovery.
Global equity markets were mixed before the U.S. open as investors assessed Warsh's comments and the outlook for AI-related investment. S&P 500 futures were up 0.2%, Dow futures gained 0.4% and Nasdaq futures slipped 0.1%. Asian equities recovered part of Thursday's sharp losses, with South Korea's Kospi rising 2.1% and Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 1.4%. European markets were mixed, with Germany's DAX up about 1.0%, France's CAC 40 modestly higher and the U.K. FTSE 100 slightly lower. The stabilization in equities has reduced some immediate defensive demand, but concerns about the financing of large-scale AI infrastructure remain supportive of Treasury bonds.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices lower and trading near $97.11 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $105.26. The U.S. dollar index is softer and trading near 101.9. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 5.11% area. The U.S. dollar index is softer and trading near 101.9. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Technically, spot gold bulls' next upside price objective is to push prices back above the $4,201.00 to $4,217.40 resistance zone, with a sustained move targeting $4,230.51 and then $4,272.41. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is a break below $4,141.97, with deeper downside targets at $4,073.55 and then $4,066.54. First resistance is seen at $4,185.25 and then at $4,201.00. First support is seen at $4,148.26 and then at $4,141.97.
Spot silver bulls' next upside price objective is to drive prices back above the $57.856 to $58.276 area, with a move above that zone targeting $59.370 and then $60.450. The next downside price objective for the bears is a break below $56.920, with deeper downside targets at $56.777 and then $56.340. First resistance is seen at $57.856 and then at $58.276. Next support is seen at $57.390 and then at $56.920.

articles.title: BoJ's Ueda signals further rate hikes as underlying inflation nears 2% - Mitrade
articles.summary: BoJ's Ueda signals further rate hikes as underlying inflation nears 2%  Mitrade
articles.full_text:
Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated on Friday that the central bank will continue raising interest rates as underlying inflation approaches its 2% target, noting that financial conditions remain accommodative.
Ueda said economic activity and price developments remain broadly in line with the BoJ's forecasts, while policymakers will discuss at their upcoming meeting whether to revise their assessment of underlying inflation. He added that the timing and pace of future rate hikes will depend on the impact of exchange rate movements, Artificial Intelligence (AI) demand and developments in the Middle East on prices.
The BoJ Governor also highlighted that some global policymakers appeared more optimistic about AI-driven demand than the Japanese central bank had anticipated, although discussions this week did not materially alter its baseline economic outlook.
No big gap in view between what we have assessed on inflationary pressure from AI demand, and what I heard from global policymakers.
I felt that there were more policymakers at this meeting who were somewhat more bullish on ai-demand than we had estimated.
We will continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaching 2%, financial conditions are accommodative.
Economic, price moves roughly in LINE with our forecasts.
Did not hear anything at this week's meetings that deviated from our baseline view.
We will discuss at upcoming meeting whether to tweak our assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%.
Timing, pace of future rate hikes will be decided looking at impact of fx, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices.
Haven't been in touch with us treasury secretary bessent since we met in asheville.
As underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, it is becoming more important than before to anchor inflation around our target.
Ueda's remarks had little impact on financial markets, with USD/JPY hovering around 157.95 at the time of writing, virtually unchanged on Friday.
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

articles.title: Wall Street’s Praise for AI Amid Inflation Concerns: Will the Fed Pause Interest Rate Hikes in October? - 36Kr
articles.summary: Wall Street’s Praise for AI Amid Inflation Concerns: Will the Fed Pause Interest Rate Hikes in October?  36Kr
articles.full_text:
Wash speaks highly of AI, will the Federal Reserve refrain from raising interest rates in October?
This is the first time Walsh has systematically elaborated on his policy stance at a multilateral occasion since he took the helm of the Federal Reserve in May.
On local time October 16, during the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank held in Bangkok, Thailand, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Walsh held a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, covering topics including AI, monetary policy and the global economy.
AI is the most profound economic transformation in a lifetime
Walsh's positioning of AI is extraordinarily rare in its high regard.
He emphasized that AI is the most far-reaching economic transformation he has witnessed in his lifetime.
In his view, AI will first impact the demand side, then unlock productivity dividends on the supply side, and ultimately make the economy more productive and create more wealth.
At present, capital expenditure on data centers, chips and power infrastructure is competing for resources and driving up prices; but in the medium term, AI will bring a positive supply shock.
However, he also warned that "the road to this goal will be very bumpy", and the impact on employment in the next 12 to 18 months remains uncertain.
"I want everyone to feel my optimism, but this optimism carries a serious mission."
To this end, he announced that the Productivity and Employment Task Force established in June will hold its first on-site hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on November 16.
This is one of five external expert task forces he set up, all of which are expected to submit policy recommendations to the Federal Reserve around the end of the year.
Wei Liang Chang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank, pointed out that Walsh's reaffirmation that AI will boost productivity in the medium term helps ease inflation expectations and reduce market concerns about successive interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, which "will reassure the market".
It is worth noting that recently, affected by concerns that the AI capital expenditure boom may cool down, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index of US stocks has fallen for the seventh consecutive trading day.
Jonas Goltermann, chief markets economist at Capital Economics, warned that more and more signs of the end of the cycle are emerging in US stocks, and a more sustained pullback may occur in the next year or so, accompanied by a decline in US Treasury yields.
He believes that this stock-bond combination exactly matches the market performance that may appear when the AI boom begins to reverse.
Manish Singh, chief investment officer of Crossbridge Capital, further said that although AI demand and long-term opportunities are real, it does not mean that every enterprise building infrastructure can bring satisfactory returns to investors.
"AI may represent the future, but debt repayment is the present."
The interest rate meetings in October and December will be data-dependent
Since the Federal Reserve implemented its first interest rate hike since 2023 in September, the market has been closely watching Walsh's statements on monetary policy.
Meghan Swiber, a US interest rate strategist at Bank of America, said before Walsh's speech that investors are closely watching whether he will "green light" further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
The answer is: No.
Walsh is unwilling to disclose in advance the possible actions to be taken at the remaining meetings this year.
He emphasized that the Fed's policy conclusions "should not have a preset stance", and it is not appropriate to send signals in advance about what actions may be taken at the remaining meetings this year at the current stage.
When talking about the September interest rate hike decision, Walsh said that the Federal Reserve "clearly demonstrated its determination to achieve price stability" and reduced the degree of monetary easing.
Regarding the next policy path, he said that the trend of the global economy is "generally in line with" the Fed's expectations. There are two remaining interest rate decision meetings in October and December this year, and policymakers will be able to more clearly assess economic output, employment and inflation at that time before determining the monetary policy path.
The timing of this statement is quite sensitive.
On the eve of the speech, the US September CPI and PPI data were released one after another, both exceeding expectations: CPI rose by 3.7% year-on-year, core CPI rose to 2.6% year-on-year, higher than expected for the second consecutive month; PPI soared by 6.3% year-on-year, the largest monthly increase since March 2022.
Despite rising inflation, most Fed watchers still expect the central bank to keep interest rates unchanged this month, postponing the next rate hike to December.
According to the CME "FedWatch Tool", the probability that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged in October is 85.1%, and the probability of a cumulative 25 basis point rate hike is 14.9%; the probability of keeping interest rates unchanged in December is 10.8%, and the probability of a cumulative 25 basis point rate hike is 76.1%.
At present, many voting members of the Federal Reserve tend to wait until the December interest rate meeting to take action.
Several senior officials including Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Governor Christopher Waller, and New York Fed President John Williams have previously sent signals that there is no urgent need to take further action after the September rate hike.
Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott, believes that although the price increase of many categories is indeed at a high level, there is no substantial evidence that inflation is accelerating.
Analysts remind that against the background of rapid economic changes, do not overreact to a single data point. Waiting until December to consider raising interest rates will allow the Federal Reserve to have more time to assess the potential trend of prices.
The global economy is in a stage of structural growth
In addition to AI and monetary policy, Walsh also talked about the global economy.
He believes that the global economy is currently in a stage of structural growth, experiencing a round of investment boom that is "not limited to the AI field".
"The economies in almost all regions of the world have shown resilience, which I could not have anticipated five or six months ago."
Walsh attributed this round of investment prosperity to a favorable policy environment, and believes that it is the single most important factor driving the improvement of the global economic development trend.
However, he also admitted frankly that he "may be too sensitive to the shadow left by the global financial crisis".
Since US President Trump launched a war against Iran in February, global energy prices have skyrocketed, triggering Tehran's retaliatory actions against US Gulf allies, plunging the Middle East into crisis.
The rise in oil and gas costs, superimposed on the AI investment boom, has pushed up inflation in many economies including the United States, forcing central banks around the world to raise interest rates.
Walsh pointed out that sustained inflation is a common challenge faced by central banks around the world. At present, most regions of the world are synchronously tightening monetary policy, and "no one can free ride".
It is worth noting that just a few days ago, the IMF released the Global Financial Stability Report, stating bluntly that the global economy is "tilted to the downside in terms of risks".
Chief Economist Silvana Tenreyro warned that the global economy has shown resilience, but this resilience is approaching its limit.
This article is from the WeChat official account "Gelonghui Finance Hotspot" (ID: glh_finance), author: Sun Over the Mountain, published with authorization from 36Kr.

articles.title: Dollar-Yen Softens to 157.80 Range as Fed Chair Remarks Dampen Rate Hike Expectations - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Dollar-Yen Softens to 157.80 Range as Fed Chair Remarks Dampen Rate Hike Expectations  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Dollar-Yen Softens to Upper 157 Range as Fed Chair Remarks Cool Year-End Rate Hike Expectations
The dollar-yen pair softened in foreign exchange markets on the 16th, sliding to the 157.80 level. Fed Chair Warsh offered no clear directional signal on future monetary policy, causing expectations for additional rate hikes this year to recede. Dollar selling prevailed as U.S. long-term yields declined.
In Tokyo trading, the pair climbed to 158.18 in the morning before grinding lower through the afternoon, touching 157.79 at one point. Speaking in a conversation with IMF Managing Director Georgieva, Fed Chair Warsh stated, "I hold no preconceptions about the FOMC's conclusions. I do not think it is appropriate to say at this point what we will do at meetings later this year." While some had anticipated hawkish remarks on inflation after the previous day's U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in above market expectations, Warsh ultimately showed no inclination to lean toward additional rate hikes.
In New York trading, dollar-yen briefly climbed to 158.34, but reversed to 157.70 as Warsh's remarks circulated. The pair later stabilized as dollar selling paused amid a rise in U.S. long-term yields tied to higher crude oil prices, finishing the session at 157.99.
EUR/USD rose to $1.1262 before retreating to $1.1213, closing at $1.1237. EUR/JPY fell from 177.90 to 177.38.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told the Upper House Budget Committee in the afternoon that she intends to "work toward maintaining orderly currency markets" while communicating with the U.S. Treasury Department, though the market reaction was limited.
At the National Association of Shinkin Banks convention, Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida read remarks on behalf of BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, stating that "underlying inflation exceeding 2% cannot be tolerated," signaling a continuation of rate hikes. Market participants largely interpreted this as maintaining the BOJ's existing stance of assessing the pace of future hikes while monitoring inflation trends, and it was noted as a yen-supportive factor.
Hiroshi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, noted: "We are currently in a wait-and-see phase on monetary policy in both Japan and the United States. Financial market attention is shifting toward European developments and trends in tech company corporate bonds."
From a technical standpoint, the 200-day moving average near 158.57 is seen as overhead resistance, while the 25-day moving average near 157.49 is viewed as downside support. With U.S. midterm elections approaching in November, some market participants suggest this is not the time to take aggressive positions.
Today's Key Ranges
| Currency Pair | Trading Range | 
|---|---|
| Dollar-yen | 157.79 - 158.18 | 
| EUR/USD | 1.1208 - 1.1241 | 
| EUR/JPY | 177.15 - 177.44 | 
Note: Trading ranges in the Tokyo market on the 16th.
Uncertainty Surrounding U.S. Monetary Policy Weighs on Dollar
The U.S. CPI released on the 14th exceeded market expectations, briefly heightening caution over additional rate hikes. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield spiked to the 5.32% level at one point. However, with Fed Chair Warsh showing no inclination toward further tightening, the probability of an additional rate hike at the October Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting declined.
Market participants increasingly see a challenging environment for discerning the direction of monetary policy in both Japan and the United States. While the BOJ has signaled its intention to continue raising rates, the Fed has maintained its data-dependent approach, leaving dollar-yen without clear directional conviction.
Crude oil price movements are also influencing currency markets. Front-month WTI futures traded in the low $97 per barrel range, below the previous day's settlement of $97.97. With the rise in oil prices pausing, upward pressure on U.S. rates through inflation expectations has eased, contributing to a slowdown in dollar-buying momentum.
Going forward, the focus shifts to U.S. economic indicators, remarks from Fed officials, and the BOJ's policy management. With U.S. midterm elections also approaching in November, a wait-and-see stance is likely to intensify in currency markets for the time being.

articles.title: Dollar Falls as Fed Rate Hike Expectations Ease and AI Fears Grow - SuaraGarut.ID
articles.summary: Dollar Falls as Fed Rate Hike Expectations Ease and AI Fears Grow  SuaraGarut.ID
articles.full_text:
The US dollar weakened on Friday, October 16, 2026, and headed toward its first weekly decline in more than a month against the euro and Japanese yen. Investors reassessed Federal Reserve policy expectations as officials signaled little urgency to raise interest rates further, while concerns about an artificial intelligence-driven stock market correction unsettled financial markets.
The dollar index, which measures the currency against six major counterparts, fell 0.17% to 101.87 and was on track to lose 0.35% for the week, according to Reuters. The euro rose 0.08% to $1.1227, bringing its weekly gain to 0.23% after a 0.56% advance on Thursday.
The British pound climbed 0.31% to $1.3314 and gained 0.63% over the week. The dollar fell 0.25% against the Swiss franc to 0.8246, leaving it down 0.67% for the week as demand for defensive assets supported Switzerland's currency.
Market pricing reflected a shift in expectations for US monetary policy. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, investors assigned an 83% probability to the Federal Reserve leaving rates unchanged later in October, compared with 49% a month earlier.
Matt Weller, global head of market research at StoneX in Michigan, highlighted the unusual relationship between the dollar and technology stocks during the week's market volatility.
"What I found most interesting today and more broadly this week, is how closely the dollar has been tied to the AI trade. Usually if we see a sell off in tech stocks you would expect the greenback to get a safe-haven bid. We are seeing an element of that into bonds, but the dollar is actually falling."
Technology shares suffered substantial declines as investors questioned whether data center operators could generate sufficient profits to service their debts. The pressure extended into parts of the credit market, raising concerns about the financial risks associated with heavy investment across the artificial intelligence supply chain.
Some relief emerged after CoreWeave-related assets recovered modestly on Thursday. ING's October 16 foreign exchange analysis attributed the rebound partly to comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said CoreWeave's financial strength was improving and its cost of capital was declining.
ING also noted that longer-dated US Treasury bonds had recovered despite persistent inflation pressures. The yield curve between two-year and 10-year Treasuries flattened by nearly 20 basis points during the week, reflecting continued support for shorter-term yields from inflation concerns.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh provided no clear indication of the next policy decision during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"prejudge meetings."
Warsh used the phrase when discussing future Federal Reserve decisions, according to Reuters. Investors continued weighing elevated inflation against the possibility that deteriorating technology-sector sentiment could weaken economic prospects.
John Velis, Americas macro strategist at BNY in New York, said a rate increase in October appeared unlikely given the level of support within the Federal Open Market Committee.
"I don't think there is enough support in (the) committee, particularly from the governors, for a rate hike in October. It still leaves December an unanswered question and there is a lot to happen between now and then,"
Velis's assessment left the December policy decision unresolved. Meanwhile, ING expected the dollar to consolidate near recent highs unless technology stocks and broader risk assets experienced another substantial decline.
European inflation and fiscal concerns also remained important for currency markets. ING expected September eurozone consumer price inflation to be confirmed at 3.8%, substantially above the European Central Bank's 2% target, while market pricing reflected expectations for nearly 75 basis points of additional tightening.
However, ING's analysts anticipated only one further ECB rate increase, with developments in French government bond markets likely to influence the policy outlook. Fiscal concerns in France remained in the background following an increase in the country's debt risk premium in early October.
ING identified the Swiss franc as a potential defensive outperformer if concerns about US technology stocks intensified. Its analysis placed resistance for the dollar index around 102.40 to 102.50 and support around 101.75 to 101.80.

articles.title: WTI Jumps 5.6% This Week as U.S. Stocks Fall 8.56M Barrels While Brent Stays Near $105 — Upside to $102.50 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: WTI Jumps 5.6% This Week as U.S. Stocks Fall 8.56M Barrels While Brent Stays Near $105 — Upside to $102.50  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
WTI Jumps 5.6% This Week as U.S. Stocks Fall 8.56M Barrels While Brent Stays Near $105 — Upside to $102.50
More than 2 dozen Hormuz attacks since October 1 and a projected global deficit through year-end support crude | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- U.S. commercial crude stocks fell 8.557 million barrels to 415.577 million, the largest weekly draw since February.
- The IEA will release its last 100 million emergency barrels plus more than 20 million barrels of diesel.
- WTI is up 5.6% this week versus Brent’s 0.4%, narrowing the spread between the benchmarks to near $8.
Brent crude for December delivery is trading at $105.36 a barrel, down 56 cents, or 0.53%, from Thursday’s settlement of $105.92. Friday’s Brent range runs from $104.92 to $106.75. West Texas Intermediate has traded between $96.98 and $97.74 this morning, below Thursday’s settlement of $97.97. That settlement capped a gain of more than 3% on Thursday, the biggest daily move of the week.
Both benchmarks are slightly lower on the day but headed for weekly gains. Brent is up 0.4% to 0.49% for the week. WTI is up 5.6% to 5.91%. The gap between those two moves is the clearest feature of this week’s trading. U.S. crude has been catching up to global prices as domestic inventories drain.
WTI’s rebound this month has been sharp. On October 7, it closed at $88.28 after trading as low as $87.96. It then climbed to $91.49 on October 8, $91.85 on October 9, $93.74 on October 12, $94.14 on October 13 and $95.09 on October 14. Thursday’s session ran from $93.59 to $98.29. From the October 7 low to Thursday’s high, WTI gained $10.33, or 11.7%.
Brent has been more stable. Over the past month, it traded between $93.68 and $108.59, averaging $102.15. The September 16 high of $108.59 is the top of that range. Brent is up 0.42% over a month and 71.73% over 12 months. A year ago, Brent traded at $61.23.
The spread between Brent and WTI has narrowed to near $8 from more than $13 earlier in the month. WTI’s 5.6% weekly gain against Brent’s 0.4% shows U.S. supply tightening faster than global supply. WTI Midland, the light sweet crude grade from the Permian Basin, traded at $98.98 on Thursday, up $3.22.
The OPEC basket price is $111.60, down 70 cents. Gulf crude is trading at a premium to both Brent and WTI because of supply disruptions in the region.
Refined products are weaker today. Gasoline futures are down 1.78% to $3.124 a gallon. Heating oil, a proxy for diesel, is down 2.00% to $4.749. European diesel margins dropped after the International Energy Agency announced a new diesel release.
The setup is a market caught between two forces. Physical supply is tight: U.S. inventories just posted their largest draw since February, the IEA projects a global deficit through year-end and attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue. Policy is pushing back: the IEA is releasing the last 100 million barrels from its March emergency agreement, the U.S. is weighing sanctions relief for shadow-fleet tankers and demand is falling at its fastest pace in years. The next sections map both sides.
The 8.56-Million-Barrel Draw: Largest Since February
Thursday’s rally came from U.S. inventory data. The Energy Information Administration’s weekly petroleum report, delayed by the Columbus Day holiday, showed commercial crude stocks fell by 8.557 million barrels in the week ending October 9. The forecast was a build of 200,000 barrels. The previous week’s draw was 3.186 million barrels.
Commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, fell to 415.577 million barrels. That is 3% below the five-year average for this time of year. The 8.56-million-barrel draw was the largest since February.
Three factors drove the draw. First, Hurricane Isaias forced production shut-ins in the Gulf of Mexico. Second, imports were low. Third, exports were high. In the prior week, U.S. crude exports were 4.765 million barrels per day, and production was estimated at 13.979 million barrels per day.
Distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, fell by 2.5 million barrels. That matters because diesel is the tightest part of the global oil market right now. Refineries operated at 93.5% of capacity, a high utilization rate for October, when many plants schedule maintenance.
The Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds 283.0 million barrels. Stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for WTI futures, are at 26.6 million barrels. Cushing levels below 30 million barrels are considered low and support WTI prices relative to Brent.
The inventory draw explains why WTI has outperformed Brent this week. U.S. crude is being pulled out of storage to meet export demand as Middle East supply remains constrained. When U.S. stocks fall and exports stay high, WTI tends to gain on Brent. The narrowing spread reflects that.
Part of the draw is temporary. Hurricane shut-ins usually reverse within weeks as production comes back online. If Gulf of Mexico output returns to normal, next week’s data could show a smaller draw or a build. That would remove some of the support behind WTI’s rally.
The structural factors are more lasting. U.S. exports have stayed high since the Middle East conflict began, as buyers in Europe and Asia replace lost Gulf barrels with U.S. crude. Inventories 3% below the five-year average show a market that has been tightening for months, not just this week.
For the forecast, the inventory picture supports WTI. A second large draw next week would push WTI toward $100. A return to builds as hurricane production comes back would pull it back toward $93 to $95.
Hormuz: More Than Two Dozen Attacks in October
The Strait of Hormuz remains the main source of supply risk. Attacks on shipping in the strait and along the Red Sea have picked up again in recent weeks.
Multiple tankers and container ships in the Strait of Hormuz either caught fire or sank this week. More than two dozen attacks have been recorded in the region since the start of October. Conflict along the Red Sea has also resurfaced, disrupting a second major shipping route.
The war began on February 28, when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran. The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed to tanker traffic for months. Before the conflict, roughly a fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait.
The supply losses have been enormous. Middle Eastern oil production shut-ins currently stand between 4 million and 6 million barrels per day, based on the latest pace of exports. Total cumulative supply losses from the region since the war began have exceeded 2.3 billion barrels as of early October.
September brought some improvement. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest level of the war in September. Export-implied shut-ins dropped to roughly 2 million barrels per day excluding Iran and just over 4 million barrels per day including Iran. October’s renewed attacks have reversed part of that gain.
Iran’s own production has collapsed. Iranian crude output fell 99,000 barrels per day in September to below 2 million barrels per day, the first time since 2020. The U.S. blockade has cut Iran’s upstream output to roughly the level of its domestic consumption, with no meaningful export route.
Escalation risk is high. President Trump said the U.S. may strike Iran’s nuclear facilities again, including a fortified site known as Pickaxe Mountain. He ruled out using nuclear weapons or sending ground troops. The Pentagon is reportedly considering using the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal.
Saudi Arabia’s backup route has also come under attack. The East-West pipeline, which carries crude from the Gulf to the Red Sea and bypasses Hormuz, was hit by drones and temporarily shut. Saudi crude production fell sharply month on month as a result.
Markets are pricing a significant risk premium because of uncertainty over whether Hormuz flows can be sustained. A durable agreement between the U.S. and Iran is likely needed to give markets confidence that Gulf exports will keep flowing.
For the forecast, Hormuz is the main upside risk. A major attack that shuts the strait again, or a U.S. strike on Iran, could send Brent above $110 quickly. A credible ceasefire or agreement would remove much of the risk premium and push Brent toward $95 to $100.
The IEA Response: 100 Million Barrels and 20 Million Barrels of Diesel
Policymakers are trying to cap prices, and their actions are limiting the upside.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market. It also committed to releasing all remaining oil from its record emergency stock release pledged on March 11. That remaining amount is 100 million barrels. Around 330 million barrels have already been released under the March agreement.
The diesel release targets the tightest part of the market. Middle distillates, which include diesel, jet fuel and heating oil, have been in short supply because Gulf refineries that normally export these products have been disrupted. European diesel margins fell after the announcement, showing the release had an immediate effect on product prices.
The G7 pushed for faster delivery. On October 2, G7 leaders announced their commitment to speed up delivery of the volumes agreed under the IEA’s March collective action, with priority on releasing diesel supplies in the coming weeks.
The release has limits. Emergency reserves are a one-time buffer. Once the remaining 100 million barrels are released, the IEA’s collective action under the March agreement will be finished. Rebuilding those reserves later will add demand to the market.
The diesel release is also unlikely to fully solve the shortage. Product tightness depends on refining capacity, which takes time to restore. The IEA itself expects constrained middle distillate supplies to persist well into 2027.
Oil prices rose overnight after the IEA announcement, a sign that traders saw the measures as insufficient. Mar

Join today
Already a member? Log in
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday he will not prejudge the U.S. central bank's upcoming interest rate decisions in October and December.
A quarter-point hike in September raised the key rate to roughly 3.9%—the Fed's first move in three years. High U.S. inflation will likely force another increase in coming months to curb spending and ease prices.
Warsh offered no fresh signals during a discussion with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at a financial summit in Bangkok.
"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
The September hike went against demands from U.S. President Donald Trump to lower rates. The president criticized the committee while still supporting Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year.
Global inflation remains a primary focus for central bankers meeting in Thailand.
Recent meeting minutes show most Fed officials think one more rate hike will likely be needed this year, raising costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards.
Warsh pointed to surging artificial intelligence investment as a key inflation driver, noting the Fed’s AI task force meets Nov. 16.
"I’d say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime to this point," he said.
Unlike military conflict or other price-raising shocks, Warsh expects AI to bring "huge benefit" to global growth long term.
For Fed economists struggling with lagging data, AI could prove invaluable, he added.
"We torture data with old-fashioned models to try to find out what’s underlying inflation trends. Not so long from now, it won’t be torture. We will have access at the fingertips of central banks to all the information in the world, and we’ll be able to use new analytical tools to distill that data," he said.

Fed Chair Warsh Flags Persistent Inflation, AI's Mixed Economic Impact Ahead of Oct. 28 Rate Decision
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged that persistent inflation is weighing on the economy and restated the commitment of policymakers to achieving price stability, speaking a little more than a week before the committee's next interest rate decision, according to USA TODAY.
Warsh said the economy has largely behaved as officials anticipated after the Federal Open Market Committee voted last month to lift the target range for short-term rates to 3.75% to 4%, a move aimed at slowing the pace of rising prices. Since that meeting, data showed year-over-year U.S. consumer price inflation reached 3.7% in September, above the Fed's 2% target and higher than the 3.4% recorded the prior month.
As is customary, Warsh did not directly indicate how the committee will vote at its next meeting on Oct. 28. Most traders expect the committee to leave the range unchanged this month and raise it by a quarter point in December, according to CME FedWatch.
Warsh commented on Oct. 16 during a fireside chat in Bangkok with Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, that discussions with central bankers consistently surface the same concern about surging prices, and he noted that the Federal Reserve has made clear its intention to deliver price stability.
Georgieva and Warsh also addressed the growth of artificial intelligence and its effect on the world economy. The Fed chair pointed to a significant investment surge tied to the technology and characterized it as probably the most important positive development in the global economy.
He said the AI buildout could be inflationary in the near term by increasing demand for certain products such as memory chips, while potentially disinflationary over the longer term as it lifts productivity. Warsh added that policymakers do not yet know how it will affect employment over the next 12 to 18 months.
Warsh expressed his belief that the technology will make economies and countries that use it well more productive and generate greater wealth, which he views as a positive outcome, though he cautioned that the path to that point is likely to be uneven.
The Fed chair also announced that his productivity and jobs task force, one of five he has created this year, will hold its first field hearing in the Bay Area on Nov. 16, where it will grapple with these issues. He added that he is fairly confident he has identified the right questions but is not certain he has the right answers.

articles.title: US Market: Fed's Goolsbee says latest US inflation data is discouraging - The Economic Times
articles.summary: US Market: Fed's Goolsbee says latest US inflation data is discouraging  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
In an interview with CNN, Goolsbee said he remained cautiously optimistic that inflation could ease if it was driven by temporary factors such as tariffs, conflicts in the Middle East and supply-chain disruptions, Reuters reported.
However, he warned that inflation stemming from excessive demand, particularly from the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centres, would be more concerning and could require a policy response.
Read more: Global Market: South Korean shares rebound, but head for biggest weekly loss in 18 years
The latest inflation readings complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring price pressures under control while supporting economic growth. Persistent inflation could limit the central bank's ability to ease monetary policy, particularly if demand-driven price increases prove difficult to contain.
Goolsbee's remarks highlight the uncertainty facing policymakers as they assess whether rising prices reflect temporary supply-side disruptions or stronger underlying demand. The distinction will be important in determining the appropriate path for US interest rates.
Read more: Global Market: Japan's Nikkei rebounds after six-session losing streak; weekly loss nears 5%
Goolsbee's comments also underscore the challenge of assessing how investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure could influence the broader economy. The construction of data centres and the associated demand for energy, equipment and other resources could add to inflationary pressures if spending outpaces the economy's capacity to meet that demand.
Policymakers will continue to monitor incoming economic data to determine whether inflation is becoming more persistent. Reuters has reported that tariffs and geopolitical disruptions remain important risks to the US economic outlook, while the strength of domestic demand could also shape the Fed's decisions on interest rates in the months ahead.

articles.title: US Treasury says Japan no longer faces deflationary environment, yen level must change - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: US Treasury says Japan no longer faces deflationary environment, yen level must change  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Andrea Shalal
BANGKOK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Japan no longer faces the deflationary environment that existed for more than a decade, and the level of its currency and monetary policy should reflect that, US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne said on Friday.
Browne, in Bangkok for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, told reporters that US and Japanese officials worked closely together to support stable, well-functioning markets and would continue to do so.
Browne and Treasury Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke met with Japan's vice minister of finance, Atsushi Mimura, this week on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, a Treasury official said.
Browne told Reuters that markets should reflect the changed conditions in Japan, having earlier told reporters that Japan's economic performance deserved "considerable confidence."
"Japan no longer faces the deflationary environment that existed for more than a decade, and the yen level and monetary policy path must change along with that," she told reporters, underscoring Washington's interest in continuing the communications with Tokyo.
"Sharp, disorderly currency moves can ... really create much wider consequences that force investors to unwind positions and creates volatility across markets, and potentially raises financing costs in both the United States, and really globally," Browne told reporters.
Brooke, Browne and other US Treasury officials will travel on from Bangkok to Hong Kong to attend a meeting of finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation group scheduled for October 20 to 21.
(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair)

articles.full_text:
Warsh said AI would ultimately generate wealth but the path may be "very bumpy."
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned of a potential "shock" to the U.S. economy delivered by a rise in artificial intelligence spending, pledging to contain price increases as a flood of private sector funds drives up demand.
"If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognize this as a shock," Warsh said in Bangkok, Thailand, at a conference organized by the International Monetary Fund.
A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters. In theory, an onrush of investment in activities like chip manufacturing and data center construction could put upward pressure in general on consumer prices, unless the demand is offset by a new supply of goods and services.
"It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s hitting the supply side of the economy," Warsh said.
Warsh, who took the helm of the Fed in May, has previously weighed in on the potential impact of AI on the labor market and wider economy.
On Friday, Warsh reiterated his optimism about AI, saying the technology would ultimately generate added productivity and wealth.
But, Warsh added, "the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one."
"We really don’t know what the market structure will be of these new technologies," Warsh said. "Who's going to be making the money?"
Warsh acknowledged other shocks faced by the U.S. economy, including "shocks of war and military conflict."
The outbreak of the Iran war in February imposed a historic oil supply shock and caused an acceleration of price increases in many countries. A U.S. government report issued this week showed inflation had climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Middle East conflict continued to drive up gasoline prices.
Prices rose 3.7% in September, according to new data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Fed's target rate of 2%.
"It’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said on Friday.
He later added: "I’ve heard resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability. I’ve certainly delivered that resolve."
Price hikes prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point in September, marking the central bank's first rate increase since 2023.
An increase to the benchmark interest rate aims to slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections.
Consistent with his approach in previous public appearances, Warsh opted against issuing a forecast about what the central bank may do at its meeting later this month.
"I don’t pre-judge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have over the balance of this year," Warsh said.
Many investors appeared to interpret Warsh's posture as a sign the Fed may hold interest rates steady later this month.
As of Friday morning, investors peg the chance of the Fed maintaining current interest rates at about 86%, which marks an uptick from about 55% on Wednesday, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, a measure of market sentiment.

articles.title: Hot US CPI Data Sends Dollar Surging While Gold And Yen Face Heavy Pressure - Foreign Policy Journal
articles.summary: Hot US CPI Data Sends Dollar Surging While Gold And Yen Face Heavy Pressure  Foreign Policy Journal
articles.full_text:
A stronger-than-expected US Consumer Price Index report sent the dollar index (DXY) surging to a multi-month high, rattling currency and commodities markets across the board.
US CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.5% year-over-year, exceeding economist forecasts of 0.3% and 3.4% respectively, signaling that inflation remains stubbornly elevated.
Core CPI, which strips out food and energy costs, also topped expectations, climbing 0.4% month-over-month and 3.8% year-over-year against forecasts of 0.3% and 3.7%.
The hotter inflation print immediately reshaped Federal Reserve rate cut expectations, with Fed swap markets now pricing in just 50 basis points of cuts for the year, down from 75 basis points the prior week.
Markets sharply reduced the probability of a rate cut at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting, pricing in only a 3% chance of a 25 basis point reduction.
The odds for a cut at the subsequent FOMC meeting were also slim, with markets pricing in just a 21% probability, reflecting a significant shift in investor sentiment following the data release.
Treasury yields spiked sharply in response to the report, amplifying pressure on rate-sensitive assets and reinforcing the dollar’s broad advance across major currency pairs.
EUR/USD dropped to a one-week low as the dollar’s surge undercut the euro, with diminished expectations for Fed easing removing a key pillar of support for the shared currency.
The Japanese yen bore some of the heaviest losses, with USD/JPY rising sharply as the yen tumbled to a 33-year low against the dollar following the spike in Treasury note yields.
Gold prices initially fell under pressure as the dollar rallied and rate cut expectations were pared back, with higher global bond yields adding an additional bearish weight on precious metals.
June gold ultimately recovered from its early session losses and finished moderately higher, drawing support from a rise in the 10-year breakeven inflation expectations rate to a five-month high.
The uptick in breakeven inflation rates boosted demand for gold as an inflation hedge, helping the metal claw back ground even as the broader macro backdrop remained challenging for commodities.
The data reinforced growing market concerns that the Federal Reserve may be forced to maintain a restrictive policy stance for longer than previously anticipated, with inflation proving difficult to tame.

articles.full_text:
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned that it remains too early to assess the full inflationary impact of the Middle East conflict amid signs that businesses are working hard not to pass higher energy costs on to customers.
Speaking at an Institute of International Finance meeting in Bangkok on Friday, Bailey suggested that the risk of rising energy prices triggering more widespread, second-round inflation had so far been limited.
"I think it's too early, but to the extent we've seen evidence, so far it's been quite subdued," he said.
Bailey also highlighted the pressure on companies to contain costs rather than increase prices. "When I go around the country, I do a lot of talking to businesses. There's a very big focus on cost-cutting and a very big focus on the difficulty of passing through [higher energy prices]," he said.
His comments came as the UK economy continued to show signs of strength despite the disruption caused by the conflict.
"[The economy] is actually turning out to be more resilient than we expected it to be", he said, though he acknowledged inflation remained "enormously frustrating".
UK consumer price inflation stood at 3.1% in August, remaining well above the Bank's 2% target. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to keep interest rates unchanged at 3.75% in September, though three members favoured a quarter-point increase.
Bailey highlighted the risks of second-round price pressures earlier this month at the İstanbul Economic Forum, saying that elevated inflation can lead households and businesses to increase wage demands and pricing decisions, meaning temporary shocks can become "persistent".
"These second-round effects are slower to emerge," he said on 8 October. "The difficulty becomes greater when shocks arrive in quick succession. A recent history of higher inflation can cause people to expect further inflation. The sequencing of Covid and the invasion of Ukraine have made this risk particularly acute."

articles.title: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh signals price stability focus amid hotter US inflation - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh signals price stability focus amid hotter US inflation  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to provide explicit guidance on upcoming interest rate decisions during a highly anticipated fireside chat at the International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Thursday, emphasizing that price stability remains the central bank's paramount objective. The remarks, delivered while many American investors were sleeping, came amid a market selloff triggered by hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data, forcing global markets to recalibrate their expectations for monetary policy in the final quarter of 2026. Warsh's measured tone signaled a continuation of his cautious approach to navigating the complex post-pandemic economic landscape.
Navigating Hotter Inflation Data
The backdrop to Warsh's appearance was a fresh round of consumer price index reports that showed persistent stickiness in core services and housing costs, undermining earlier market hopes for a rapid sequence of rate cuts. Financial markets had previously priced in an aggressive easing cycle, but the latest data has prompted traders to increase bets on a potential rate hike or a prolonged pause in easing. Addressing this volatility, Warsh praised the global trend toward monetary tightening, noting that coordinated central bank action has been instrumental in preventing inflation expectations from becoming unanchored.
However, when pressed on whether the Federal Reserve would follow suit with another rate hike at its upcoming policy meeting, Warsh firmly shied away from pre-committing to any specific path. He reiterated that the Federal Open Market Committee remains data-dependent, assessing each incoming report on employment, wage growth, and inflation before making structural adjustments to the federal funds rate. This refusal to provide forward guidance is a hallmark of Warsh's tenure since he assumed the chairmanship in June 2026, reflecting a deliberate shift away from the highly prescriptive communication strategies employed by his predecessors during the emergency phases of the pandemic recovery.
The Chairman's Monetary Philosophy
Warsh's approach to monetary policy is deeply influenced by his belief in the importance of central bank credibility and the dangers of over-reliance on theoretical economic models. Having served as a Fed governor during the 2008 financial crisis, he has consistently warned against the risks of keeping interest rates artificially low for extended periods, arguing that such policies distort asset prices and encourage excessive risk-taking in financial markets. His current stance suggests a willingness to tolerate short-term market volatility if it serves the longer-term goal of decisively eradicating inflationary pressures from the U.S. economy.
Market analysts interpret his Bangkok comments as a signal that the Fed is prepared to maintain a restrictive policy stance for longer than Wall Street currently anticipates. By emphasizing price stability over immediate economic growth or stock market performance, Warsh is attempting to reset market expectations and anchor long-term inflation forecasts. This strategy carries inherent political and economic risks, as prolonged high interest rates could dampen business investment and slow the housing market, potentially drawing criticism from political figures seeking stronger economic growth ahead of future electoral cycles.
Macroeconomic Uncertainty and the AI Factor
Beyond the immediate mechanics of interest rates and inflation, Warsh dedicated a significant portion of his address to the broader structural shifts reshaping the global economy, particularly the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence. He warned that the integration of AI into the workforce and production processes will be "very bumpy," creating significant transitional friction that could complicate traditional macroeconomic forecasting. The potential for AI to simultaneously boost productivity while displacing workers presents a dual challenge for monetary policymakers, who must distinguish between temporary supply-side shocks and permanent shifts in the economy's productive capacity.
Warsh suggested that central banks must remain agile and avoid rigid adherence to historical correlations that may no longer apply in an AI-driven economy. The uncertainty surrounding the pace and scale of AI capital expenditure adds another layer of complexity to the Fed's dual mandate, as massive investments in data centers and computing infrastructure could temporarily inflate demand for energy and materials, exerting upward pressure on prices. As the IMF meetings continue, global leaders will be watching closely to see how Warsh's nuanced understanding of these technological disruptions translates into actionable policy frameworks for the world's largest economy.
Global Spillovers and Emerging Market Resilience
The implications of Warsh's steadfast commitment to price stability extend far beyond the borders of the United States, profoundly impacting emerging markets and developing economies. A prolonged period of elevated U.S. interest rates typically strengthens the dollar and increases the cost of servicing dollar-denominated debt for nations across Asia, Latin America, and Africa. By maintaining a restrictive stance, the Federal Reserve forces other central banks to make difficult choices between defending their currencies and supporting domestic growth. Warsh acknowledged these global spillovers in Bangkok, emphasizing the need for robust international financial safety nets and structural reforms in vulnerable economies to withstand the ongoing normalization of global monetary policy.

articles.title: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says AI will force the central bank to change how it sets rates - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says AI will force the central bank to change how it sets rates  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
Kevin Warsh isn't a Fed governor angling for the top job. He's already Fed chair, and on Thursday he told the IMF that artificial intelligence is big enough to make him rewrite his own institution's playbook.
Speaking at an IMF event in Bangkok on October 16 in a fireside chat with Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Warsh said AI will change how the Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy, calling it potentially the most consequential economic shift of his lifetime. He framed the technology as a positive supply shock, the kind that should push prices down over time even as it strains the economy right now. He also said the Fed itself plans to lean on AI tools to read incoming data faster and more accurately, treating the technology as both the subject of policy and an instrument of it. He stopped short of signaling what the Fed will do at its October 27-28 meeting.
Worth pausing on who's saying this. Warsh was confirmed by the Senate 54-45, the narrowest margin ever for a Fed chair, and took the oath from Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas on May 22, succeeding Jerome Powell. He isn't floating a theory from the sidelines. He's the person who sets the policy he's describing.
His bet is specific: AI capex causes short-term price pressure but drives a real productivity surge later, and the Fed's models need to catch up to that lag rather than reacting to today's data as if it were the whole story. He has pushed this view before. At Jackson Hole in August, on his hundredth day in office, he called AI a potential fourth factor of production and argued official statistics are already understating productivity gains that haven't shown up in the numbers yet. He has separately described AI as structurally disinflationary, distinct from the kind of one-time price bump that central bankers usually have to fight.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee isn't buying the timeline. Goolsbee told Semafor on October 12 that AI-driven demand is spilling well past data centers and their direct suppliers, into electricity, construction, land and equipment, and that prices are climbing in industries that have nothing to do with chips. "I'm getting increasingly nervous that that's just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand," he said. Fed governors Philip Jefferson and Michael Barr have made similar points in recent weeks, warning that AI spending could lift inflation in the near term and push up the Fed's estimate of the neutral interest rate over the long run.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says AI hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Oracle are driving up borrowing costs for everyone by flooding the bond market to fund data centers. Their 2025 bond issuance hit $121 billion, four times their historical average, and Morgan Stanley expects AI-linked debt to approach $570 billion in 2026. - why AI companies are driving up interest rates - how AI infrastructure spending affects borrowing costs
The arithmetic underneath that disagreement is roughly $700 billion in AI infrastructure spending this cycle, money for chips, power and data centers landing in the economy today against productivity gains that, if they come, arrive later. Warsh is making the opposite call, and he's the one with the gavel.
Markets gave his optimism an unfriendly backdrop this week. Semiconductor stocks led a broader selloff after a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue was running well below figures previously cited in media reports, reviving doubts about whether AI infrastructure spending will generate returns anywhere near its cost. None of that proves Goolsbee right or Warsh wrong. It does mean the chair is arguing for patience on rates at the exact moment the market is losing patience with AI valuations.
Here's the real stakes for anyone watching rate policy: if Warsh is right that AI is disinflationary, the Fed has room to cut even with hot headline numbers, because he'll read a strong GDP print as capacity catching up with demand rather than an economy overheating. If Goolsbee is right, that same strong print is a warning sign, and holding rates, or raising them, is the correct response. Those two readings of the same data point to opposite policy moves. That's not a technical dispute about one chart. It is the entire question of whether the Fed eases or tightens next, routed through how one data series gets interpreted.
Warsh isn't just picking a side in that argument. He's telling the IMF, and by extension every central banker watching, that the old model for separating signal from noise in inflation data no longer works cleanly when a single technology can be inflationary in the short run and disinflationary in the long run at the same time. Whether the rest of the Fed's committee ends up reading the data his way is the question the October 27-28 meeting will start to answer.

articles.title: BOE’s Bailey sees little evidence of second-round inflation - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: BOE’s Bailey sees little evidence of second-round inflation  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
(Oct 16): Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said there is little evidence yet of inflation becoming embedded in UK price and wage-setting.
The central bank is watching closely for signs that companies and workers are pushing up prices and wages to cover their own rising costs, setting off a second round of the inflation shock, Bailey said on Friday at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok.
“To the extent we have seen evidence, it’s quite subdued,” the governor said. “It’s too early.”
Inflation is above the BOE’s 2% target at 3.1% and forecast to rise to 4% in the coming months, a level that the bank itself says should provoke a policy response.
Bailey and his colleagues on the Monetary Policy Committee make their next interest-rate decision on Nov 5, when the markets expect a quarter-point hike to bring the benchmark to 4%.
The committee is increasingly split over policy and its last vote in September was tight, with a 6-3 vote in favour of holding rates.
Two of Bailey’s committee colleagues — external member Megan Greene and chief economist Huw Pill — have warned at other events in Bangkok against waiting for more inflation evidence. Both have been voting for rate increases, citing concern about the potential for second-round effects and the need to move fast.
Bailey has argued that policy is restrictive because the BOE was going to cut rates this year before the Iran conflict began in February. At that point, “the market was pricing a couple of cuts, and I thought that was probably pretty reasonable,” he said on Friday at the IIF event.
He was speaking after the International Monetary Fund raised its growth forecast for the UK to 1.3% this year from 1% and official UK GDP data this week showed the economy is expanding faster than expected. GDP rose 0.7% in the three months to August.
The UK economy is proving to be “more resilient than we expected it to be,” Bailey said.

articles.summary: Bank of England Chief Economist: Any Future Rate Hike Would Not Mark the Start of a Continuous Tightening Cycle  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Bank of England Chief Economist Huw Pill said in Bangkok on Thursday that investors should not interpret any future rate hike by the UK central bank as the start of a new round of consecutive increases. The remarks were aimed at cooling market expectations and avoiding a repeat of the panic surrounding the aggressive tightening path seen between 2022 and 2023.
Pill made the comments during a panel discussion at the Bangkok Economic Festival, held alongside the International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings in the Thai capital. "We should not give the market the impression that because we act now, it means we are going to step into a staircase of consecutive rate hikes again, as we did in 2022 and 2023. This is a different shock," he said.
The chief economist stressed that the macroeconomic backdrop driving any potential policy adjustment is fundamentally different from the previous tightening cycle. The earlier round of rate increases stemmed from a broad-based inflation shock triggered by surging energy prices and supply chain disruptions, whereas the current pressures stem more from stickiness in the labor market and the wage-setting mechanism.
Pill reiterated his concerns about what he has described as a potential "hidden catch-up effect" in UK inflation. This effect refers to a dynamic in which, as price levels continue to rise, workers demand higher wages to compensate for lost purchasing power, and businesses in turn pass those wage costs on to consumers—creating a self-reinforcing wage-price spiral. "It may be necessary to maintain restrictive monetary policy for a longer period to contain that trend," he said.
The assessment implies that even if the Bank of England chooses to raise rates at some point, the policy path would more likely be a "one-off adjustment" rather than a "systematic pivot." For investors, this means they should not mechanically extrapolate the future policy trajectory from a single rate decision.
The Bank of England raised rates fourteen consecutive times between 2022 and 2023, lifting the benchmark rate from near zero to a peak of 5.25%, before gradually pivoting toward easing in 2024. While UK inflation has fallen significantly from double-digit highs, services inflation and wage growth remain at levels that continue to unsettle policymakers.
Pill's remarks come against a backdrop in which major central banks around the world are grappling with the "last mile" of the inflation challenge. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and other major central banks have recently signaled caution about easing policy prematurely, while concerns about inflation persistence within the Bank of England are similarly on the rise.
Market participants view Pill's comments as revealing a delicate balance within the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee: the central bank is reluctant to be seen by markets as about to embark on a new round of aggressive tightening, yet it is equally unwilling to rule out further rate hikes prematurely. This stance of "conditional tightening" reflects the difficult trade-off policymakers face between sticky inflation and slowing economic growth.
For sterling assets, Pill's remarks help alleviate concerns about an abrupt policy reversal, while also confirming the reality that a restrictive interest rate environment may persist for longer. The front end of the UK gilt yield curve may see a recalibration of rate-hike expectations, while the direction of the pound will depend more on the evolution of upcoming economic data and inflation indicators.

articles.summary: Dollar Pressured as Fed Chair Powell Refrains from Forward Guidance  TradingView
articles.full_text:
The dollar index DXY tumbled to a 2-week low today and is down by -0.34%. The dollar came under pressure today after Fed Chair Powell refrained from providing guidance on monetary policy or the economy during a speech at the annual IMF meeting in Bangkok. Mr. Powell’s lack of guidance reduced the chance of a Fed rate hike later this month to 13% from 27% on Thursday. A stronger Chinese yuan is also weighing on the dollar after it rose to a 4-year high today.
The dollar recovered from its worst level after US import prices ex-petroleum rose the most in 5 months last month, a hawkish factor for Fed policy, and after manufacturing production rose as expected last month.

Markets are pricing in a 13% chance of a +25 bp Fed rate hike at the next FOMC meeting on October 27-28.

ECB Governing Council member and Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said. "The ECB has raised interest rates twice, and if the situation remains as it is, we don't rule out the possibility that we may have to take further action."

articles.full_text:
European stock markets advanced on Friday, extending gains from the previous session as stronger corporate earnings and declining global bond yields supported investor sentiment. The latest increases followed Thursday's trading, when regional equities reached their highest levels in more than two weeks.
Technology shares recovered some of their recent losses, while positive company announcements provided support across aerospace, industrial manufacturing and renewable energy stocks.
Germany's DAX rose 0.9%, while France's CAC 40 gained 0.3%. The UK's FTSE 100 traded marginally below the unchanged level.
Technology Stocks Recover as AI Sector Remains in Focus
European technology stocks rebounded following a period of selling pressure, supported by comments from Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang regarding the financial position of AI computing infrastructure provider CoreWeave Inc.
Huang defended CoreWeave's financial health, helping to ease some concerns surrounding companies involved in the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
AI also featured prominently in discussions at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh described artificial intelligence as the most consequential economic transformation of his lifetime for both the United States and the global economy.
However, Warsh avoided offering specific guidance on forthcoming Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, leaving investors to assess the potential direction of monetary policy.
Eurozone Inflation Rises to 3.8% in September
Currency markets remained relatively stable, with the euro trading close to unchanged against the US dollar over the week.
Preliminary economic figures showed that annual inflation in the eurozone accelerated to 3.8% in September, compared with 3.2% in August.
The increase highlighted continued inflationary pressures across the currency bloc, even as global government bond yields eased.
Lower bond yields can support equity valuations by reducing the discount rates applied to expected future corporate earnings.
Nevertheless, the latest inflation figures remain relevant to expectations surrounding European monetary policy.
Airbus Gains Following 75-Aircraft Order
Airbus (EU:AIR) shares advanced in Paris after the aerospace manufacturer secured an order from Aviation Capital Group for 75 aircraft from the A320neo Family.
The agreement adds to Airbus's commercial aircraft order book and reflects continuing demand for narrow-body aircraft.

In this live blog, Investment Week collates all the breaking market news, analysis and opinion on equity, bond and currencies, as well as the impact of regulation, economics and key market figures.
The euro area annual inflation rate was 3.8% in September 2026, up from 3.2% a month before and 2.2% a year prior, according to estimates from Eurostat today (16 October).
Annual inflation fell in one member state, remained stable in three and rose in 23 year-on-year.
France's CAC 40 index rose by 0.4%, Germany's DAX increased by 1.1%, and the STOXX 600 grew by 0.7%, according to data from MarketWatch. Meanwhile, the FTSE 100 was largely flat, up by 0.2% at time of writing.

GianLuigi Mandruzzato, senior economist at EFG Asset Management, said: "With inflation staying close to 4% in the coming months, barring a sudden resolution of the tension in the Middle East, it would be unsurprising if the ECB increased the policy rates again before the end of 2026."

Chip companies fared worse as Western Digital shares plummeted by 6.8% while Sandisk and Micron stock value fell by 8.7% and 5.7%, respectively, before clawing some value back.
