“The tech sell-off has continued with pace, exacerbated by US inflation data, which increased expectations for US interest rate hikes this month,” said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.
The CME's FedWatch tool currently predicts the Fed is around 70% likely to hold rates at its next meeting on 28 October, but a hike in December is currently priced in as an 88% probability.
Coatsworth added: “Tech investors are getting uncomfortable with the amount of debt being used to fund the AI build-out. There is a growing fear that big names in the tech space are running too fast, and they are primed to trip up.
"Reports about Anthropic’s third quarter revenue suggest it is not growing as fast as expected, which added to fears that the AI euphoria might be hard to sustain."
US inflation hit 3.7% in September, the highest since May and an increase from the 3.4% recorded in the 12 months to August, according to the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures today (14 October).
Core inflation – which strips out food and energy – also outpaced analysts’ expectations, suggesting price increases are feeding into the wider economy.
It comes three weeks before November’s midterms, where affordability and the cost of living will be front and centre in voters’ minds.
Richard Carter, head of fixed income interest research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “President [Donald Trump] has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”
Despite rising energy costs driving most of the increase, the Federal Reserve could find it more challenging to contain inflation should elevated energy prices feed into broader price pressures, added Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar.
Analysts at Principal Asset Management, Quintet Private Bank and Moneyfarm predicted a further rate hike could be on its way in December – after the midterms.
“The Fed’s job is not yet done,” said Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.
The inflation figures have caused Treasury yields to spike – just as they had shown signs of plateauing after weeks of rises – with 10-Year Treasury notes up 9bps to 5.3% and 30-Year counterparts up 6bps to 5.6% at the time of reporting, according to data from MarketWatch.
“It is not inconceivable that 10-Year Treasury yields continue to march higher,” warned Carter.
Markets have opened lower as bond yields surged, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both down, 0.4% and 0.6%, respectively.
Brent crude has been flat through the day at $105.6 per barrel. On Friday (9 October), Trump unveiled a plan to temporary lift US sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal decried by political opponents as a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
US indices responded differently and cautiously to big banks' quarterly results figures today (13 October).
JP Morgan (JPM) reported Q3 net income of $15.3bn as equity markets revenue grew by 49% year-on-year to reach $5bn, while fixed income markets revenue fell by 4% to $5.4bn.
Goldman Sachs (GS) net revenues for the quarter totalled $18.7bn with net earnings at $5.3bn.
The S&P 500 opened flat while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shrunk by 0.1% and the Dow Jones jumped by 0.5%, according to data from MarketWatch.
US 10-Year Treasury note yields fell to 5.21% while the yield on their 30-Year counterparts dropped by 5bps to 5.56%.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said: "This is not quite the uniformly positive set of figures from JPM and GS that investors might have wished for, but it still looks like a solid outlook overall.
"Goldman itself still expects 8,000 on the S&P 500 before too long, and if the rest of earnings season goes like this then that target looks more than achievable."
Brent crude oil prices dropped 0.8% today (12 October) below $104 a barrel following US President's Donald Trump's announcement of an "energy ceasefire".
Trump posted on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
It is unclear if such a ceasefire exists at present as Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenksy posted on X yesterday evening that it would be "good news for everyone – and it is important that it become reality".
EU high representative for foreign affairs and security policy Kaja Kallas added: "We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We have not yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
West Texas Intermediate has also decreased, by 0.9%, to reach close to $91 a barrel.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: "Trump’s deal with Putin to import Russian diesel helped ease oil prices slightly, but it has failed to make a significant dent in the cost of crude, given the situation in the Middle East remains so tense.
"[Brent crude] remains more than 40% higher than before the conflict with Iran broke out. The devastating Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport demonstrate how complex the crisis has become, with the Iran-backed rebels increasingly audacious and destructive in their strikes on Saudi Arabia."
"What began as a US-Iran war has broadened out, with dire implications for the safety of shipping and for oil supplies too. While earnings season will be a key driver this week, investors should expect oil news to keep making headlines, weighing heavily on sentiment," added Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG.
The FTSE 100 opened 0.5% up today, while France's CAC 40 and Germany's DAX jumped by 0.5% and 0.6% respectively.
The FTSE 100 opened in the green today (9 October), up 0.9% at the time of reporting, after a volatile week, according to data from MarketWatch.
European indices followed suit, with France’s CAC 40 up around 0.7%; Germany’s DAX rising 1%, and the STOXX Europe 600 up 0.9%.
This came in tandem with a drop in UK gilt yields, which had risen to multi-decades highs this week, currently at 5.4% and 5.9% for 10- and 30-Year bonds, respectively, after the latter surpassed the 6% mark earlier in the week.
At the same time, the price of Brent crude oil was down 1.3% to $103 per barrel.
According to Russ Mould, investment director at AJ bell, the “yo-yo” movement in markets mirrored short-term investors’ view to “flip flop” between inflation and interest rate concerns to corporate earnings strength.
“The trading week is set to finish on a positive note as European equities moved higher and Brent crude oil eased back,” he continued. “This is a welcome development but the past few weeks and months have taught us that sentiment can switch on the smallest thing.
“The FTSE 100 jumped as investors dipped their toes back in the water with riskier assets, with miners among the key names moving the market.”
US Treasury yields have surged again today (7 October) as the global bond sell-off resumed, with borrowing costs at their highest level since 2002.
The yield on 10-Year Treasuries was up 7bps to 5.36%, at the time of reporting, while yields on its 30-Year counterpart were up 6bps to 5.73%, according to data from MarketWatch.
Major indices were also down at the open, including the S&P 500 (-0.6%) and Nasdaq (-0.9%) – which have both retreated from record highs registered this week – and the Dow Jones (-0.9%).

articles.title: BoU sells $30m to halt shilling slide as emergency rate hike bites - Daily Monitor
articles.summary: BoU sells $30m to halt shilling slide as emergency rate hike bites  Daily Monitor
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has returned to direct intervention in the foreign exchange market for the first time since June 2022, selling approximately $30 million (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday in an aggressive bid to arrest the local currency's slide past the psychological Shs4,000 threshold against the US dollar.
The direct market sale capped a dramatic week in which the central bank was forced to convene an emergency Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting and deliver its largest benchmark interest rate increase in 15 years.
In his weekly market assessment, Mr. Stephen Kaboyo, Partner at Alpha Capital and forex market analyst, noted that the local unit experienced significant volatility following BoU’s multi-pronged approach.
"Uganda Shilling experienced major shifts after the BoU stepped in with a hike in the benchmark rate following an emergency Monetary Policy meeting. In a multi-pronged approach, the Central Bank, in a surprise move, also intervened in the market, an action last seen in June 2022 by selling about 30 million dollars (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday. The move triggered a strong rebound, driving the shilling back below the 4000 threshold. However, in subsequent market sessions, the currency surrendered its short-lived gains," Mr. Kaboyo said.
Looking ahead, Mr. Kaboyo warned that market fundamentals remain fragile. "In the coming days, the outlook indicates that underlying pressures remain intact. The shilling will continue facing persistent downward market forces that will keep it on the back foot, with the primary driver being the substantial outstanding exposure of portfolio investors to the local bond market. The unpredictable nature of these flows will keep the unit on the edge," he added.
The central bank's intervention briefly halted eight consecutive sessions of losses after the currency hit a record low of Shs4,143 per dollar—its weakest level since 1993, making it the worst-performing currency among 144 tracked globally by Bloomberg this month. Data from LSEG showed the shilling temporarily gaining over 2 percent on the day following the action.
In an official statement detailing the outcomes of the special MPC meeting held on October 14, 2026, BoU Governor Dr. Michael Atingi-Ego announced a dramatic 225-basis-point increase in the Central Bank Rate (CBR), lifting it from 9.75 percent to 12.0 percent. The hike represents the largest monthly increase since October 2011 and elevates the benchmark rate to its highest level since December 2016, ending a two-year period of unchanged monetary policy. Additionally, the central bank raised the Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) for commercial banks from 11.0 percent to 13.5 percent, effective September 24.
The central bank linked the drastic tightening to heightened Middle East geopolitical conflicts, surging global energy prices, and tighter international financial conditions. These external headwinds expanded Uganda's current account deficit by $1.4 billion (Shs5.6 trillion) to a total of $4.6 billion (Shs18.4 trillion), while headline inflation accelerated to 4.6 percent in September up from 4.1 percent in August.
Adding to the liquidity strain, estimates from Citigroup reveal that over $200 million (Shs799.8 billion) exited Uganda's domestic market in just two weeks as offshore investors reallocated capital from local government bonds into higher-yielding US dollar assets.
Introduced in July 2011 at 13 percent under BoU's Inflation Targeting Lite framework, the CBR serves as a key signal for the cost of money and aims to anchor core inflation around 5 percent.
The policy rate reached a historic peak of 23 percent in November 2011 when inflation approached 30 percent, before gradually easing to 9.5 percent by October 2017. During the COVID-19 pandemic in June 2021, the rate hit an all-time low of 6.5 percent to stimulate economic activity. Prior to the latest decision, the rate was last raised during an emergency meeting in July 2022 to 8.5 percent and had remained steady at 9.75 percent since October 2024.
Financial experts and economists remain divided on whether monetary tightening is the effective remedy for current market conditions.
Mr. Uthman Mayanja, Country Senior Partner at PwC Uganda, explained that the central bank's primary objective is mitigating imported inflation pressures.
"The Bank of Uganda's decision is about controlling inflation. As the shilling weakens, imports such as fuel and machinery become more expensive. Eventually, this drives prices for consumer goods higher. The typical response is to raise interest rates to make saving more attractive and borrowing more expensive, thereby easing pressure on prices. In turn, higher interest rates strengthen local and international demand for Ugandan treasury bills and bonds, which should reduce pressure on the Shilling. In short, the Bank is tightening money supply today to contain inflation risks from a weaker shilling, while also making shilling-denominated investments more attractive," Mr. Mayanja noted.
Conversely, Dr. Fred Muhumuza, a senior economist at Makerere University, argued that hiking interest rates is an inadequate solution for external supply-side shocks.
"The central bank is trying to also tell people to think twice before you borrow," Dr. Muhumuza stated, pointing out that "BoU is emphasising the message of risk aversion, but to even tell them that this is not a risk, it is a reality…that is the space we are in." He maintained that raising domestic interest rates cannot resolve imported fuel price inflation or structural foreign exchange shortages.
Adding to these concerns, Dr. Susan Kavuma warned that commercial banks will rapidly transmit the higher central bank rate to end-user borrowing costs, severely dampening private sector credit growth. She highlighted that Uganda’s average lending rate of 17.3 percent recorded in July was already higher than neighboring regional peers like Kenya.
Similarly, Ms. Jane Nalunga, Country Director at SEATINI Uganda, cautioned that the ultimate economic burden will fall on vulnerable households and small businesses.
"BoU has raised the CBR by 225 basis points to respond to the record depreciation of the shilling, worsening BoP amid the mounting inflation pressure. It's important to note that this is a remarkable increase marking the end of the 2 years of unchanged rates," Ms. Nalunga said. "While the increase in the CBR intends to curb inflationary pressures and exchange rate depreciation, it comes at a cost."

articles.title: Fed’s flexible rate outlook offers emerging markets temporary relief - The Nation (Pakistan )
articles.summary: Fed’s flexible rate outlook offers emerging markets temporary relief  The Nation (Pakistan )
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve’s flexible approach to future interest rate decisions offers emerging markets a potential reprieve from abrupt tightening in global financial conditions.
The Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4% in September after keeping rates unchanged for nine months. Its latest communication indicates that future decisions will depend on incoming economic data rather than a predetermined schedule of rate increases.
Recent US economic indicators have presented a mixed picture. Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September, while unemployment remained at 4.2%. Average hourly earnings rose 3% year-on-year, suggesting some moderation in labour market momentum and adding uncertainty to the outlook for further monetary tightening.
Inflation, however, remains above the Fed’s objective. US consumer prices increased 3.4% year-on-year in August,while inflation excluding food and energy stood at 2.4%. September inflation figures are scheduled for release on October 14 and are expected to influence market expectations ahead of the Fed’s October 27–28 meeting.
Ubaid Ullah Khan, former Unit Head at the State Bank of Pakistan, told Wealth Pakistan that the significance of the Fed’s policy flexibility for emerging economies lay less in whether interest rates eventually increased again and more in whether further tightening occurred gradually enough for global financial markets to adjust.
“When monetary policy is not tied to consecutive rate increases, emerging markets get some breathing space. It reduces the risk of sudden repricing in currencies, bonds and external financing and gives central banks more room to manage their own policy response,” he said.
Khan cautioned that greater flexibility in the timing of interest rate decisions should not be interpreted as a shift towards monetary easing, particularly while inflation remained a concern for US policymakers.
“The Fed is still signalling concern about inflation. For emerging economies, the benefit is that the adjustment may be spread over time rather than delivered through a rapid sequence of rate increases. That distinction matters significantly for countries managing external debt and foreign exchange pressures,” he added.
The Fed’s data-dependent approach has implications extending well beyond the United States because changes in American interest rates influence global borrowing costs, international investment decisions andthe movement of capital between developed and emerging economies.
When US monetary policy becomes more restrictive, higher returns on dollar-denominated assets can increase pressure on emerging-market currencies and make it more expensive for governments and businesses to raise financing in international markets.
Conversely, greater predictability in the pace of monetary tightening can reduce uncertainty and provide additional time for emerging economies to manage debt repayments, strengthen foreign exchange reserves and adjust domestic financial policies.
The importance of these developments has increased as emerging economies have become more exposed to international portfolio investment and shifts in global financial conditions.
According to research published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) this year, portfolio debt liabilities now average around 15% of GDP across emerging markets, compared with approximately 9% in 2006.
The research found that nonbank investors supply about 80% of this capital, highlighting the growing role of international investment funds and other nonbank financial institutions in emerging-market financing.
Separate IMF research identified changes in US monetary policy as an important driver of emerging-market borrowing spreads and capital flows, demonstrating how shifts in expectations about the Fed’s future decisions can influence financing conditions across developing economies.
Adil Mustafa, Director Compliance at Khushhali Bank, said greater predictability in US monetary policy could temporarily improve funding conditions for emerging economies by reducing uncertainty surrounding dollar liquidity and international borrowing costs.
“For banks and businesses in developing markets, the challenge is not only the level of US interest rates but the volatility surrounding their future direction. A more flexible and data-dependent approach allows institutions to plan liquidity, foreign currency exposure and refinancing requirements with greater confidence,” he told Wealth Pakistan.
Mustafa said the impact of the Fed’s policy direction could also extend to international investor behaviour, particularly in countries that depend on external financing and foreign portfolio inflows.
“When markets fear rapid US tightening, international investors tend to become more defensive and emerging market assets face greater pressure. If rate increases are spaced out, it can reduce that immediate pressure, although countries with weak external positions will still need to maintain strong buffers,” he said.
The changing outlook for US interest rates is particularly relevant for developing economies already facing substantial external debt obligations and elevated refinancing costs.
According to World Bank estimates, low- and middle-income countries paid a record $415 billion in interest on external debt in 2024, while their combined external debt reached $8.9 trillion.
These figures underscore the financial pressures facing developing economies, where high borrowing costs can constrain fiscal resources, limit development spending and increase the burden of servicing existing obligations.
For countries such as Pakistan, which must manage external financing requirements alongside domestic economic priorities, greater stability in global interest rate expectations planning could offer some relief for financial planning.
However, experts stressed that any improvement in international financing conditions would depend on broader economic fundamentals, including foreign exchange reserves, debt sustainability, investor confidence and the availability of external financing.
Mustafa said financial institutions and businesses in emerging economies needed to use periods of reduced market volatility to improve liquidity planning and manage foreign currency exposure more effectively.
He emphasised that a slower pace of US monetary tightening would not eliminate the risks associated with elevated global interest rates, particularly for economies with weak external positions.
Khan similarly cautioned that the current flexibility in US monetary policy should be viewed as an opportunity for emerging economies to strengthen their financial resilience rather than increase their dependence on external borrowing.
He said countries facing substantial refinancing requirements needed to focus on extending debt maturities, building up reserve buffers and reducing vulnerabilities to sudden changes in international capital flows.
“For emerging economies, breathing room is valuable only if it is used to lengthen maturities, strengthen reserves and reduce refinancing vulnerabilities. The global interest rate environment remains restrictive, so policy flexibility in Washington should be treated as an opportunity to prepare, not as evidence that financing risks have disappeared,” he said.

articles.title: China moves to stabilise stock market with share buybacks and curbs on selling - Business Upturn
articles.summary: China moves to stabilise stock market with share buybacks and curbs on selling  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
China is intensifying efforts to support its stock market by encouraging listed companies to increase share buybacks, expanding sources of long-term investment and strengthening market-stabilisation mechanisms. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) outlined these priorities during a meeting with company executives and financial-sector experts in Beijing on October 10, as policymakers seek to sustain investor confidence and improve the resilience of the country’s capital markets.
The meeting, chaired by CSRC Chairman Wu Qing, focused on the financial outlook and measures to promote stable market development. According to the regulator’s official statement, participants called for stronger stabilisation mechanisms, broader channels for medium- and long-term capital, increased dividends and share repurchases by eligible companies, and closer oversight of trading activity and cross-border risks. The statement did not announce a new blanket ban on stock selling.
Share buybacks are a central part of the approach. When a listed company repurchases its own shares, it reduces the number of shares available in the market or holds them for permitted corporate purposes. Such purchases can signal management confidence and support shareholder returns, although they do not guarantee that a company’s share price will rise.
China has already revised its buyback framework. In December 2023, the CSRC introduced rules intended to make repurchases easier for listed companies while strengthening oversight. The framework allows companies to use buybacks to protect corporate value and shareholder interests, subject to legal requirements and disclosure obligations. Regulators have warned against using repurchases for insider trading or market manipulation.
The latest push comes as authorities try to attract patient capital and reduce excessive short-term volatility. In January, the regulator said market stability would remain a priority for 2026, alongside efforts to broaden long-term investment channels and improve corporate governance. These policies reflect a wider effort to make China’s equity market a more reliable source of financing for businesses.
Restrictions on selling shares have also featured in discussions of China’s market interventions. However, the CSRC said in February 2024 that regulatory measures taken by the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges targeted abnormal trading behaviour and were not intended to limit normal share sales. Any claims of new selling restrictions therefore require confirmation from a current regulatory notice.
The strategy faces a key test: whether stronger corporate buybacks and greater institutional investment can generate sustained demand rather than a temporary improvement in sentiment. Share prices will also depend on company earnings, economic growth and investor expectations.
The next steps are likely to involve implementation of regulatory priorities, new corporate buyback announcements and further measures to broaden long-term investment. Investors will watch for concrete policy announcements and market data to assess whether the support effort produces lasting stability.

articles.title: Euro gains as US Dollar weakens following Fed Warsh’s comments at IMF chat - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: Euro gains as US Dollar weakens following Fed Warsh’s comments at IMF chat  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
EUR/USD remains stronger after posting modest gains the previous day, trading around 1.1230 during Asian hours on Friday. The currency pair inches higher as the US Dollar (USD) declines following recent comments from key financial leaders.
Speaking at a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve (Fed) Chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed’s commitment to price stability while refusing to prejudge upcoming policy meetings. Warsh highlighted that an investment surge is currently the most significant upside force in the global economy.
Meanwhile, US Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne, called on the IMF to take a more assertive approach to identifying global imbalances and urged a balanced outlook considering positive US-led economic shocks. She further cautioned that sharp, disorderly currency moves could trigger volatility across broader financial markets.
However, the Greenback gained support from stronger-than-expected inflation data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Thursday. The US Producer Price Index (PPI) surged 6.3% year-over-year in September, its largest gain since 2022, easily topping the market consensus of 5.3% and following a revised 5.6% increase in August. On a monthly basis, the PPI rose 1.3%, significantly outpacing the 0.5% analyst estimate. Core PPI, which excludes food and energy, also came in hotter than expected, rising 0.7% month-over-month and 5.0% year-over-year.
Despite the elevated inflation figures, market expectations regarding Federal Reserve interest rate decisions remained largely unchanged. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, traders are pricing in a 72% probability that the central bank will keep rates steady. However, expectations for a rate increase in December have climbed to 92%.
On the European front, upside momentum for the EUR/USD pair remains constrained due to political uncertainty in Europe, particularly in France. European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde emphasized that France must address its national debt challenges through fiscal consolidation, dampening speculation that the ECB might intervene by purchasing French bonds to contain rising yields.
While Lagarde noted that energy-driven inflation has not yet spread to the broader euro-area economy, supporting a cautious policy stance, ECB policymaker Gediminas Šimkus asserted that a rate hike this month remains an option if necessary. Markets continue to price in another ECB rate increase in December.
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

articles.full_text:
Brent holds near $105 as Iranian tanker attacks and multiple geopolitical conflicts keep oil markets on edge.
October 16, 2026
Oil prices have been relatively rangebound this week as the current modus operandi of frequent Hormuz transits and frequent Iranian drone attacks found an equilibrium point around $105 per barrel for ICE Brent. Production shut-ins triggered by Hurricane Isaias no longer provide bullish support as total offline capacity in the US Gulf of Mexico dipped to 200,000 b/d by Friday, with offshore production returned to its pre-Isaias state at some point next week. Hence, oil markets are back to watching and analyzing wars – be it US vs Iran, Russia vs Ukraine or Saudi Arabia vs Yemen’s Houthis.
Houthi Strikes Move Closer to Saudi Oil’s Nerve Centre. Houthi drone strikes caused extensive damage to Saudi Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters, as the Yemeni militia vowed further attacks on airports and oil facilities, widening risks to critical energy infrastructure amidst recovering Saudi oil export flows.
The Diesel Squeeze Is Becoming a 2027 Problem. The International Energy Agency warned that global diesel tightness would extend into 2027, with persistent supply shortages making it unlikely that stocks will be rebuilt before Q3 2027 as diesel production fell 1.7 million b/d year-on-year to 27.2 million b/d.
China Flooded Fuel Markets Before Policy Tightened. Chinese exports of refined products surged to a 4-year high of 1.88 million b/d in September, up 39% year-on-year, as refiners maximized exports of middle distillates amidst looser controls, only to see October exports halve to 933,000 b/d so far.
Trump Hypes Up a Greenland Resource Boom. US President Donald Trump stated that massive oil, gas and mineral exploration would begin in Greenland soon, even though the island’s 2021 ban on new oil exploration remains in force and the US-Denmark security deal granted Washington no drilling rights.
Russia-Ukraine Energy Truce Collapses Again. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian refineries after an awkward 4-day energy truce allegedly negotiated by US President Trump, striking Rosneft’s 340,000 b/d Ryazan plant as the public rift of Ukraine President Zelenskiy with the White House escalates further.
Taiwan Raises Alaska LNG Hopes, Trump Declares Victory. Taiwan stated that it was making progress in talks to buy LNG from the $54 billion Alaska LNG project and would invest $4.4 billion in the project, only for US President Trump to claim that Taipei would buy 30% of the liquefaction plant’s entire output.
Washington Seeks to Ease Sanctions on the Shadow Fleet. The Trump administration is considering removing sanctions from selected vessels, believed to be part of Russia’s so-called shadow fleet or previously linked to Venezuelan deliveries, so that they can carry oil, particularly from Gulf countries.
Taranto Labour Blockade Spreads into Southern Italy’s Fuel Supply. Italian oil major ENI (BIT:ENI) might be forced to shut its 84,000 b/d refinery in the southern city of Taranto as protesters continue blocking essential chemical and gas deliveries to the plant, with shortages already declared at regional airports.
China’s Solar Overcapacity Leads to Firing Spree. China’s largest solar manufacturers have jointly fired 21% of their staff in 2025, a total of 40,589 positions, as the Chinese economy continues to solve its structural overcapacity issues, as China’s solar capacity remains twice the size of global demand.
Venezuela’s Oil Recovery Barely Moves in September. Venezuela’s crude oil production boom is gradually hitting a capacity wall as September output edged up by just 5,000 b/d to 1.22 million b/d, as prolonged power outages and delayed infrastructure upgrades continued to constrain growth.
Pipeline Attacks Deepen Syria’s Energy Shortage. Syria’s national oil firm SPC reported two separate pipeline attacks this week, with explosions rocking the al-Jabsah gas pipeline and the Baniyas-Homs product pipe, compounding diesel shortages as Syrian retailers increasingly rely on imported fuels.
Trump Reaches for Wartime Powers to Expand Refineries. The White House is reportedly working with smaller refiners to award funds for capacity expansions under the 1950 Defense Production Act, tapping into $1 billion allocated by the Republican-led Congress, starting with Delek’s 74,000 b/d Tyler plant. 
IEA Looks to Build LPG Strategic Stocks. The International Energy Agency is in talks with member governments to develop an emergency reserve mechanism for liquefied petroleum gases (LPG), replicating its own model for crude SPRs, claiming the role of LPG is often overlooked in energy security. 
Aramco’s Chinese Refining Megaproject Nears Start-Up. China’s newest refinery, the 300,000 b/d Panjin plant jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and Chinese conglomerate Panjin Xincheng, has received its first crude cargo from Saudi Arabia, bringing the refinery one step closer to commissioning in early 2027.
Iran Finds Cracks in the US Oil Blockade. Shipping and intelligence data suggest that Iran has managed to export some LPG and jet fuel cargoes since the US Navy reinstated its maritime blockade of the Gulf of Oman, with at least 8 LPG carriers delivering an estimated 4.1 million barrels flowing through.
By Tom Kool for Oilprice.com

articles.title: Indonesia stocks plunge after MSCI says market could be cut from indices - Financial Times
articles.summary: Indonesia stocks plunge after MSCI says market could be cut from indices  Financial TimesIndonesia gets 'wake-up call' as MSCI prepares to expel it from global indexes  ReutersIndonesian Stocks Plunge as MSCI Threatens to Drop Market from Indexes  The New York TimesIndonesia Stocks Log Worst Day Since 1998 on MSCI Downgrade Warning  WSJMSCI Ignites Indonesia Market Reckoning After Months of Warnings  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Indonesia’s stock market tumbled on Friday after global index provider MSCI warned it could exclude the country from its main indices, deepening concerns about investability in south-east Asia’s largest economy.
The country’s benchmark Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent, triggering a trading halt, after MSCI warned it could downgrade Indonesia to standalone market status.
MSCI’s indices are closely followed by emerging-market investors and the warning, a significant escalation, could trigger billions of dollars of outflows.
Friday’s fall is the Indonesian market’s largest single-day drop since January 1998, when the country’s stocks were buffeted in the wake of the Asian financial crisis.
MSCI warned in January that it could downgrade Indonesia from emerging market status to frontier market, signalling greater investment risk. It cited concerns over market opacity, concentrated shareholdings and insider trading.
Indonesia is the world’s worst-performing stock market this year, having lost more than 40 per cent. Foreign investors have pulled close to $5bn from the country’s stock market this year.
“Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems,” a statement from the index provider said on Thursday.
Indonesian regulators have unveiled reforms to address market concerns but MSCI said investors believed these had not gone far enough.
“Market participants have indicated to MSCI that, to date, sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market,” it said, noting “significant concerns” around market dysfunction.
“Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate and is launching a consultation on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a Standalone Market.”
MSCI classifies countries including Ukraine, Argentina and Zimbabwe as standalone markets.
Investors have been particularly concerned about Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s costly welfare policies and their impact on an already strained budget and growing state interventionism.
The MSCI announcement sent Indonesian assets spiralling further. The rupiah slipped as much as 0.8 per cent against the dollar to Rp18,087 while yields on the country’s 10-year bonds rose 0.1 percentage points to 7.32 per cent. Bond yields rise when prices fall.
Indonesia’s financial regulator said it was “carefully reviewing and paying serious attention to MSCI’s assessment”. The Indonesian stock exchange said it would request “further clarification from MSCI regarding the basis for the considerations and assessments behind this announcement”.
Some investors were taken aback by the MSCI statement. “For us it really came as a surprise,” said Gary Tan, an emerging markets portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments. “Standalone status to us seems a little far-fetched,” he added.
Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier, said the threat of a downgrade to standalone status might be a “negotiation tactic” by MSCI to signal to Indonesia that a reclassification to frontier market status was a real possibility and reforms were needed.
A downgrade to standalone status “basically means the international investment community will turn its back on the Indonesian market”, said Chris Leahy, executive director of Barbican Advisory, a global research firm. “It’s quite a significant impact.”
He said the announcement gave Indonesian regulators time to introduce reforms. The index provider was “basically saying you’re in limbo for another seven months”, he said, adding that the country’s authorities had already “had plenty of time”.
Investors have complained about the lack of transparency in shareholding structures for listed companies. “The biggest thing that needs to change is the ownership structure,” said Allspring’s Tan. “That’s the biggest bugbear.”
Later on Friday, Indonesian financial services regulator OJK announced fines and sanctions against “traders, underwriters, parties who carry out fixed allocations, and UBO [ultimate beneficial ownership] of issuers, who are proven to have violated the provisions of capital market regulations”.
It said it had imposed fines of Rp1.5tn ($83mn) related to the share sales of Dian Swastatika Sentosa, which is part of the Sinar Mas conglomerate, owned by tycoon Franky Widjaja.
The regulator also imposed fines of Rp500bn ($27.8mn) and Rp100bn ($5.6mn) related to trading in Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi respectively. Both companies are owned by Indonesia’s second-richest person, Prajogo Pangestu.
OJK said shares sold during the companies’ public offerings were “intended for a group of parties related to the controlling shareholder”.
It did not name the targets of the fines or the nature of the sanctions.
Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi both said they respected the regulator’s decisions, that their businesses were running “normally” and that they were committed to supporting reforms to foster an investment climate positive for the national economy.
Dian Swastatika did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Bad News for Trump. The US Is In Its Worst Bond Crisis Since Alexander Hamilton Was Leading the Treasury - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: Bad News for Trump. The US Is In Its Worst Bond Crisis Since Alexander Hamilton Was Leading the Treasury  24/7 Wall St.U.S. Treasury yields waver as traders wrap up volatile week  CNBCTreasuries rally as investors seek shelter from AI turbulence  Financial TimesDow Industrials, Treasurys Rise as Investors Rotate Out of Tech  WSJLong-term Treasury yields plunge as tech stocks selloff  MarketWatch
articles.full_text:
Treasury yields are punishing bond investors in ways not seen since the nation's founding debt crisis, and the fallout reaches well beyond Wall Street into mortgage rates, retirement portfolios, and the federal government's own borrowing costs.
While stock traders have spent most of 2026 focused on the benchmark S&P 500, the bond side of the classic portfolio has been stuck in a historic slump. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.19% on October 14, 2026, up 1.16 percentage points from a year earlier. BofA Global Research data, shared on X by Mike Zaccardi, CFA, ranks the current slide as the second-longest bond drawdown in US history. That record runs back to the federal debt Alexander Hamilton organized as the first Treasury secretary.
Mike Zaccardi, CFA (@MikeZaccardi), sharing BofA Global Research: “BofA: The 2nd longest bond drawdown in US history”
In more than two centuries of American borrowing, only one period has kept bondholders waiting longer. Hamilton’s plan to have the new federal government take on the states’ Revolutionary War debts created the Treasury market investors trade today. For retirees who count on bond funds to cushion their portfolios, this ranking hits the part of the plan that was supposed to be safe.
Inflation Refuses to Cool, and Bond Prices Keep Falling
Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September 2026. The Federal Reserve had held the upper bound of its target range at 3.75% since December 2025, then raised it to 4.00% on September 17. That rise was a warning to anyone holding bonds bought earlier this decade, when yields sat near much lower levels.
A bond pays a fixed coupon, so when new Treasuries pay more, older bonds have to drop in price until their yields match. The longer the maturity, the more years a holder is stuck with the lower coupon, so long bonds take the steepest price cuts. Over the past year, the 10-year yield rose from a low of 3.97% on February 27 to a high of 5.31% on October 5.
Higher Yields Hand Washington a Bigger Interest Bill
The political problem follows from the same math. Every Treasury the government sells or rolls over at today’s rates locks in higher interest costs for years, and the Trump administration has to pay that bill on top of whatever fiscal agenda it pursues. On October 15, every maturity from 7 years through 30 years still yielded above 5%. The 30-year paid 5.43%, compared with 4.17% for one-month bills. I flagged this pressure when the Treasury faced a heavy auction calendar earlier this month.
Those yields spread through the rest of the economy. Mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs track longer Treasury maturities, so a long-lasting selloff pressures homebuyers and companies refinancing debt. Higher Treasury yields also raise the return stocks have to beat, which is why Wall Street watches the long bond so closely.
Long Bond Funds Took the Deepest Hits
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT) is a widely followed long bond ETF, and it holds Treasuries that mature well after the 10-year note. The table shows adjusted price performance through the October 15 close for TLT and three related funds: the iShares 10-20 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLH), the iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:IEF), which is the closest match to the 10-year note, and the iShares 1-3 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:SHY).
| Fund | Year to Date | 1 Year | 5 Years | 
|---|---|---|---|
| TLT | -5.05% | -7.69% | -34.05% | 
| TLH | -4.33% | -5.53% | -23.11% | 
| IEF | -3.19% | -3.22% | -8.07% | 
| SHY | 0.79% | 1.52% | 9.63% | 
The longer the duration, the deeper the damage. Over five years, TLT lost 34.05%, TLH gave up 23.11% and IEF fell 8.07%, while SHY gained 9.63%. TLT closed at $79.97 after a 2.7% one-week bounce as the 10-year eased to 5.1% on the October 15 Treasury curve. One good week barely dents a five-year hole.
Retirement savers should check what their bond funds actually own. A fund heavy in long Treasuries carries TLT-style risk, while one built on short maturities acts more like SHY. TLT charges 0.15% according to its latest prospectus, and its annualized forward distribution works out to about a 4.68% yield at the current price. I recently looked at whether TLT is a bargain or a trap at these levels. For anyone drawing down a portfolio into this kind of bond market, a loss in the first period of retirement does far more lasting damage than the same loss later, which is the whole case we laid out in a free guide on defending those early years: The First Five Years.
What It Would Take for Bonds to Recover
Bond bear markets have historically ended when inflation turns lower and yields peak. I expect this one to follow that pattern once CPI falls meaningfully below 3.7%. The level I’m watching is the 10-year yield’s 5.31% high from October 5. If the 10-year stays below that ceiling while inflation eases, the October bounce in long funds could turn into a permanent recovery. If the 10-year breaks above it, the second longest drawdown on record would drag on, and TLT would take the biggest hit. For a sense of valuation, the 10-year TIPS yield is at 2.78%, so buyers are now paid a healthy inflation-adjusted return to wait.
Over the long run, Wall Street has historically worked through every bond bear market, and higher starting yields tend to set up stronger future returns. Until the 10-year stays below 5.31% and inflation cools, long bonds remain the riskiest corner of the fixed-income market.

articles.full_text:
- South Korean won hits 2-week low
- Taiwan dollar slips to early August levels
- Philippine peso hits record low
- South Korean chipmakers dive 10%-12%
- Singapore, Indonesian shares down 1%
Most currencies in emerging Asia weakened on Thursday against the US dollar, after hotter-than-expected US inflation fuelled expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike to push the dollar higher, while stocks in South Korea tanked 8%.
The Philippine peso  hit a record low of 63.09 per dollar, while the South Korean won  weakened 0.8% to a two-week low of 1,352.84 a dollar. Taiwan’s dollar  fell sharply to early August lows of 32.320 a dollar.
Overnight, Latin American currencies clocked their worst session in nearly two weeks, with Brazil’s real  and Mexico’s peso  slipping 0.4% and 0.7%, although the latter recovered some ground in early Asia trading hours.
An MSCI gauge of global emerging market currencies  dipped 0.4% on its worst day in two weeks.
US consumer prices rose faster than expected last month, data showed, lifting expectations for an interest rate hike by the central bank over the course of the year ahead, possibly as soon as this month.
Fed rate hikes tend to boost the US dollar, putting pressure on emerging market currencies, fuelling capital outflows from their bond and stock markets, and increasing borrowing costs for dollar-denominated debt.
The US dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of major currencies, scaled a fresh 18-month high after the inflation data but had given up most of those gains to trade slightly lower by 0230 GMT on Thursday.
Emerging Asian equities were also on the backfoot, led by an a fall of 8% in South Korean stocks , putting it on track for a seventh consecutive session of losses.
Samsung Electronics  and SK Hynix , the world’s leading memory chipmakers, dived 10% and 12%, respectively, for their worst day since late July.
Taiwan stocks  also fell more than 3% to a near one-month low. TSMC , the world’s top contract chipmaker, also shed about 3% to hit a one-month low.
Stocks in Indonesia  and Singapore  and fell 1% each, taking those in the city-state to a three-month low, where top lenders DBS Group  and OCBC  slipped about 1% each.
Equities in Malaysia  and the Philippines  edged lower.

articles.title: PPI Jumps 1.3% in September, Fastest Since March 2022 | Inflation Pressure Builds - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: PPI Jumps 1.3% in September, Fastest Since March 2022 | Inflation Pressure Builds - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Archer-Daniels-Midland Company (ADM)
Major grain buyer and processor
U.S. producer prices climbed last month at their quickest rate since March 2022, according to CFO Dive, intensifying pressure on the Federal Reserve as the inflation outlook grows more concerning. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, a 6.3% increase on an annual basis, surpassing forecasts. The reading followed an unexpected 3.7% annual surge in the Consumer Price Index last month. Over the twelve months ending in September, the PPI excluding energy, food and trade services increased 5%, indicating that a war-driven jump in fuel costs is lifting expenses throughout the economy.
Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank, noted in a research note that the PPI and CPI reports show no indication of inflation returning to the Fed's 2% target, leaving the central bank with additional work to do, echoing a phrase used by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh in his August Jackson Hole speech.
As with consumer prices, rising energy costs accounted for a substantial portion of the producer price increase. The BLS said prices for final demand goods, meaning physical products alone, jumped 2.6% in September, the largest gain since data collection began in December 2009. A measure of energy prices spiked 10.8% last month and accounted for more than 80% of the increase in goods costs, according to the BLS. Prices for goods excluding energy and foods rose only 0.3% last month.
Adams said the PPI report demonstrates that the economy faces persistent inflationary pressure from the global energy shock and its secondary effects, pointing to a surge in prices for agricultural feed products including corn, hay and oilseeds. He added that these will place upward pressure on consumer prices for meat next year.
High fuel costs also inflated the retail sales calculation last month. The Census Bureau reported Thursday that total sales rose 0.8% in September, largely due to a 6.4% surge in receipts at gasoline stations.
Fed policymakers in recent weeks, including as recently as Wednesday, have expressed no urgency to raise the main interest rate this month after increasing it by a quarter-point in September. Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Wednesday that even with inflation above the Fed's target, policymakers have some time to wait and observe how financial conditions and the economy develop. She indicated she feels no urgency toward taking further action at this point and that time is needed to understand how the economy will evolve.
Warsh is scheduled to speak Friday at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok. It is the final scheduled comment by a Fed official before a two-week blackout period ahead of the central bank's October 27-28 monetary policy meeting.

articles.title: 3.7% US inflation sends the Pound to an 11-month low - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: 3.7% US inflation sends the Pound to an 11-month low  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
Hotter US inflation figures knocked GBP/USD to its lowest since late November 2025, and the pair is back near 1.3200, the floor of its range since late September. It dropped from just above 1.3250 on the release to just under 1.3150 at the low, and has recovered about two-fifths of that since.
US consumer prices were up 3.7% on the year in September against a 3.6% forecast, and the 10-year Treasury yield jumped from about 5.19% to about 5.33% on the release. The yield has since come back to about 5.20%, but the Pound has lost more against the Dollar than any other major currency on Wednesday.
Bank of England (BoE) Chief Economist Pill voted with external members Greene and Mann in September to raise the UK's Bank Rate from 3.75%. On Wednesday he said he's a bit sceptical of the four hikes markets price over the next year, which leaves traders expecting more from the BoE than one of its keenest advocates of a hike does. The UK side of the rate gap GBP/USD follows was being talked down before the US release pushed the other side up.
The UK's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figure for August, due on Thursday, is forecast to show a 0.1% contraction after 0.4% growth in July, with factory output forecast down 0.1% after a 0.9% rise. Chief Economist Pill speaks again on Thursday and BoE Governor Bailey on Friday, ahead of the November 5 decision. A shrinking economy would make the four hikes in market prices harder to defend.
US retail sales, due on Thursday with producer prices and weekly jobless claims, are forecast to rise 0.3% in September after a 1.2% jump, and Fed Chair Warsh is due to speak on Friday. Traders already put a December Fed hike near 95%, so the US figures bear mostly on whether it arrives on October 28 instead.
Wednesday's low went just under the late-June low, where the climb to the August 21 high just under 1.3700 began, so GBP/USD has given back that whole rally. The pair has traded beneath both its 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), now near 1.3350, and its 200-day EMA, short of 1.3400, since September 17, and both averages are falling.
The Pound Sterling (GBP) is the oldest currency in the world (886 AD) and the official currency of the United Kingdom. It is the fourth most traded unit for foreign exchange (FX) in the world, accounting for 12% of all transactions, averaging $630 billion a day, according to 2022 data. Its key trading pairs are GBP/USD, also known as ‘Cable’, which accounts for 11% of FX, GBP/JPY, or the ‘Dragon’ as it is known by traders (3%), and EUR/GBP (2%). The Pound Sterling is issued by the Bank of England (BoE).
The single most important factor influencing the value of the Pound Sterling is monetary policy decided by the Bank of England. The BoE bases its decisions on whether it has achieved its primary goal of “price stability” – a steady inflation rate of around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is the adjustment of interest rates. When inflation is too high, the BoE will try to rein it in by raising interest rates, making it more expensive for people and businesses to access credit. This is generally positive for GBP, as higher interest rates make the UK a more attractive place for global investors to park their money. When inflation falls too low it is a sign economic growth is slowing. In this scenario, the BoE will consider lowering interest rates to cheapen credit so businesses will borrow more to invest in growth-generating projects.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact the value of the Pound Sterling. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, and employment can all influence the direction of the GBP. A strong economy is good for Sterling. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the BoE to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen GBP. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Pound Sterling is likely to fall.
Another significant data release for the Pound Sterling is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought-after exports, its currency will benefit purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

The Dow Jones index corrected by more than 7% between the beginning of August and the end of September and has now been recovering since the beginning of October. It is true that this stock market index is increasingly overlooked compared with the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq, yet it is one of the oldest US stock market indices and has a particular feature that makes the analysis of its underlying trend a relevant indicator of the health of the US equity market.
In this new analysis published on TradingView, I will remind you of the history of the Dow Jones and how it is calculated. We will then see that its underlying trend remains firmly bullish according to technical analysis of the financial markets.
To begin with, here is the TradingView page showing the current real-time composition of the Dow Jones index: tradingview.com/symbols/DJ-DJI/components/
1) Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is price-weighted
Created in 1896 by Charles Dow and Edward Jones, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is one of the oldest stock market indices in the world and remains a key Wall Street benchmark. Originally composed of 12 US industrial companies, it now includes 30 major US-listed companies from a wide range of sectors.
Its historical peculiarity lies in its calculation method: unlike the S&P 500, which is weighted by market capitalization, the Dow Jones is a price-weighted index. The higher a stock’s price, the greater its influence on the index, regardless of the size of the company.
A $500 stock therefore carries more weight than a $50 stock, even if the latter company has a much larger market capitalization. Ultimately, this helps reduce the dominant weight of the technology sector and provides a broader representation of the health of the US equity market.

The message from technical analysis of the financial markets regarding the underlying trend of the Dow Jones index is bullish. After a 7% correction between early August and late September, the index rebounded near its 200-day moving average.
The underlying trend remains bullish as long as the index stays above the following combination: the 200-day moving average and the weekly Ichimoku cloud.

articles.title: European Stocks Rebound as AI Debt Concerns Rattle Markets, Dollar Heads for Weekly Loss - Tekedia
articles.summary: European Stocks Rebound as AI Debt Concerns Rattle Markets, Dollar Heads for Weekly Loss  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
European stocks rose on Friday as global markets attempted to recover from a technology-led selloff that exposed growing investor concerns about the cost of financing the artificial intelligence boom, the sustainability of corporate profits and the prospect of higher US interest rates.
The rebound followed a turbulent week in which stronger-than-expected US inflation data intensified expectations of further monetary tightening, while mounting concerns about debt-financed investment in AI infrastructure weighed on technology and semiconductor stocks. Although European equities recovered some ground, the broader market remained on course for a weekly decline, suggesting investors were still cautious about the durability of the AI-driven rally.
At 10:55 GMT, the MSCI World Equity Index was up 0.4% but remained set for a weekly loss. Europe’s STOXX 600 advanced 0.6%, Germany’s DAX rose approximately 1%, and France’s CAC 40 gained 0.5%. London’s FTSE 100 was up less than 0.1%.

Join Tekedia Capital Syndicate and co-invest in great global startups.
US stock futures also pointed to a modest recovery, with S&P 500 futures rising 0.2%. Nasdaq futures, however, remained in negative territory as investors continued to reassess the financial risks associated with the AI investment cycle, particularly among heavily indebted data-center operators.
The divergent performance between broader US equity futures and the technology-heavy Nasdaq highlighted a central concern facing markets: investors are increasingly questioning whether the revenue and profits generated by AI will justify the enormous capital expenditure required to build the infrastructure supporting the technology.
Amelie Derambure, a senior multi-asset portfolio manager at Amundi in Paris, said the ability of AI companies to translate investment into sustainable earnings remained unresolved.
“The question of monetization to me is still the big question that is not fully answered. There are still some doubts about the sustainability of the profits and the margins from some actors in the sector,” Derambure said.
Despite those concerns, she said she remained overweight US equities, expecting strong corporate earnings to limit the extent of any market correction.
Her position captures the tension driving investor sentiment. Expectations of robust earnings continue to support equities, but rising financing costs and questions about AI profitability are making investors more selective about which companies can sustain their valuations.
The week’s selloff reflected growing unease about the financing structure behind the AI boom, particularly the reliance on borrowing to fund data centers and other computing infrastructure.
Companies are committing substantial sums to servers, advanced chips, power supplies and data-center capacity in anticipation of continued demand for AI services. Yet the returns on these investments remain uncertain, with the pace of monetization varying across the industry.
That gap between immediate capital spending and the eventual generation of cash flows has become necessary as interest-rate expectations rise. Higher borrowing costs can increase the expense of financing infrastructure, weaken the economics of projects dependent on future demand, and put pressure on valuations that assume sustained growth over many years.
CoreWeave, a major provider of AI computing infrastructure, emerged as a focal point for those concerns. Its heavily indebted business model has drawn scrutiny as investors assess the credit risks associated with the rapid expansion of AI computing capacity. Concerns surrounding companies such as CoreWeave contributed to Thursday’s market selloff.
The implications extend beyond individual technology stocks. If investors become less willing to finance data-center expansion on existing terms, companies across the AI supply chain could face higher capital costs or more demanding conditions for raising funds. That could affect infrastructure developers, chip suppliers and technology companies relying on continued expansion in computing capacity.
The market’s reaction also suggests that strong demand for AI technology may no longer be sufficient on its own to support valuations. Investors now want evidence that spending will translate into durable revenue, healthy margins and cash generation rather than a prolonged cycle of investment financed by debt.
Monetary policy has added another source of uncertainty. Stronger-than-expected US inflation data released on Wednesday prompted traders to increase bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes. The prospect of tighter policy has weighed on risk assets by raising the potential cost of capital and challenging valuations built around expectations of lower interest rates.
The resulting shift in sentiment has encouraged investors to reduce exposure to some technology shares while seeking protection in government bonds. That rotation helped stabilize fixed-income markets on Friday, even as equities remained vulnerable to renewed selling.
Dollar Weakens As Government Bonds Regain Safe-Haven Appeal
The US dollar fell as lower Treasury yields reduced its appeal, putting the currency on track for its first weekly decline after three consecutive weeks of gains. The dollar index dropped 0.4% to 101.65. The euro rose 0.4% to $1.1257, recovering from a recent 17-month low as the dollar weakened.
The currency movement underpinned how concerns about the AI trade and changing expectations for US monetary policy were influencing broader financial markets. Analysts said further deterioration in sentiment around AI companies could put additional pressure on the dollar.
Government bonds also recovered some of their safe-haven appeal as investors sought assets perceived as less exposed to corporate financing risks. European government bond yields edged higher on Friday, with Germany’s 10-year yield at 3.4355%, but yields remained lower over the week.
Government bond markets across the Group of Seven advanced economies were on course for their strongest weekly performance since late May, reflecting demand for fixed-income assets during the equity market turbulence.
The relationship between German government bond yields and the STOXX 600 also turned positive during the week for the first time since August. The shift suggests government debt is regaining some of its defensive appeal, although one week’s price movements do not establish a lasting change in market behavior.
That relationship had weakened earlier in the year amid concerns that the war in Iran could drive energy prices higher, fuel inflation and force central banks to maintain restrictive monetary policies for longer. The latest market moves show investors balancing those inflation risks against concerns about corporate credit and the sustainability of technology-sector investment.
Asian markets mostly advanced on Friday as investors reversed some of the previous session’s moves. However, the recovery was uneven, with Indonesia and Turkey experiencing sharp declines following decisions by index provider MSCI.
Indonesian equities suffered their largest drop since 1998 after MSCI said the country’s market no longer merited emerging-market status and outlined plans to remove it from key indexes tracked by investment funds. Turkey’s main stock index fell more than 3% after MSCI froze certain changes to its Turkish equity indexes.
The developments underscored how index classifications and changes to benchmark composition can influence capital flows, particularly in markets that depend on foreign portfolio investment. The Indonesian selloff also introduced a separate source of pressure into an otherwise broad regional recovery.
Oil and Gold
Commodity markets remained sensitive to developments in the Middle East and movements in the dollar. Brent crude futures traded at $106.14 a barrel and remained on course for a weekly gain as concerns about supply disruptions persisted. Attacks around the Strait of Hormuz had intensified over the preceding 10 days, raising concerns about the security of a critical route for global oil shipments.
Elevated oil prices pose a potential complication for central banks already confronting inflation uncertainty. A sustained rise in energy costs could push headline inflation higher, limit the scope for interest-rate cuts and increase pressure on consumers and businesses. That would make it more difficult for equity markets to recover if financing costs remain elevated.
Gold, meanwhile, rose to approximately $4,174.52 an ounce, supported by the weaker dollar. The metal’s performance reflected demand for an alternative store of value amid uncertainty over interest rates, geopolitical developments and financial-market stability.
The broader outlook remains unsettled. Friday’s gains indicate that investors were willing to buy into some of the week’s declines, but the weakness in Nasdaq futures and continued concerns about AI-related credit exposure indicate that confidence has not fully recovered.
For equities to regain sustained momentum, analysts say investors will likely need clearer evidence that AI investment can generate returns commensurate with its financing costs. Strong earnings could cushion the market against a deeper correction, as Derambure expects, but higher interest rates and mounting debt obligations could expose companies whose valuations depend on growth arriving faster than cash flows can support.

articles.title: Nifty, Sensex investors alert! US bond yields remain above 5% - 5 ways this could impact your investments, portfolio - TradingView
articles.summary: Nifty, Sensex investors alert! US bond yields remain above 5% - 5 ways this could impact your investments, portfolio  TradingView
articles.full_text:
US Bond Yield Rise, Oct. 16 -- The sharp reversal in US Treasury yields has drawn attention to the outlook for global financial markets, with implications for capital flows, currencies, borrowing costs and equity valuations.
The US 10-year Treasury yield retreated from a peak of 5.33% following Wednesday's inflation data to 5.086% by Thursday's close, holding near that level on Friday. The 10-basis-point decline on Thursday marked its biggest single-day fall since August 2025, despite September consumer inflation accelerating to 3.7%, producer prices rising 6.3% year on year, stronger retail sales and crude oil prices remaining above $100.
Sandip Jha, Chief Product Officer at Godrej Wealth, cautioned that the decline may not signal a sustained turnaround in the bond market.
"The decline in US 10-year yields looks more like a tactical correction than a change in the underlying trend. While yields have eased amid risk-off flows and a flight to safe-haven assets, the underlying macro backdrop remains far from supportive of a sustained bond rally. With inflationary pressures expected to remain sticky and economic activity remaining resilient, the fundamental case for a sustained rally in Treasuries remains weak. Unless the macro data begin to soften meaningfully, yields could reverse course and move higher again," Jha said.
The US 10-year Treasury yield had climbed from 4.76% at the end of August 2026 to 5.33% on Wednesday, reaching a multi-decade high.
The increase comes amid elevated crude oil prices, resilient US economic activity, widening fiscal deficits and growing investor demands for higher compensation for holding long-term government debt. These factors have reinforced expectations of interest rates remaining elevated for longer.
For Indian investors, the development matters because US Treasury yields serve as a global benchmark for borrowing costs and influence how international investors allocate capital across markets.
Here are five ways rising US yields could affect investments and what investors should consider doing, according to a report by IndusInd Bank.
Higher US Treasury yields can make American fixed-income investments more attractive relative to emerging-market assets. As the return available on US government debt increases, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) may become more selective about investing in Indian equities, particularly when the additional returns do not adequately compensate for currency and market risks.
Such a shift could put pressure on Indian stock prices and contribute to volatility, especially if foreign investors continue to withdraw money from domestic markets.
The IndusInd Bank report noted that rising US yields can affect the relative attractiveness of Indian assets and influence international capital flows.
Movements in US Treasury yields can influence domestic bond-market sentiment and Indian government security (G-sec) yields. Higher global borrowing costs may push domestic yields upwards, increasing the cost of raising money for governments and companies.
The IndusInd Bank report showed that India's 10-year benchmark government bond yield rose to 7.18% on September 30, 2026, from 6.95% at the end of August. It attributed the increase to rising global yields, elevated crude oil prices, domestic inflation concerns and tighter banking-system liquidity.
For existing bondholders, rising yields can mean falling market prices for bonds, particularly those with longer maturities. However, higher yields can also improve the returns available to investors entering the market at the new levels.
Higher US yields can strengthen the dollar by improving the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated investments. A stronger dollar could put pressure on the Indian rupee, particularly when foreign capital flows are volatile.
A weaker rupee can increase the domestic cost of imported goods, including crude oil. This may add to imported inflation and complicate the policy outlook for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
Currency movements can also affect companies differently. Businesses dependent on imported raw materials may face higher costs, while exporters earning revenues in dollars could benefit from favourable currency translation, depending on their cost structures and hedging arrangements.
Higher global interest rates influence overseas borrowing costs for companies. If elevated yields persist, businesses that depend heavily on external financing could face more expensive debt, potentially affecting profitability and investment plans.
Higher interest rates can also reduce the present value of future corporate earnings, putting pressure on equity valuations. This can be particularly relevant for companies whose valuations depend heavily on profits expected several years into the future.
The report identified elevated fiscal deficits and Treasury issuance as factors that could keep US yields high, reinforcing the possibility of a prolonged higher-interest-rate environment.
Rising yields are part of a broader global picture involving inflation, geopolitical uncertainty, energy prices and uneven economic growth. These factors can influence investor sentiment and trigger sharp market movements even when a company's long-term business outlook remains intact.
IndusInd Bank's report highlighted India's resilient domestic fundamentals but cautioned that global developments can affect markets in the short term.
For investors, the key is not to predict the exact peak in US yields but to understand how prolonged high rates could affect their holdings. A disciplined approach, periodic portfolio reviews and diversification can help manage risk without abandoning long-term investment objectives.
