articles.title: Is Gold's Rise Driven by US Inflation or Safe-Haven Demand, and What Does It Mean for Newmont (NYSE:NEM) and Northern Star (ASX:NST)? - Kalkine
articles.summary: Is Gold's Rise Driven by US Inflation or Safe-Haven Demand, and What Does It Mean for Newmont (NYSE:NEM) and Northern Star (ASX:NST)?  Kalkine
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Gold traded above USD 4,150 per troy ounce on 16 October 2026 as safe-haven demand provided support amid financial market uncertainty.
- US consumer inflation reached 3.7% in September 2026, maintaining attention on the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.
- Newmont (NYSE:NEM) and Northern Star Resources (ASX:NST) remain exposed to gold price movements, production costs and operating conditions.
- Interest rates, US dollar movements and geopolitical uncertainty remain important influences on precious metals markets.
Gold traded above USD 4,150 per troy ounce on 16 October 2026, according to Trading Economics. The quotation represents a contract-for-difference market reference rather than an official COMEX futures settlement.
The precious metal recovered following recent market weakness, with changing economic expectations and increased demand for defensive assets contributing to market attention.
Gold's performance reflects competing influences. Persistent inflation and expectations of higher interest rates can create pressure on precious metals, while financial market uncertainty can encourage demand for assets traditionally regarded as stores of value.
Consequently, the gold market remains sensitive to changes in monetary policy expectations, bond yields, currency movements and geopolitical developments.
US Inflation Remains an Important Market Influence
The US Consumer Price Index increased 3.7% over the twelve months to September 2026, while monthly consumer prices rose 0.6% on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Energy prices contributed substantially to the monthly increase, highlighting the continuing influence of fuel costs on broader inflation.
Elevated inflation can affect gold through several channels.
Persistent price pressures may encourage monetary policymakers to maintain restrictive interest rates or consider additional tightening. Higher interest rates can increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest income.
However, inflation can also support demand from investors seeking exposure to assets perceived as potential stores of value.
The direction of gold prices therefore depends on how inflation affects interest rates, economic expectations and demand for defensive assets.
How Interest Rates Influence Gold Prices
Gold prices are closely watched alongside movements in government bond yields and monetary policy expectations.
When interest rates increase, interest-bearing assets may become relatively more attractive than non-yielding commodities.
Conversely, declining bond yields can reduce the opportunity cost associated with holding gold.
Changes in US monetary policy expectations can also affect the US dollar, which plays an important role in international gold trading.
Because gold is commonly priced in US dollars, currency appreciation can make it more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
A weaker dollar may provide support to demand, although this relationship does not operate consistently during every trading session.
These interconnected factors help explain why gold prices can fluctuate despite relatively stable physical supply conditions.
Safe-Haven Demand Adds Another Dimension
Gold is frequently considered a defensive asset during periods of heightened uncertainty.
Volatility in equity markets, concerns about economic growth and geopolitical tensions can influence demand for precious metals.
Investors may seek gold exposure as part of broader portfolio diversification or as a means of reducing exposure to certain financial market risks.
However, gold does not always rise during periods of uncertainty.
Sudden increases in liquidity requirements, changes in interest-rate expectations or currency movements can lead to temporary selling pressure.
The relationship between safe-haven demand and inflation-related monetary policy concerns is therefore complex.
Rather than operating independently, these influences can reinforce or offset each other.
Central Bank Activity and Long-Term Gold Demand
Central banks hold gold as part of their international reserve assets.
Gold can contribute to reserve diversification because it is not directly linked to the credit obligations of an individual sovereign issuer.
Changes in central bank purchasing behaviour can influence longer-term market expectations, although the impact depends on the scale and timing of transactions.
Physical gold demand also comes from jewellery manufacturing, investment products and industrial applications.
Gold exchange-traded products and investment-related purchases provide additional channels through which financial market sentiment can influence demand.
Nevertheless, short-term price changes cannot be attributed to central bank activity without supporting transaction and market evidence.
What Does the Gold Price Environment Mean for Newmont (NYSE:NEM)?
Newmont Corporation (NYSE:NEM) is a major international gold mining company with operations across multiple geographic regions.
Its financial performance is influenced by realised gold prices, production volumes, mining costs and capital expenditure requirements.
Higher realised gold prices can support revenue when other operating factors remain unchanged.
However, profitability also depends on the costs associated with extracting, processing and delivering gold.
Energy expenditure, labour requirements, equipment maintenance and sustaining capital investment contribute to the economics of mining operations.
Newmont (NYSE:NEM) also faces operational risks associated with geological conditions, regulatory requirements and project execution.
As a result, changes in gold prices do not necessarily translate directly into equivalent movements in company earnings or share prices.
How Northern Star Resources (ASX:NST) Is Positioned
Northern Star Resources (ASX:NST) is a major Australian-listed gold producer with operations in Australia and North America.
The company's financial performance is sensitive to realised gold prices, operating expenditure and production efficiency.
Gold is primarily priced internationally in US dollars, while a substantial portion of costs at Australian mining operations is incurred in Australian dollars.
Consequently, movements in the AUD/USD exchange rate can influence revenue translated into Australian dollars and operating margins.
Northern Star Resources (ASX:NST) must also manage mining costs, capital investment and operational execution across its asset portfolio.
Higher gold prices may support revenue, but production constraints or rising expenses can offset some of the potential benefit.
Other Major Listed Gold Producers
Evolution Mining
Evolution Mining (ASX:EVN) operates gold and copper assets in Australia and Canada.
Its financial performance reflects precious metals prices, copper exposure, production volumes and operating costs.
Barrick Mining Corporation
Barrick maintains international exposure to gold and copper production.
Its earnings are influenced by commodity prices, operating performance and capital allocation across mining assets.
Agnico Eagle Mines (NYSE; TSX)
Agnico Eagle Mines operates gold mining assets across several international jurisdictions.
Its financial outlook depends on realised gold prices, production efficiency and the cost of maintaining and developing its mining operations.
Although these companies operate within the precious metals sector, their sensitivity to changes in gold prices varies according to production costs, geographic exposure and business structure.
Why Mining Costs Matter Alongside Gold Prices
The relationship between gold prices and mining profitability depends substantially on operating costs.
All-in sustaining costs are commonly used to assess the expenditure associated with maintaining gold production, although the measure is non-standardised and can differ between companies.
The calculation generally incorporates operating expenses and certain sustaining capital requirements.
Changes in labour costs, energy prices, equipment expenditure and production grades can influence the cost of producing an ounce of gold.
A higher gold price may improve operating margins when costs remain stable, while increasing expenditure can reduce the financial benefit.
Investors assessing mining companies therefore need to distinguish between movements in the commodity price and changes in company-specific operating performance.
What Could Strengthen or Weaken Gold Prices?
Gold prices may receive support from increased safe-haven demand, declining real interest rates or a weaker US dollar.
Demand for defensive assets could also increase during periods of financial market volatility or geopolitical uncertainty.
Conversely, stronger economic activity, rising real yields or additional monetary policy tightening could create pressure on the precious metal.
Physical demand, central bank reserve activity and investment flows represent additional influences.
The interaction between these factors makes near-term gold price movements difficult to predict with certainty.
Key Developments to Watch
The Federal Reserve's next scheduled monetary policy meeting will take place on 27–28 October 2026, followed by another meeting on 8–9 December 2026.
Future inflation releases, employment indicators and changes in government bond yields may influence expectations regarding the direction of interest rates.
Quarterly production and financial disclosures from Newmont (NYSE:NEM), Northern Star Resources (ASX:NST) and other gold miners will also provide insight into operating costs, output and realised pricing.
For gold producers, the relationship between commodity prices and financial performance remains dependent on operational efficiency, production continuity and capital expenditure.
The broader gold market will continue to reflect the interaction between inflation, monetary policy expectations and demand for defensive assets.

articles.title: Bonds Are Breaking, the Fed Is Boxed In: Why Stocks Can Keep Rising - I/O Fund
articles.summary: Bonds Are Breaking, the Fed Is Boxed In: Why Stocks Can Keep Rising  I/O Fund
articles.full_text:
·OCT 16, 2026·16 min read
On this page
In last week’s report, we laid out the case for a continuation of the secular bull market for months to years, which would be led by AI. From our analysis, we believe the best gains are yet to come; however, we will have to contend with a brief period of volatility, which we warned our readers about.
“On a shorter timeframe, the S&P 500 appears to be setting up for a high of some kind into this cycle window…At minimum, we would then expect a pullback to the 7,300–7,265 area. If 7,265 breaks, the next target is 7,000–6,683.”
Since that report, Semiconductors dropped ~10%, signaling this period of volatility has likely begun. How long and deep this correction runs depends largely on the deteriorating macro backdrop, which is forcing a readjustment to risk exposure while the market digests a new norm.
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury just broke to a new high, reaching roughly 5.35% intraday – a level not seen since 2002. This may not seem like much, yet when analyzed in the context of growing US deficits, it quickly becomes a major problem. This breakdown in bonds is causing a chain reaction in Monetary Policy and the U.S. Dollar, which is depleting global liquidity.
In this report, we will unpack the current macro-backdrop. We will explain why this breakout in yields matters, why the U.S. Dollar remains the key, and why growth in the economy should put a floor under any extended period of volatility.
Record Consumer Spending Is Putting a Floor Under Stocks
There are a handful of macro forces that have a history of affecting equity markets, ranging from growth, inflation, liquidity, sentiment, fiscal and monetary policy. Of these, one of the most important factors which largely determines secular shifts in the equity market’s trend is growth.
While the market is focused on bond yields moving higher, and FED policy becoming more restrictive, not many are discussing the unusually high level of growth unfolding in the economy. We are in a rare period where nominal private sector growth, as measured by domestic private demand, grew at a 9.5% annualized rate in Q2. This is more than double the pre-COVID growth of 4% to 4.5%. Roughly half of this growth is real, at 4.6% after inflation, which is still well above pre-COVID trends.
Furthermore, when we dive into the data, what we find challenges the assumption that the AI CAPEX buildout is the primary driver of economic activity. While this narrative was true in 2025, it doesn’t represent the full picture in 2026.
Most AI spending shows up in GDP under business investment (nonresidential fixed investment). That category covers software, information processing equipment, R&D, structures such as data centers, and other equipment. Its contribution to real GDP growth decreased from 1.4 percentage points in Q1 2026 to 1.2 percentage points in Q2, using BEA’s revised data released September 30th.
While the business investment share of the total contribution to GDP decreased, the QoQ growth figure was +3.6% in Q2. What this means is that investments in US businesses were not the primary driver of Q2 GDP, which may surprise many readers. The biggest driver of growth was consumer spending. This segment’s contribution jumped from 0.5 percentage points in Q1 to 2.5 points in Q2, more than all of Q2’s 2.2% growth rate. So, not only is AI spending in the economy still expanding, but the US consumer is also leading the current growth in the economy.
It is unlikely to see the start of a meaningful bear market in equities when growth is this robust. The growth picture alone confirms the larger secular trend higher that we outlined in last week’s report. However, this does not mean that we cannot see other meaningful macro forces cause a temporary period of volatility.
10-Year Treasury Yields Hit 2002 Highs as $40 Trillion Debt Boxes In the Fed
While the growth backdrop is historically very strong, which would typically support a secular uptrend in equities, the two segments that could lead to a correction now are Monetary Policy and Liquidity.
The above-trend growth in the economy we just discussed has been happening while inflation was running well above the FED’s arbitrary 2% target. The FED has been easing into this environment with their rate cutting campaign that started in 2024, until they reversed course with a rate hike on September 16th.
As a result of an economy running hot in tandem with a Fed that has been stimulating, bond yields are starting to break out (and bond prices to break down) to levels not seen in nearly 25 years.
What drives yields in long-duration bonds is growth and inflation expectations. A stronger economy pushes prices higher to meet a growing demand for goods and services. Rising inflation is not an environment in which one wants to hold a fixed yield, as the purchasing power of that yield diminishes the higher inflation goes.
Fiscal Dominance Is Limiting the Fed’s Options
The breakdown in bonds is the market signaling loudly that the FED has been too accommodative by demanding a higher yield for holding this debt. However, unlike over the prior decades, the FED is very limited in what it can do to address inflation concerns due to the current fiscal problems in the U.S.
Our debt sits at $40 Trillion, while our GDP sits at roughly $32.5 Trillion. We are currently spending ~21% of all tax receipts just to service interest on the debt. The last time the 10-year yield was this high in 2002, we were only spending 9% of tax receipts to service the debt.
Furthermore, our tax receipts are unable to fund our spending needs. In fiscal year 2026, the government spent $7.4 Trillion while collecting $5.4 Trillion in taxes, leaving a $2.0 Trillion deficit that we have to borrow/create. This equals roughly 6% of our total GDP.
Now consider what happens when the FED raises rates to fight inflation. It only increases the borrowing costs of the U.S. Government. In other words, we now have to increase our deficit due to the increase in yields the FED caused. This means more borrowing, which means more inflation over time.
So, while the FED is attempting to look tough on inflation, the fact that they raised the short end of the curve will only exacerbate the US debt problem. And, keep in mind, bonds are breaking down because the FED was too accommodative. They were making borrowing too easy, which also puts more money into the system, causing inflation over time. This no-way-out scenario is what is called “fiscal dominance.”
In our view, no matter what the FED does, it will likely increase inflation due to the massive deficits we are running. This effectively removes the FED as the primary driver of monetary policy in exchange for the Treasury.
Why a Strong U.S. Dollar Is Driving Global Bond Yields Higher
This chain reaction is spreading into the Dollar Index, which can be seen in the breakout in the chart below.
The U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) has broken above a key resistance zone near 101.8, confirming a stronger uptrend after months of consolidation. If the breakout holds, the chart suggests potential upside toward the 106-110 range, reinforcing the view that a stronger dollar could tighten global liquidity, pressure foreign borrowers with dollar-denominated debt, and contribute to rising global bond yields.
As bond yields break out in the US, the FED has been forced to tighten monetary policy in reaction, raising rates on September 16th for the first time in three years. When rates go higher, this naturally makes the US dollar scarcer, which creates its own liquidity issues, and it also attracts money into the US considering bonds are now paying higher yields.
Considering there is an estimated $84 trillion of dollar obligations outside of the US, the higher the dollar moves in comparison to foreign currencies, the more foreign borrowers must spend of their local currency to service their dollar debt. Foreign investors naturally sell assets like equities and bonds to meet their obligations, which is why global liquidity is so linked to the behaviors of the U.S. Dollar.
Another consequence of a rising dollar is that money must leave a foreign economy to access a more expensive dollar, which pushes foreign government yields higher – i.e., foreign governments now must borrow more to fund spending, just like the U.S.
This behavior is clearly seen in global bond yields, which are rising along with the U.S. 10-year yield. In fact, since bond yields bottomed in 2020, the U.S. has not been alone: 10-year yields in the U.K. and France have hit multi-decade highs, and Germany’s has reached its highest level since 2008.

This matters because foreign corporations and governments owe an exorbitant amount of debt in a currency they can’t print. The higher the dollar goes, the harder it becomes to service this debt, increasing global risk. As foreign currencies are sold to chase a higher dollar, money inherently flows into the US markets, which pushes yields on foreign debt higher. Not only does a rising dollar exert pressure on foreign private sectors, but a growing yield on foreign government bonds exerts pressure on their public sector.
As bad as the U.S.’s fiscal situation is, and as bad as the breakout in bond yields could become, it’s worse in other countries. Most importantly, there is a persistent demand for U.S. dollars in the world while there is a very limited demand for almost every other country’s currency. We can print the money we owe, while other countries cannot. This puts the U.S. in a unique situation.
Seeing the United States within the context of this global system makes our debt burden, fiscal dominance and bond market breakdown much more palatable and preferable on a relative basis. articles.full_text:
- Rate decisions can influence liquidity and appetite for risk-sensitive cryptocurrencies.
- Trading activity, blockchain adoption, liquidity, and ecosystem developments may affect each token differently.
- Bitcoin’s direction, trading volume, and macroeconomic signals could help clarify the broader trend.
The Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision could shape cryptocurrency market sentiment, placing Hyperliquid (HYPE), Sui (SUI), Pi (PI), Avalanche (AVAX), Celo (CELO), and Raydium (RAY) on traders’ watchlists. Whether policymakers hold rates steady, cut them, or consider another hike may influence liquidity, risk appetite, and short-term price movements across digital assets.
Why the Fed’s Next Move Matters for Altcoins
Interest rates continue to be a significant issue in the financial markets because the rate of interest affects investment. High rates might lead investors to seek out safer options, and smaller cryptocurrencies might experience falling demand and increased selling pressure. The rate cut does not always lead to rally, however, traders also consider the inflation, growth and the Fed’s guidance.
A rate-hike decision would have mixed reactions if the majority of investors already have that expectation. An unexpected cut could have a positive effect on sentiment, but sentiment may be held back by worries about economic weakness. A rate hike could push caution to all markets that are sensitive to rates, and may lead to higher volatility among smaller cap altcoins.
In this context, the six cryptocurrencies are the various portions of the market. The price action of their stocks may provide some insights into what traders will do when the central bank sends out contrary signals on monetary policy. However, the market situation, project-related developments, volume of trade and liquidity would still be critical in their performance. The trading activities of Hyperliquid and Sui Reflect are extremely high.Hyperliquid and Sui Reflect Trading Activity is very high.
Hyperliquid and Sui Reflect Trading Activity
Hyperliquid (HYPE) is linked to decentralized derivatives trading, so everything that happens in the perpetual futures market is applicable to this. Traders might shift trades around the Fed announcement, which could impact changes in leverage, trading volume and open interest.
SUI (SUI) is an operating layer-1 blockchain for Decentralized Application (DecApp) operations, however. The performance of its market might mirror market needs for blockchain assets, in addition to network activity and the development of its ecosystem. A sustained recovery would need to be driven by increased buying interest not monetary policy expectations.
Pi, Avalanche, and Celo Face Different Market Conditions
In the banking sector, they are experiencing a wide range of market conditions.The banking sector has different market conditions for Pi, Avalanche, and Celo.
Traders might watch for news regarding liquidity, access to the exchange and broader activity in its ecosystem that might make it a focal point for Pi. The Fed’s reaction to its decision would also depend on market liquidity and demand as well.
Avalanche (AVAX) is another indicator of sentiment and positivity for smart-contract platforms. It could be affected by network adoption, decentralized finance activity and competition between blockchain ecosystems as well as macroeconomic factors.
Celo (CELO), on the other hand, is a blockchain platform specializing in mobile-friendly services and payments, presenting an alternative perspective on the cryptocurrency development landscape. The price fluctuations may be influenced by the overall ecosystem activity, market liquidity, and investor sentiment towards blockchain payment solutions.
Raydium Adds a Decentralized Finance Perspective
Raydium (RAY) is a decentralized finance (DeFi) project under the Solana blockchain, and trading activity in the DeFi ecosystem and their liquidity conditions may impact market demand. Rising volume in decentralized exchanges will be beneficial to the token’s interest, though it may put further pressure on it in market conditions.
What Traders May Watch Next
The Fed’s move could set the short-term tone for the market, but a confirmation via price action would be crucial. The traders can watch the way Bitcoin responds, the strength of the dollar, the yields of the treasury bills and trading volume of the altcoins before arriving at any conclusion.
In conclusion, as the monetary policy outlook changes, HYPE, SUI, PI, AVAX, CELO and RAY are worth keeping an eye on. They will be performing based on liquidity, market sentiment and developments – and there is no certainty after the announcement.

articles.title: Fed’s Warsh hails economic resilience but sees ‘bumpy’ AI road ahead - Euronews
articles.summary: Fed’s Warsh hails economic resilience but sees ‘bumpy’ AI road ahead  Euronews
articles.full_text:
US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in Bangkok on Friday that the global economy has proved surprisingly resilient and called AI the most consequential change of his lifetime, but gave no hint on interest rates ahead of the Fed’s meeting this month.
The global economy has held up better than Kevin Warsh would have predicted earlier this year, the US central bank chief said on Friday, calling AI the biggest economic shift he had seen.
Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, Warsh offered no clue on the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision, due on 28 October.
Almost everywhere, the economy is showing a resilience "I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," Warsh said in a discussion on stage with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva.
The Fed chair was most upbeat about the US, stating during the event that a broadening investment surge that "isn’t just AI" had given the economy "plenty of tailwinds", momentum "certainly not found everywhere in the world".
Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. This, along with an AI investment boom, has fuelled inflation in many economies, forcing central banks to raise rates.
The Fed, which has seen inflation run above its 2% target for over five years, raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75-4% in September, its first hike since July 2023.
"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability," argued Warsh, who took over as chair in May.
He said he had heard the same "resolve" from central bankers in Bangkok, calling the wave of rate hikes, including two by the European Central Bank, a "synchronous tightening" that leaves "no free riders".
The IMF on Tuesday nudged up its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but said risks were tilted to the downside. Rich countries also face soaring borrowing costs, with the 10-year US bond yield above 5% and the French bond yield trading around 4.8% at the time of writing.
A 'bumpy' road for AI
Much of Friday's discussion focused on AI, which Warsh said was "probably the most consequential change" for the US and global economies in his lifetime.
Before taking office, he had argued that an AI-driven productivity boom could curb inflation and make room for lower interest rates. On Friday, he acknowledged that for now, the investment frenzy was pushing prices up by fuelling demand.
Minutes of the Fed's September meeting noted that data centre construction had driven up the cost of chips, computer equipment and electrical components.
However, over time, Warsh expects AI to boost the economy’s capacity to produce, bringing a "huge benefit" at home and abroad.
He also expects it to change central banking as "we torture data with old-fashioned models," he said. "Not so long from now, it won’t be torture."
Despite the optimism, the Fed chair also warned that the road ahead was "likely to be a very bumpy one", both in understanding the technology and because "we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be".
Eyes on the next Federal Reserve meeting
Warsh, who has promised fewer hints about where policy is heading, kept to that pledge.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," he said, though he noted the world had "broadly conformed" to the Fed’s expectations since September.
US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% as petrol prices surged, though core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%.
Wholesale prices rose 6.3% year on year, the most since 2022, while the economy added just 29,000 jobs last month.
Bets on an October hike have swung this week, jumping from about 22% to around 50% after Wednesday’s inflation figures before falling back to about 30%, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks market pricing.
Markets currently put the chance of a December hike at around 90%, while the September minutes showed that most Fed officials expect another hike this year.
New York Fed President John Williams, vice chair of the Fed’s committee, told Bloomberg on Tuesday that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike", but saw no need for more in 2027.
On the other hand, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said at the Bangkok meetings on Wednesday that she felt no urgency to act.
The decision comes days before the 3 November US midterm elections.
September’s hike defied US President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates, though he still backs Warsh, his pick for the job.

articles.title: Gold Price Forecast, Prediction: Gold Buyers Look Past Next Fed Decision - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: Gold Price Forecast, Prediction: Gold Buyers Look Past Next Fed Decision  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
Gold Prices for 2026-2027: Julius Baer Sees Support Beyond the Inflation Shock
Gold has recovered after the US inflation shock, while Julius Baer sees central-bank demand and concerns about US debt supporting its longer-term outlook.
Gold prices regained ground after Wednesday's inflation-driven decline, but the recovery faces another test from US interest rates as producer prices deliver a further upside shock.
The gold price in US Dollars traded near $4,151 an ounce on Thursday afternoon, up 0.95% from the previous close.
Julius Baer's longer-term view rests on buyers whose decisions extend beyond the next Federal Reserve meeting: central banks adding to their reserves and investors concerned about the burden of US government debt.
"In the longer term, gold should again benefit from continued strong central-bank buying and renewed concerns over US debt and its rising interest burden," says Carsten Menke, an analyst at Julius Baer.
That support has not insulated bullion from abrupt changes in expectations for US monetary policy.
Wednesday's consumer-price figures prompted an initial jump in Treasury yields and the Dollar, making interest-bearing assets more attractive relative to gold, which pays no income.
David Meger, director of metals trading at High Ridge Futures, described the immediate consequence: "As a result, we've seen the dollar rise and pressure added to the gold market."
Inflation complicates the recovery
The following day's data offered little reassurance that price pressures were fading.
The US producer-price index rose 1.3% in September, the largest monthly increase since March 2022, keeping the possibility of further Fed tightening in focus.
However, the market reaction has been less straightforward than a sustained rise in yields.
Treasuries recovered after their initial post-CPI sell-off as concerns about technology companies and their funding needs encouraged demand for government bonds.
Gold's rebound therefore comes amid competing pressures: persistent inflation supports higher interest rates, while a retreat from riskier investments can restore demand for bullion and lower the yields against which it competes.
The separation between short-term selling and longer-term buying also featured in Exchange Rates UK's coverage of resilient gold ETF demand despite futures liquidation.
Central-bank purchases give the bullish case substance
There is recent evidence behind Menke's emphasis on official-sector demand.
The World Gold Council recorded 39 tonnes of reported net central-bank purchases in August, led by China, Uzbekistan and Poland.
The council describes much of that activity as part of multi-year accumulation programmes, suggesting reserve objectives remain important even when market prices fluctuate.
Such buying provides a persistent source of demand, but does not establish a minimum price or prevent investors responding to changing real yields.
Goldman Sachs separately projects $4,605 an ounce for Q4 2026 and $4,765 for Q1 2027, leaving room for a recovery beyond Thursday's level.
These are quarterly projections, distinct from Menke's directional assessment and its broader time horizon.
The debt concern he identifies may also develop more slowly than the interest-rate response to an inflation release.
Higher borrowing costs initially increase the appeal of bonds, but they also make financing a large public debt more expensive, potentially strengthening demand for assets held outside government liabilities.
For gold's recovery to last, that longer-term demand will need to withstand further episodes in which inflation sends investors back towards higher-yielding Dollar assets.
Near-term gold price FAQ
Why does Julius Baer expect support for gold?
Carsten Menke points to continued central-bank buying and concerns about US debt and its rising interest costs.
What is Goldman's near-term gold forecast?
Its latest projections are $4,605 an ounce for Q4 2026 and $4,765 for Q1 2027.
Why can inflation hurt gold?
If inflation prompts higher interest rates and real yields, interest-bearing assets can become more attractive relative to bullion.

articles.title: BoE's Bailey says energy price pass-through remains limited, rate risks persist - The Economic Times
articles.summary: BoE's Bailey says energy price pass-through remains limited, rate risks persist  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
According to the report, Bailey said the evidence of wider price pressures remained subdued, with businesses focusing heavily on cutting costs and struggling to pass higher energy expenses on to customers.
Most economists now expect the Bank of England (BoE) to begin raising interest rates next month, according to a Reuters poll, after the central bank kept monetary policy unchanged following the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February.
Also Read |Global Market: South Korean shares rebound, but head for biggest weekly loss in 18 years
The BoE held its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% last month, with six members of its Monetary Policy Committee voting to keep rates unchanged and three favouring a different decision. Bailey was among the majority but had indicated that monetary tightening could become necessary if the risk of second-round inflation effects increased.
Speaking at a meeting of the Institute of International Finance in Bangkok, Bailey said policymakers needed more time to determine whether the initial energy price shock would translate into broader and more persistent inflation.
Also Read | Global Market: Japan's Nikkei rebounds after six-session losing streak; weekly loss nears 5%
The governor has previously argued that the sharp increase in British mortgage rates and other borrowing costs since the start of the US-Iran war had given the central bank some time to assess whether an interest rate increase was necessary.
However, other BoE policymakers have warned that waiting for conclusive evidence of second-round effects could leave the central bank behind the curve. Annual pay settlements expected in early 2027 could provide a clearer indication of whether higher energy costs are feeding into wages and sustaining inflation.
Bailey also said the British economy was proving more resilient than policymakers had anticipated. Data released on Thursday showed that annual economic growth in August was the strongest since October 2022, providing a more encouraging picture of economic activity despite persistent price pressures, as per the report.
Nevertheless, inflation remains a significant concern for the central bank. Bailey described the August inflation rate of 3.1% as deeply frustrating, as it remained well above the BoE's 2% target. He attributed the overshoot primarily to conflicts in the Middle East, which have pushed energy prices higher.
The geopolitical turmoil has also contributed to volatility in British government bond markets. Bailey said developments in the Middle East were the principal driver of sharp movements in government bond yields, some of which reached their highest levels since 1998 last week, Reuters reported.
The BoE faces a difficult balancing act as it weighs the risk of persistent inflation against the potential impact of higher borrowing costs on households and businesses. A rate hike could help contain inflation expectations, but it could also put pressure on mortgage borrowers and companies already facing higher costs.
Bailey's remarks suggest that policymakers remain cautious about drawing firm conclusions from the initial impact of higher energy prices. The extent to which businesses pass on costs, workers seek higher wages and inflation expectations rise will be crucial in determining the timing and scale of any further monetary tightening.
The Institute of International Finance meetings are being held in Bangkok alongside the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where policymakers and financial leaders are assessing the economic implications of geopolitical tensions, higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions.

articles.title: Bank of America Warns AI Bubble Burst Could Trigger Simultaneous U.S. Stocks & Treasury Yields Decline – OpenAI Revenue Incident Serves as Early Preview - 36Kr
articles.summary: Bank of America Warns AI Bubble Burst Could Trigger Simultaneous U.S. Stocks & Treasury Yields Decline – OpenAI Revenue Incident Serves as Early Preview  36Kr
articles.full_text:
Bank of America: The burst of the AI bubble may trigger a simultaneous decline in U.S. stocks and U.S. Treasury yields, and the OpenAI revenue incident has already served as an advance preview.
The derivatives team at Bank of America warns that when the AI bubble finally bursts, the market will move in a drastically different pattern from what we have seen in the past months — it will not be a "stocks down and bonds down" scenario (falling stock prices and rising U.S. Treasury yields), but a synchronous decline in stock prices and yields.
On October 8, the UK's Financial Times revealed that OpenAI's annualized revenue is far lower than the figures circulated in the market. On the same day, the Nasdaq Index plunged by more than 1%, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell by 3.4%, and U.S. Treasury yields also moved lower immediately — the bond market showed a rare risk-averse property.
In the latest issue of the Global Equity Volatility Insights report, the Bank of America derivatives team defined this single-day flash crash as "the best rehearsal for AI position unwinding", and pointed out that a more critical signal lies in: U.S. Treasury yields moved down synchronously with the stock market at that time, instead of the "stocks down and bonds up" pattern that the market has been accustomed to for months.
This pattern was then replicated on October 14. On that day, U.S. CPI inflation data exceeded expectations, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield once surged, and the probability of interest rate hike expectations briefly broke through 50%. However, as the share price of cloud computing infrastructure enterprise CoreWeave plummeted by more than 15% and the credit default swap spread widened by 135 basis points, the upward trend of bond yields reversed rapidly, and the yield finally closed nearly flat.
On the 15th, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield continued to fall sharply by 10 basis points to 5.09%, touching a three-week low. At the same time, the MSCI Asia Pacific Stock Index plunged by more than 3%, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index once plummeted by 9% in a single day, and the declines of Samsung and SK Hynix once reached double digits. S&P 500 futures fell 0.4%, and Nasdaq 100 futures fell by more than 1%.
Bank of America believes that this is exactly the "transmission chain" of the AI bubble burst: The pressure from the private AI ecosystem hits the Nasdaq first and most violently, and pulls the bond market into risk-aversion mode at the same time.
AI-specific risk shocks, Nasdaq bears the brunt
Benjamin Bowler, Nitin Saksena, Arjun Goyal and other members of Bank of America's equity-linked team pointed out that the Nasdaq's significant underperformance relative to the broader market on October 8 is highly consistent with the performance of every AI-specific risk event in the past few years — from the DeepSeek shock in January 2025 to the semiconductor sector correction this summer, the pattern is identical.
The report believes that this reflects the Nasdaq's high exposure to the "private AI ecosystem". Once cracks appear in private AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, the Nasdaq 100 Index will be the first underlying target to bear pressure in the public market. The bank defines it as the preferred index for AI trading, whether long or short.
This transmission path is now facing a new stress test. Anthropic opened its financial data to Wall Street on October 14, while the $20 billion "gap between total revenue and net income" of OpenAI remains unresolved, and the transmission channel from the private sector to the public market is expected to continue to be tested.
Abnormal bond market movement: Both AI shocks trigger synchronous decline in yields
What deserves more attention is the behavioral pattern of the bond market. In the past few months, U.S. stocks and U.S. Treasury yields have continued to show an inverse relationship, and the function of bonds as a hedging tool has almost failed. However, the two AI risk events on October 8 and October 14 both broke this pattern, with yields moving lower in step with the stock market.
Bank of America attributes this to the macro logic of AI slowdown: In addition to the inflow of traditional risk-averse capital, the cooling of the AI investment cycle means reduced capital expenditure, lower power and resource consumption, coupled with the dual suppression of economic growth and inflation, which will form additional positive factors for bonds. In other words, if the AI bubble really bursts, bonds will resume their hedging function.
The historical reference cited in the report is the burst of the dot-com bubble in 2000: At that time, the Nasdaq 100 Index crashed, and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield fell from about 6.5% to the mid-4% range. Bank of America acknowledges that the two data points do not yet constitute a complete pattern, but believes that the mutual verification of historical precedents and macro logic is sufficient to provide structural references for investors.
CoreWeave triggers credit-side crisis, AI stocks underperform broader market by 840 basis points this week
The market sell-off on October 14 revealed another potential burst path for the AI bubble: the credit side.
CoreWeave (CRWV) is the center of this storm. After the G-spread of its 2032-maturity bonds broke through 1000 basis points and the yield rose to 15%, its share price then plummeted by more than 15%, marking the third largest single-day decline since its listing. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria defined CoreWeave as the "subprime mortgage tranche" in the AI field, and warned that if the company cannot repay its debts, its share price will go to zero — its financing cost is about 9%, while the return on investment is only about 1%. CoreWeave's credit default swap spread widened by 135 basis points on the same day, and the current market-implied default probability within five years has reached 63%.
Panic spread rapidly. DigitalOcean (DOCN) fell 14%, Hut 8 (HUT) fell 10%, Nebius (NBIS) and IREN each fell by about 9%; Oracle (ORCL) fell 9%, and the deviation from its credit default swap level has not been closed. Market research firm Gartner then issued a warning, predicting that 80% of emerging cloud computing enterprises will cease independent operations before 2030.
This week, the cumulative underperformance of the AI sector relative to non-AI constituents of the S&P 500 has reached 840 basis points. BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky also believes that the current pain trade points to "falling interest rates and falling Nasdaq". If the "Magnificent Seven" also begins to fall synchronously with interest rates like semiconductor stocks, it will further confirm his "Red October" judgment.
BofA recommends hedging portfolio: Let the bond market subsidize option costs
Faced with this potential risk, Bank of America's derivatives team has proposed a hedging structure of "using bond proceeds to offset equity hedging costs".
The difficulty of traditional AI bubble hedging lies in timing: if you buy put options too early, the continuous rise of the market will keep making the strike price lag behind the market. Bank of America's solution is the "max lookback put" — its strike price keeps moving up as the market rises, but this feature itself comes with a relatively high cost. The bank's innovation lies in setting the option to take effect only when the 10-year SOFR is 25 basis points below the current forward rate, so as to convert the expectation of falling interest rates into option premium subsidies.
The specific trading plan is: buy a daily observation max lookback put option on the Nasdaq 100 Index, which expires in September 2027 with a strike price of 90% of the current price, attached with an interest rate trigger clause. The indicative option premium is 3.62%, which is 46% lower than the pure lookback put option, and 23 basis points lower than the ordinary put option.
Backtest data shows that after simulating and pricing this structure over the past 30 years, its trigger probability is 13% (11% for ordinary 90% put options), the average in-the-money payout multiple is 7.2 times (6.1 times for ordinary put options, 3.9 times for pure lookback options), and the maximum excess return appeared during the dot-com bubble burst.
The main risk of this structure lies in the 2022-style "stocks down and bonds up" scenario, that is, the pattern of stocks and bonds falling in the same direction caused by inflation shocks or unexpected Federal Reserve tightening — which is exactly the operating mode of the bond market for most of 2026, not a real tail risk.
In addition, Bank of America simultaneously recommends a VIX call spread trade: buy the VIX November expiry 19-24 point spread, with an indicative cost of $0.63 and a maximum payout multiple of about 7.9 times, which is suitable for the judgment of a moderate rise in volatility around the mid-term elections.
How severe is the bubble: Indicators show it is concentrated in local areas rather than comprehensive
The latest reading of Bank of America's Bubble Risk Indicator (BRI) provides a more detailed perspective. At present, only 13 stocks in the S&P 500 have a BRI exceeding 0.8, accounting for about 2.4% of the total index weight; in contrast, during the peak of the dot-com bubble, 50 to 100 stocks hit this threshold, accounting for 20% to 40% of the index weight.
The current bubble characteristics show obvious concentration: at the single-stock level, Moderna (MRNA), CrowdStrike (CRWD), Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), Zebra Technologies, Revvity and Palo Alto Networks (PANW) rank top in readings; at the sector level, the BRI of Bank of America's U.S. cybersecurity theme basket and Brazil election theme basket both reach a high level of 0.92.

New York (AFP) – The supervisor of New York City’s pension funds, one of the largest in the United States, asked Anthropic to postpone its stock market debut until risks posed by its artificial intelligence technology are better controlled.
Issued on: Modified:
New York City Comptroller Mark Levine cited growing concerns about safety and security in a letter addressed to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has himself called for an industry-wide slowdown of developing advanced frontier models.
"Prudence should not only be shown with respect to the pace of the frontier, it should be also shown with respect to the timing of an IPO," Levine wrote in the letter.
"I therefore urge Anthropic to pause the IPO process so that the company may fully address these key issues, ones which investors must also assess," he continued.
Levine oversees the city's financial entities, which include several pension funds for city workers, teachers, police and firefighters.
These funds provide retirement benefits to more than 750,000 people, and their assets under management totaled $330 billion at the end of August.
A small fraction of those assets, around $7 million, are currently exposed to Anthropic, the Comptroller's office told AFP.
However, that exposure will grow if Anthropic goes public because its shares would become included in several stock indices, including the Russell 3000, which New York City tracks for its own investments.
So the city's funds would "automatically become long-term investors when the company is integrated into the index fund," a spokesperson for the Comptroller's office said.
On Wednesday, prosecutors from eight US states also sued ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, a rival AI lab that could go public next year, for allegedly concealing certain risks and implementing inadequate safeguards.

articles.summary: Is Anthropic worth $2 trillion? How about $1.5 trillion?  Yahoo Finance'Not good enough. It's over': The AI doomers are going off on Anthropic's revenue figures  Yahoo Finance UKInvestors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations over revenue growth slowdown, sources say  ReutersSandisk, AMD Stocks Fall as Anthropic Adds to AI Concerns  Barron'sAnthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) work will contribute to massive changes in the US economy and workforce, but how much is the leading AI lab actually worth as a public company?
Reuters, citing several people familiar with the matter, reported that current and prospective investors in Anthropic's initial public offering who attended an investor day at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters this week discussed a valuation of the Claude maker at about $1.5 trillion, down from earlier expectations of $2 trillion.
"What's $500 billion between friends in the AI trade?" Yahoo Finance's Jake Conley quipped (video above) before adding, "It does get to the point of you're trying to justify these huge valuations: Do your numbers justify it?"
Anthropic's third quarter revenue reportedly rose 45% from the second quarter to $16.8 billion, and the company stayed profitable on an adjusted basis. Reuters, which got its hands on Anthropic's IPO prospectus, previously reported that revenue more than doubled in the second quarter, to $11.6 billion from $4.7 billion.
"While those numbers assuaged some concerns about the massive costs of developing AI systems," Reuters reported, "some investors were disappointed by the slowing sequential growth rate in the latest quarter."
Yahoo Finance co-host Julie Hyman called the lower price "a reading-the-room moment," with AI stocks selling off this week. "All of this would seem to indicate that there's at least enough concern out there that you're not going to go out and try and overprice."
Hyman also noted that one quarter may not settle it: "We don't know if it's going to reaccelerate in the fourth quarter."
Conley wants a different yardstick than annual recurring revenue (ARR), the run-rate figure AI companies like to cite.
"ARR, that's not a real number," he said. "Give me some GAAP numbers."

articles.summary: BoE to hike interest rates by 25 bps to 4% in November – Reuters poll  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
According to the latest Reuters poll, 54 of 63 economists have voted in favor of a 25 basis point (bps) interest rate hike by the Bank of England (BoE) in policy meeting on November 5.
The Bank of England (BoE) decides monetary policy for the United Kingdom. Its primary goal is to achieve ‘price stability’, or a steady inflation rate of 2%. Its tool for achieving this is via the adjustment of base lending rates. The BoE sets the rate at which it lends to commercial banks and banks lend to each other, determining the level of interest rates in the economy overall. This also impacts the value of the Pound Sterling (GBP).
When inflation is above the Bank of England’s target it responds by raising interest rates, making it more expensive for people and businesses to access credit. This is positive for the Pound Sterling because higher interest rates make the UK a more attractive place for global investors to park their money. When inflation falls below target, it is a sign economic growth is slowing, and the BoE will consider lowering interest rates to cheapen credit in the hope businesses will borrow to invest in growth-generating projects – a negative for the Pound Sterling.
In extreme situations, the Bank of England can enact a policy called Quantitative Easing (QE). QE is the process by which the BoE substantially increases the flow of credit in a stuck financial system. QE is a last resort policy when lowering interest rates will not achieve the necessary result. The process of QE involves the BoE printing money to buy assets – usually government or AAA-rated corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Pound Sterling.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE, enacted when the economy is strengthening and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the Bank of England (BoE) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to encourage them to lend; in QT, the BoE stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive for the Pound Sterling.

articles.full_text:
MUMBAI : Global investors and sovereign wealth funds, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Qatar Investment Authority, GIC Pte. Ltd, Norges Bank Investment Management and Mubadala Investment Co., are queueing up for allocations in the anchor book of Jio Platforms Ltd’s public offering, alongside asset managers BlackRock Inc. and FMR LLC, according to four people familiar with the matter.
About 15 domestic asset managers, including HDFC Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Nippon Life India Asset Management and Motilal Oswal Asset Management, have also submitted indications of interest for a share of Jio's ₹8,000-crore anchor book, the people said on the condition of anonymity.
The asset management arms of Goldman Sachs and Franklin Templeton are also vying for a slice of the pie, the people said.
While ADIA, Motilal and Norges declined to comment, representatives of Jio's parent company, Reliance Industries Ltd, as well as other institutional investors and fund managers, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The mega IPO
The telecom giant's parent filed its red herring prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Board of India on Wednesday for an initial public offering (IPO) that will raise around ₹ 30,200 crore, or about $3.2 billion, at the upper end of the 1,069-1,119 per share price band announced.
The anchor allocation window, which precedes the public subscription period, allows institutional entities to secure share allotments before the main issue opens.
Under capital market regulator rules, up to 60% of the portion reserved for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) can be allocated to anchor investors. Half of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds.
Final share allocations for the anchor book are scheduled to be finalized ahead of the opening of the retail and non-institutional bidding windows.
The subscription window opens on 21 October and closes on 23 October. Shares are slated to start trading on the exchanges on 28 October.
Jio operates digital services and telecommunications infrastructure across India. Existing equity holders in Jio Platforms include Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc.’s Google, KKR & Co., Silver Lake and General Atlantic.
At a press conference in Navi Mumbai on Wednesday, which saw Anant Ambani, Shloka Ambani and other key CXOs of Jio Platforms seated in the front row, Uday Kotak, chairman of left lead merchant banker Kotak Investment Banking, said, “Reliance Industries (...) has always believed in making it attractive for investors to be long-term with the group."
Anant Ambani is an executive director on the board of Reliance Industries and non-executive director on the board of Jio Platforms, while Shloka is the wife of managing director Akash Ambani.
On the company's prospects, Kotak said: "Akash Ambani has discussed in detail (at institutional roadshows) the various trends of Jio Platforms, including scale, growth, and the fact that significant capital expenditure has already been done and it's already put in place.”
Kotak said the price band factored in investor feedback from the roadshows, and it aimed to keep the offering attractive for investors. "We believe (the price band) is appropriate. We priced for investors to have returns in this IPO," he said.
Jio Platforms' IPO comes at a time when revenue per user has stagnated across quarters. The average revenue per user (Arpu) is a closely watched industry metric that tracks paying users. The firm's monthly Arpu rose marginally quarter-on-quarter to ₹215.6 from ₹214 at the end of March. In the previous quarter too, the growth was flat.
Commenting on this sluggish growth trend, Akash Ambani said, "Today, our Arpu is measured strictly against our licenced services, but we believe we can achieve higher realization per user from offerings outside of our licenced businesses—one key example being our voice AI service."
Ambani said the company aims to deliver more value by launching new services across its customer base and extracting value from it. "While we always retain the ability to raise prices, our goal is to deliver more services to keep customers satisfied, rather than relying on price hikes as our primary lever for Arpu growth."
Analysts, however, expect the organic increase in Arpu to be restricted going forward as smartphone prices rise, particularly at the entry level. Higher prices could slow feature-phone-to-smartphone upgrades and weaken the premiumization trend.

articles.title: WTI trades near $94.00 after paring recent losses amid escalating Middle East conflict - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: WTI trades near $94.00 after paring recent losses amid escalating Middle East conflict  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil price pares its daily losses, remaining in negative territory and trading around $94.00 per barrel during European hours on Thursday. Oil prices have found support following an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, alongside renewed attacks on maritime shipping in the region.
Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to continue strikes targeting Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, shortly after an attack that reportedly caused extensive damage to the headquarters of state oil giant Saudi Aramco. Describing these facilities as legitimate targets, the Houthis cited retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, signaling a further escalation of a conflict reignited by the broader US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
The maritime situation in the region has deteriorated rapidly, with a container ship and a dry bulk carrier sinking near the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours after being struck by projectiles in separate incidents. Attacks around the vital waterway have surged over the past ten days, with Iran stating it is stepping up strikes in response to a US port blockade and tougher sanctions introduced last month. Additionally, ongoing Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure continue to keep market participants on edge.
However, crude oil price gains have been capped by potential regulatory shifts in the United States. The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on "shadow fleet" vessels that transport oil and petroleum products from sanctioned nations including Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.
A US official confirmed on Wednesday that the proposed policy shift aims to lower record-high global freight rates. The discussions come on the heels of President Donald Trump temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move that has drawn sharp criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European allies, and several Senate Republicans.
Analysts at Deutsche Bank highlight that the earlier move higher in Brent came “amidst no signs of progress in the US-Iran conflict,” noting that the price action “added to the inflationary concerns that had already mounted after the CPI print.” This combination of unresolved geopolitical tension and fresh US inflation data reinforced a more cautious near-term stance on the Oil complex.
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.

articles.title: Global X India Nifty 50 ETF (ASX:NDIA) Fund Review: How India's Demographic and Infrastructure Expansion Shapes Emerging Market Exposure - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Global X India Nifty 50 ETF (ASX:NDIA) Fund Review: How India's Demographic and Infrastructure Expansion Shapes Emerging Market Exposure  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- NDIA tracks India's leading companies through the [Nifty 50] index.
- It offers exposure to India's demographic expansion and banking credit growth.
- The fund is positioned around India's broader economic growth story.
Introduction and Market Relevance
The Global X India Nifty 50 ETF (ASX:NDIA) Global X India Nifty 50 ETF (ASX:NDIA) 59.57 AUD +0.450 0.761% Last Updated at: 2026-10-16T05:00:00Z gives Australian portfolios direct exposure to India's leading listed companies through the [Nifty 50] index. India is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies, supported by a large, young population, expanding infrastructure and a rapidly developing financial system. NDIA provides a simple, ASX-traded way to participate in that story. The fund sits within the broader universe of ASX ETF Stocks.
For many portfolios, India has been underrepresented relative to its growing economic importance. A dedicated India fund allows holders to decide their level of exposure directly rather than relying on India's weight within broad emerging market indices.
Fund Structure and Objective
NDIA aims to track the performance of the [Nifty 50] index, before fees and costs. The index represents leading Indian companies listed on the National Stock Exchange of India and is widely regarded as a key benchmark for the Indian share market.
As an exchange-traded fund, NDIA trades on the ASX during market hours. This removes the need for Australian holders to open overseas accounts or navigate Indian market regulations directly.
What the Nifty Index Represents
The [Nifty 50] covers India's largest and most liquid companies across major sectors, including banking and financial services, information technology, energy, consumer goods, automobiles and healthcare. These companies are often leaders in their industries and have significant influence on the wider Indian economy.
Because the index is weighted by market capitalisation, the largest companies have the biggest influence on performance. Financial services and technology typically account for significant portions of the index.
Demographic Expansion
India's demographics are a central part of its growth outlook. The country has one of the largest working-age populations in the world, and a high proportion of young people entering the workforce over the coming years. As more people join the workforce and incomes rise, demand for housing, consumer goods, financial products and services is expected to grow.
This demographic profile contrasts with many developed economies, where ageing populations are slowing growth. For companies in the index, a growing customer base can support long-term revenue expansion.
Banking and Credit Growth
Banking and financial services are among the largest parts of the index. As India's economy develops, more households and businesses are gaining access to formal banking, credit cards, home loans and insurance. Digital payment systems have also expanded rapidly, bringing many people into the formal financial system.
This growth in banking credit can support earnings for India's leading banks and financial institutions. Well-capitalised lenders are positioned to benefit as demand for credit rises across consumers and businesses.
Infrastructure Expansion and Economic Growth
India has been expanding its infrastructure, including roads, railways, ports, power generation and digital networks. Large infrastructure programmes can boost productivity, reduce costs for businesses and support economic growth across many sectors.
Companies in construction, energy, materials and industrial services can benefit directly, while improved infrastructure also supports manufacturing and services more broadly. This spending forms an important part of the broader economic growth story that NDIA is positioned around.
Technology and Services Strength
India's information technology services sector is a global leader, supplying software development, consulting and outsourcing to companies around the world. These businesses earn significant revenue from overseas clients, which adds a global dimension to the index.
How NDIA Compares with Broad Emerging Market Funds
Broad emerging market funds spread their holdings across many countries, including China, Taiwan, South Korea, Brazil and others. India is only one part of these portfolios, and its weight depends on the index methodology. As a result, exposure to India through a broad fund may be smaller than some portfolio holders intend.
A dedicated India fund such as NDIA allows a more targeted allocation. It also removes exposure to other emerging markets, which can be useful for those who already hold broad emerging market funds and want to add a specific tilt towards India.
Market Access and Liquidity
Accessing Indian shares directly can be complex for foreign participants, due to registration requirements and local market rules. NDIA simplifies this by packaging exposure into a single ASX-listed fund with daily trading, transparent holdings and Australian tax reporting. Market makers help support liquidity, so units can generally be traded close to the value of the underlying holdings during ASX trading hours.
Currency Considerations
NDIA's holdings are priced in Indian rupees, so returns for Australian unitholders are affected by movements between the rupee and the Australian dollar. Currency changes can add to volatility and may either improve or reduce returns depending on their direction.
Costs and Distributions
NDIA charges a management fee for its index exposure. Distributions depend on dividends from Indian companies, which are often modest because many businesses reinvest earnings to fund growth.
Principal Risk Factors
Key risks include emerging market volatility, political and regulatory change, currency movements and sector concentration, particularly in financial services. Indian shares can also trade on relatively high valuations, which may make them sensitive to shifts in sentiment or capital flows.
Global factors, including oil prices, interest rates and foreign capital flows, can strongly influence Indian markets. These risks mean NDIA may experience larger swings in value than funds focused on developed markets.
Strategic Outlook
Before using NDIA, it is important to review the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) and Target Market Determination (TMD). Many portfolio holders treat India exposure as a satellite allocation, sized to reflect their comfort with emerging market volatility and their long-term goals.
For those seeking broad, low-friction exposure to India's leading companies and its demographic, banking and infrastructure growth themes, NDIA offers a straightforward ASX-traded option.

articles.title: Citi Slashes Lead Intelligent Equipment Target Price by 62%, Downgrades to Neutral - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Citi Slashes Lead Intelligent Equipment Target Price by 62%, Downgrades to Neutral  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Citi released a new research report downgrading Lead Intelligent Equipment (00470.HK) from "Buy" to "Neutral," slashing its target price from HK$63 (approximately $8) to HK$24 (approximately $3.1), a cut of 62%. The bank noted that while Lead Intelligent Equipment's management remains optimistic about order visibility, early signals of slowing battery capital expenditure are already observable in operating data from automation equipment suppliers.
Citi stated in its report that its battery research team forecasts a significant cooling in global battery production capacity growth. Global battery production capacity is still expected to grow 46% year-over-year in 2026, but growth is projected to decelerate to 24% in 2027 and 15% in 2028. This suggests that the battery capacity expansion boom driven by electric vehicle and energy storage demand over the past few years is gradually entering a downcycle.
Based on the assessment of slowing capacity expansion, Citi simultaneously adjusted its earnings estimates for Lead Intelligent Equipment. The bank lowered its profit forecasts for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by 2%, 19%, and 37%, respectively. Citi explained that the downward revisions stem from two main factors: first, revenue expectations have been reduced, reflecting the likelihood that battery manufacturers will scale back procurement of lithium battery equipment as they turn more conservative on capital expenditure; second, asset impairment risks will rise significantly during the industry downcycle, further eroding profitability.
Lead Intelligent Equipment is a major Chinese supplier of lithium battery production equipment, with customers including large battery manufacturers such as CATL and BYD. In recent years, driven by rapid growth in the global electric vehicle market, battery makers expanded capacity on a massive scale, propelling Lead Intelligent Equipment's orders and revenue sharply higher. However, as EV penetration rates in major markets gradually rise, the growth base becomes higher, and concerns about overcapacity at some battery manufacturers emerge, the market has begun to reassess the growth prospects of the lithium battery equipment industry.
Citi's move to cut the target price from HK$63 to HK$24 in one stroke reflects its increasingly conservative stance on Lead Intelligent Equipment's profitability over the next two years. The HK$24 target price translates to approximately NT$99. The downgrade from "Buy" to "Neutral" signals that Citi believes the stock lacks sufficient upside momentum in the near term, but does not recommend that investors actively sell; instead, the bank suggests adopting a wait-and-see approach.
From an industry perspective, the signs of slowing battery capital expenditure observed by Citi are consistent with recent signals from multiple lithium battery equipment peers. Some automation equipment suppliers reported that order intake in the latest quarter was not as strong as the same period last year, indicating that battery manufacturers are beginning to tap the brakes on capacity planning. If this trend persists, revenue growth momentum across the lithium battery equipment supply chain could face further pressure.
For investors, Citi's downgrade sends an important signal: the high-growth phase of the lithium battery equipment industry may be nearing its end, and the industry environment over the next two years will be less favorable than in recent years. Lead Intelligent Equipment's future order visibility, the pace at which its order backlog converts to revenue, and the actual magnitude of asset impairments will be key areas of focus for the market.

articles.title: Fed officials: Raising interest rates may be necessary but not urgent. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Fed officials: Raising interest rates may be necessary but not urgent.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Mary Daly, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, believes the Fed will likely need to continue raising short-term interest rates to curb inflation, but that immediate action is not necessary at the meeting on October 27-28.
Ms. Daly stated that the Fed may need further policy adjustments, but the timing is still under consideration. She added that the Fed is not under pressure to rush a decision given the limited information available, and that it has ample time to assess the situation.
In recent weeks, several other Fed officials have also signaled the possibility that the Fed will not raise interest rates this month. Currently, the Fed's policy interest rate is in the range of 3.75%-4.00%.
Meanwhile, long-term borrowing costs are even higher, with interest rates for 30-year mortgages reaching 7.5%, significantly impacting and reducing demand in some sectors of the economy .
Commenting on the market's reaction, Ms. Daly stated that investors have a clear understanding of the Fed's policy response mechanism. Data released on the same day, October 14th, showed that the US consumer price index (CPI) for the 12 months ending September 2026 rose to 3.7%, slightly higher than economists' forecasts. The Fed's inflation target is 2%.
Following the release of CPI data, traders rushed to bet on the possibility of the Fed raising interest rates by the end of October 2026. However, the market later calmed down after a closer analysis of the data, realizing that the overall increase was mainly due to rising gasoline prices, while core inflation, although persistent, did not surge dramatically.
Ms. Daly assessed that the new data shows that inflation risks remain high and are increasing, but the risks are not yet a reality. Therefore, rushing to react to the risks while there is still time to consider them would be imprudent. She also emphasized that the continued stability of the labor market is creating room for the Fed to focus on the goal of price stability.
In financial markets, the probability of the Fed raising interest rates for the second consecutive time at its upcoming meeting is around 40%. Although this percentage has increased compared to before the release of inflation data, the market no longer considers a rate hike this month to be the most likely scenario.
