Market News
SUMMARY
Demand for gold jewellery is expected to remain an important driver for the sector, with the September-quarter (Q2 FY27) business updates of several listed jewellers reinforcing optimism about demand.
Gold prices fell for the third straight day, shedding ₹1,800 to ₹1.5 lakh per 10 grams in the national capital on Wednesday.
The festive season is already underway, with Navratri in progress, while Diwali, Dhanteras and the wedding season lie ahead. Gold and jewellery stocks are likely to remain in focus as the yellow metal holds cultural and emotional significance for Indian households, particularly during festivals and weddings.
Business updates for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from several listed jewellers have reinforced optimism about demand, with companies also expressing confidence in the upcoming festive and wedding season. However, this year’s festive period comes with a few additional factors for investors to consider.
Gold prices have corrected from their August highs and remain volatile. Rising inflation could weigh on household budgets, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s appeal to defer gold purchases for a year could influence consumer buying decisions.
In addition, the shift in the festive calendar has moved some demand from Q2 into Q3 compared with last year, making the October-December quarter particularly important for jewellery companies.
Gold prices in the national capital fell for the third consecutive session on Wednesday, declining by ₹1,800 to ₹1,50,800 per 10 grams for 99.9% pure gold, inclusive of taxes, according to the All India Sarafa Association. Prices stood at ₹1,52,600 per 10 grams in the previous session.
Silver prices also extended their decline, falling ₹5,000 to ₹2.21 lakh per kilogram from the previous close of ₹2.26 lakh per kilogram.
The latest declines add to the correction in domestic bullion prices from their August highs. Gold has seen bouts of volatility in recent sessions, with a stronger rupee adding to the pressure on domestic prices.
Traders said a stronger rupee makes dollar-priced bullion cheaper to import, weighing on domestic prices. For jewellery retailers, the key question is whether the correction improves affordability enough to encourage consumers to make festive and wedding-related purchases.
However, falling gold prices do not necessarily translate into an immediate increase in jewellery demand. Consumer buying decisions will also depend on household budgets, expectations about further price movements and the timing of purchases.
Rising inflation could add to the pressure on household budgets during the festive season. India's retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September 2026 from 4.83% in August, while food inflation climbed to 7.74%, according to government data.
Higher living costs could make consumers more cautious about discretionary spending, including jewellery purchases. However, wedding-related buying and traditional demand during festivals could provide some support to the sector.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's appeal to Indians to avoid buying gold for a year, including for weddings, is another factor to watch this festive season.
In May 2026, stressing the need to save foreign exchange due to the crisis, PM Modi called for postponing the purchase of gold and foreign travel for one year. "We have to save foreign exchange by any means," he said, adding that due to the West Asia conflict, prices of petrol and fertilisers had increased significantly.
When there is pressure on the supply chain, difficulties increase despite various government measures to address the situation, he said. "That's why, during a global crisis, keeping the country above all else, we have to take resolutions," he added.
For listed jewellers, the key monitorable will be whether traditional festive and wedding-related purchases remain resilient despite the appeal.
Several listed jewellery companies reported healthy year-on-year growth in their Q2 FY27 business updates, despite some moderation in demand towards the end of the quarter as the festive calendar shifted into Q3.
Titan's jewellery business grew 21% year-on-year, Kalyan Jewellers' India revenue rose 27%, Senco Gold's revenue increased 31%, and PC Jeweller reported 28% growth in consolidated revenue.
Jewellery companies remain optimistic about the October-December quarter, with Diwali, Dhanteras and the wedding season expected to support demand. Kalyan Jewellers and Senco Gold have expressed confidence in the upcoming season, while the shift in the festive calendar could support a stronger contribution from Q3 compared with last year.
However, whether this optimism translates into higher sales volumes remains to be seen, particularly amid volatile gold prices and affordability concerns.
Shares of Titan Company have fallen 2% over the past six months, while PC Jeweller has jumped over 50%. Kalyan Jewellers India has rallied over 27%, and Thangamayil Jewellery shares have surged nearly 13%. Senco Gold has remained flat, while Sky Gold and Diamonds have skyrocketed 139%. P N Gadgil Jewellers have slipped over 9% during the period.

articles.title: Have Reliance's old physical shares?: Convert into demat format before JIO IPO; get step-by-step guide here - Bhaskar English
articles.summary: Have Reliance's old physical shares?: Convert into demat format before JIO IPO; get step-by-step guide here  Bhaskar English
articles.full_text:
Do you hold Reliance's physical shares?:Convert them into demat format before the JIO IPO — here's a step-by-step guide
Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) has opened a special window for investors to transfer and convert physical share certificates into dematerialised form by 4 February, 2027. The facility applies to shares purchased before April 1, 2019, under recent SEBI guidelines.
RIL Shareholder Quota In Jio IPO:
According to Jio Platform's RHP, RIL shareholders will get a reservation of shares of Jio Platforms (the company that is bringing Jio IPO).
Reliance Opens Facility for Conversion of Physical Shares To Digital Ahead Of Jio IPO
RIL has given a special facility to investors holding old paper share certificates. This facility allows eligible shareholders to transfer ownership and convert physical shares into electronic form.
What Is Dematerialisation?
In stock markets, converting paper share certificates into digital format is called dematerialisation or demat. Shareholders who hold demat shares can hold, track, and trade their stock through a digital demat account linked to their bank account.
Eligibility Criteria for RIL Physical Shareholder Requests
Not all physical share requests qualify for this special scheme. The table below explains which requests are accepted under the official notice issued by Reliance Industries:
Mandatory Documents Required for Application
To complete the transfer and demat conversion, investors must submit five specific documents to RIL's transfer agent:
Original Security Certificate(s): The physical paper share certificate.
Transfer Deed: Form executed prior to April 01, 2019.
Proof of Purchase: Any available transaction receipt or purchase record.
KYC Documents: Updated identity and address proofs
Client Master List (CML): Demat account summary copy not older than 2 months, duly attested by the broker.
Submission Process and Contact Details
Investors who hold original physical share certificates and valid transfer deeds must send their documents to the official Registrar and Transfer Agent (RTA) of Reliance Industries Limited.
Requests must include the original share certificate, transfer deed, updated Know Your Customer (KYC) identity proofs, and the latest Client Master List (CML) of the investor's demat account.
RTA Contact Details:
Registrar Name: KFin Technologies Limited (Unit: Reliance Industries Limited)
Office Address: Selenium Tower-B, Plot Nos. 31 & 32, Gachibowli, Financial District, Nanakramguda, Hyderabad – 500 032
Investor Support Email: rilinvestor@kfintech.com
Eligible investors must submit their complete applications before the February 4, 2027 deadline to ensure their physical paper shares are converted into demat format.
Can You Sell RIL's Physical Shares?
According to the rules and regulations of the capital market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), you cannot sell those shares and get the money as share certificates would be available in the physical form. The market watchdog no longer accepts physical shares.
- You will first have to convert those physical holdings into dematerialised (demat) form as mentioned above
- Then, those shares will get credited to your demat account
- Then you can sell the electronic version of those scrips lying in your demat account to book profit for encashment
RIL Share Conversion Special Window Exception:
If the physical securities were not claimed by any family member for a consecutive period of seven years then the shares along with the dividends declared would be transferred to the government of India's IEPF, which has been set up by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
In such cases, the investor needs to contact the IEPF to get hold of the shares bought by his ancestors.
JIO IPO Details
Jio IPO will open for subscription from October 21 to October 23, making it the largest public issue in Indian stock market history. Through this IPO, the company plans to raise approximately ₹30,213 crore by issuing 27 crore fresh equity shares.
India's Biggest IPO
At over ₹30,200 crore, Jio Platforms will dethrone Hyundai Motor India (which raised ₹27,858 crore in 2024) to become the biggest IPO ever launched in India.

articles.title: Leveraged Products Launched Despite Regulatory Warnings - 조선일보
articles.summary: Leveraged Products Launched Despite Regulatory Warnings  조선일보
articles.full_text:
A report commissioned by the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) seven months before the launch of single-stock leveraged products—allowing bets twice the daily volatility of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix—warned of the need for “caution in domestic introduction.” Concerns included investor losses, amplified stock market volatility, and global regulatory tightening trends.
Despite these warnings, the single-stock leveraged products were rapidly introduced four months after discussions began in January. When the KOSPI plummeted in June–July, the products were cited domestically and internationally as a key driver of market volatility. Critics argue financial authorities rushed the launch without adequately assessing risks, despite prior warnings.
◇Ignoring Warnings and Launching, Followed by a Sharp Decline
According to materials received by Rep. Park Dae-chul of the People Power Party from the FSS on the 16th, the Korea Capital Market Institute submitted a 151-page report titled “Analysis of Successful Cases in the Overseas Asset Management Industry and Implications” to the FSS in October last year. The report noted the U.S. might strengthen regulations on single-stock leveraged ETFs and warned, “Korea should exercise caution in explicitly allowing such products, as it could lead to inconsistencies with global regulatory trends.”
Despite this, the introduction of single-stock leveraged products accelerated from early this year. Kim Yong-beom, then-Cheong Wa Dae policy chief, stated in a January media interview, “I asked the Financial Services Commission, ‘Why can’t we do what’s possible on Nasdaq?’” The FSS announced a revised enforcement decree of the Capital Markets Act in late January and amended regulations on April 28 to permit domestic listings. Just one month later, on May 27, 16 products based on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were listed.
At the time, the market was buoyed by a semiconductor boom. President Lee Jae Myung remarked at a June 8 press conference marking his first year in office, “Stock prices have risen faster than expected,” but added, “I still believe they are slightly undervalued.” The KOSPI briefly surpassed 9,300 points on June 19 but began a steep decline afterward. Concerns grew that single-stock leveraged products exacerbated volatility in Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Lee Chan-jin, Governor of the FSS, later stated, “I regret not doing everything to block it.” Amid criticism, the FSS raised the minimum deposit for these products from 10 million Korean won to 30 million Korean won. Daily trading volume, which averaged 11.86 trillion Korean won in July, fell to 560 billion Korean won this month.
◇U.S. Warnings…Discussions on Sales Restrictions
The FSS-commissioned report highlighted that while single-stock leveraged ETFs exist in the U.S., regulators did not actively permit them and emphasized investor risks. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) simplified ETF approvals in 2019 but excluded leveraged products. However, a 2020 derivatives regulation revision allowed leveraged ETFs to use the simplified process, unintentionally enabling single-stock leveraged ETF listings without SEC approval. The report called this an “unintended consequence.”
U.S. regulators strongly warned of risks. In 2021, then-SEC Chair Gary Gensler stated, “Just because a product is listed does not mean it is suitable for all investors,” cautioning that rapid market shifts could threaten the financial system. The SEC’s Office of Investor Education later warned that single-stock leveraged ETFs are “highly unsuitable for retail investors with long-term strategies.”
The report also noted the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) sought public input in 2022 on stricter investor risk assessments for complex products like leveraged ETFs. The report interpreted this as “concrete moves to restrict retail investor access.”
Rep. Park Dae-chul criticized, “Did financial authorities prioritize product launches over investor protection?” He demanded clarity on how risks were evaluated at the time.

articles.title: USD/JPY Price Forecast — Dollar-Yen (157.79) Retreats From 159.05 as Ueda Signals Hikes and Katayama Warns — 156.75 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY Price Forecast — Dollar-Yen (157.79) Retreats From 159.05 as Ueda Signals Hikes and Katayama Warns — 156.75 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
USD/JPY Price Forecast — Dollar-Yen (157.79) Caught Between a 216-Basis-Point Yield Gap and Tokyo’s 160 Intervention Line
Markets price a 75% chance of a December BoJ hike and an 85% chance of a Fed hold on October 28.
Key Points
- USD/JPY fell 0.12% to 157.79, down 126 pips from Wednesday’s one-month high of 159.05 after the hot U.S. CPI.
- Katayama said Japan is ready to intervene again, after buying ¥11.74 trillion of yen this spring and a joint U.S.-Japan intervention in July.
- The U.S.-Japan 10-year yield gap stands at 216 basis points, with Treasuries at 5.09% and JGBs at 2.93%.
USD/JPY is trading at 157.79, down 0.12% on the day. Thursday’s close was 158.00. Other Friday quotes put the pair between 157.95 and 158.18, with the session holding a tight range near 158 for most of the European morning before easing in New York trading.
The pair has pulled back from this week’s high. After the hot U.S. consumer price report on Wednesday, USD/JPY climbed to 159.05, the highest level in a month and the weakest yen of October. On Thursday, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned that Japan was ready to intervene again, and the yen strengthened past 158 to a one-week high. From 159.05 to 157.79, USD/JPY has fallen 126 pips, or 0.79%.
The week’s path shows a market pushing against an official ceiling. USD/JPY traded at 158.64 on Monday, October 12. It eased toward 158 on Tuesday as Japanese investors returned from a holiday weekend. It spiked to 159.05 on Wednesday after U.S. CPI rose 3.7%. It fell back on Thursday after Katayama’s warning and has stayed near 158 since.
The 30-day range is 154.88 to 159.05, with an average of 157.75. USD/JPY is trading almost exactly at its one-month average. The pair has risen 1.33% over the past month and the yen has lost 4.96% against the dollar over 12 months.
The 52-week range is 150.26 to 163.86. The low came on October 16, 2025, exactly one year ago. The high came on July 29, 2026, just before Tokyo and Washington carried out a joint intervention to support the yen. At 157.79, USD/JPY sits 753 pips above its 52-week low and 607 pips below its 52-week high.
The 2026 average is 158.47, compared with 149.67 in 2025. The yen has spent most of this year near historically weak levels.
Three forces are pulling on the pair. First, a wide interest rate gap still favors the dollar. Second, Japanese officials are warning they will intervene again if the yen weakens too fast. Third, the Bank of Japan is signaling more rate hikes, while the Fed may be pausing. The next sections examine each force and what it means for the outlook.
Katayama’s Warning: “Prepared to Take Action Again”
Japan’s Ministry of Finance is the biggest obstacle to a higher USD/JPY.
On Thursday, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned speculators that she was prepared to take action in the currency market again if needed. Her comments came after the yen touched its weakest level against the dollar this month following the hotter U.S. inflation report. Katayama said there had been no change in the stance of Washington and Tokyo since their joint intervention to support the yen in July.
The yen reacted immediately. It strengthened past 158 per dollar to a one-week high on Thursday.
Katayama also spoke after meetings with finance chiefs in Bangkok. She said Japan reaffirmed its existing commitments on foreign exchange at the Group of 20 and other meetings. She called for G20 policymakers to closely monitor financial markets with urgency, against a backdrop of renewed pressure on the yen and a global bond selloff.
Japan has a recent record of acting. Between April 28 and May 27, 2026, the Ministry of Finance bought ¥11.74 trillion of yen. Then, in late July, Tokyo and Washington carried out a joint intervention after USD/JPY moved above 160. Katayama has described levels above 160 before that intervention as an extremely weak yen.
The warnings have intensified since September. On September 28, Japan’s top currency diplomat, Atsushi Mimura, urged markets to heed the very clear message from Tokyo and Washington on the yen. After his comments, the yen broke through 157 to trade around 156.75. Mimura also dismissed concerns that Japan lacked the funds for another intervention.
Washington is aligned. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Katayama reaffirmed in phone talks that the yen’s undervaluation is a matter of concern. President Trump raised yen weakness during a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. That U.S. backing makes Tokyo’s threats more credible.
The intervention line appears to be 160. Japan intervened jointly with the U.S. after USD/JPY moved above 160 in July. Markets treat 160 as the level where intervention becomes highly likely. Between 158 and 160, verbal warnings and possible rate checks are the main tools.
For the forecast, intervention risk caps the upside. Traders have been buying dips in USD/JPY but avoiding chasing the pair higher. Any move toward 159 to 160 is likely to meet stronger warnings and possibly action.
Ueda in Bangkok: “Cannot Tolerate” Inflation Above 2%
Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda gave a hawkish message on Friday at the IMF meetings in Bangkok.
Ueda said the BoJ will continue to raise interest rates, with underlying inflation approaching 2% and financial conditions still accommodative. He said policy has entered a new phase and that the BoJ cannot allow underlying inflation to rise further above its 2% target. Anchoring inflation around 2% has become a major policy objective.
He said economic activity and price developments remain broadly in line with the BoJ’s forecasts. He added that the board will discuss at its next meeting whether to tweak its assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%. Changing that wording would signal more confidence that inflation is at target, opening the door to faster rate increases.
Ueda named three factors that will decide the timing and pace of future hikes: exchange rate movements, AI-driven demand and developments in the Middle East. He said more policymakers at the Bangkok meetings were bullish on AI demand than the BoJ had expected.
The yen is part of the BoJ’s calculation. A weaker yen raises import prices, which adds to inflation. If the yen keeps weakening, the BoJ has more reason to hike sooner.
Ueda also discussed the neutral rate. He said the BoJ wants to gauge its estimate of the neutral rate, taking into account the cumulative impact of past rate hikes. He said it is hard to say anything clear about Japan’s neutral rate. A higher neutral rate estimate would imply more hikes ahead.
U.S. officials are pushing for tighter policy. U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne said on Friday that Japan must adjust its monetary policy to reflect that it no longer faces a deflationary environment. That pressure aims to prevent disorderly yen declines.
The BoJ policy rate is 1.25%. The BoJ raised rates in September, three months after a hike in June. That marked an acceleration from the previous pace of roughly one hike every six months.
For the forecast, Ueda’s comments support the yen over the medium term. They confirm that the BoJ is on a tightening path. But they did not signal an October move, so the near-term impact is limited.
BoJ October 29–30: Hold Expected, December Hike 75% Priced
The BoJ’s next meeting is October 29–30, and markets expect a hold.
Markets see little chance of a hike at the October 30 meeting. The probability rises to 75% for the December 18 meeting. Economists generally expect the BoJ to keep policy unchanged in October.
Many BoJ officials prefer to wait. Having just raised rates in September, many officials would like to hold steady in October and wait for more evidence on how earlier increases have affected economic and financial conditions.
Some see a chance of an October move. Former BoJ executive director Kazuo Momma said in late September that the BoJ could raise rates at consecutive meetings. He put the odds of an October hike at 20% to 30%. He said the basic pace will probably be once every three months, which points to December.
The October meeting is still important. The BoJ will release new quarterly growth and inflation forecasts. Ueda said the bank will discuss anchoring inflation at the meeting. A change in the assessment of underlying inflation would be a strong signal for a December hike.
Japan’s economy is mixed. Second-quarter GDP grew at an annualized rate of 1.1%, well below the 2.0% forecast. Quarter on quarter, growth was 0.3%, below the 0.5% forecast. Weak growth argues for caution.
Inflation pressures are easing slightly at the producer level. Japan’s producer prices rose 6.8% in September, below the expected 7.6%. That was the slowest increase since May. Lower producer prices could reduce pressure on consumer prices in coming months.
The BoJ meeting overlaps with the Fed. The Fed meets October 27–28, and the BoJ announces its decision on October 30. A Fed hold followed by a hawkish BoJ outlook would be the strongest combination for the yen.
For the forecast, the October BoJ meeting is a moderate catalyst. A hold with hawkish forecasts and a change in the inflation assessment would support the yen. A dovish hold with no change would weaken it.
The Yield Gap: 216 Basis Points Between U.S. and Japanese 10-Year Bonds
Interest rate differentials remain the main force supporting the dollar against the yen.
The U.S. 10-year Treasury yields 5.09%. The Japanese 10-year government bond yields 2.93%. The gap is 216 basis points. Investors earn 2.16 percentage points more per year holding U.S. bonds than Japanese bonds.
Policy rates show an even wider gap. The Fed’s target range is 3.75% to 4.00%. The BoJ’s policy rate is 1.25%. The gap is 250 to 275 basis points.
The carry trade depends on that gap. Investors borrow in yen at low rates and invest in higher-yielding dollar assets. As long as the gap stays wide, the carry trade supports USD/JPY.
The gap has narrowed slightly

articles.title: HR Ratings Downgrades Mexico, PEMEX to BBB - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: HR Ratings Downgrades Mexico, PEMEX to BBB  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
Summary: HR Ratings downgraded Mexico’s long-term sovereign debt rating and PEMEX’s global-scale debt rating from BBB+ to BBB, citing persistent fiscal pressures, a weaker economic growth outlook and continued challenges in managing public-sector debt. The downgrade comes as PEMEX seeks to expand domestic fuel production and reduce refined-product imports, despite declining crude oil output, lower export volumes and the financial demands of its refining strategy. For investors and businesses, the rating changes underscore the importance of fiscal consolidation, economic growth and PEMEX’s operational performance in shaping Mexico’s credit outlook and energy-sector investment environment.
HR Ratings downgraded Mexico’s long-term sovereign debt rating to BBB from BBB+, citing persistent deterioration in public finances and a weaker economic growth outlook that could increase the country’s debt burden. The agency also lowered PEMEX´s global-scale debt rating to BBB, adding pressure to the financial outlook for the state-owned oil company.
The rating agency said the deterioration in key fiscal balances is expected to continue over its projection period, while slower economic growth will further constrain the government’s capacity to manage its debt. The combination of these factors is expected to sustain pressure on Mexico’s indebtedness.
The decision comes as the government faces competing demands on public spending, including transfers, subsidies and personnel costs, while PEMEX continues to navigate production constraints and the financial requirements of its refining strategy.
Fiscal Pressures Weigh on Mexico’s Credit Outlook
HR Ratings’ decision reflects the challenge of reducing the public deficit while maintaining spending commitments and supporting economic activity. Although the agency acknowledged the Finance Ministry’s efforts to contain the public-sector deficit following the historically high level recorded in 2024, it concluded that the measures have not been sufficient to bring the Public Sector Borrowing Requirements (RFSP) below 4% of gross domestic product.
The agency also recognized efforts to increase tax revenue. However, it warned that higher collections would not be enough to ease fiscal pressures without stronger economic activity to support revenue growth and offset rising expenditure.
The weaker growth outlook is particularly relevant because slower economic expansion can limit the increase in tax receipts while making existing debt obligations more difficult to manage relative to the size of the economy.
The downgrade therefore reflects both current fiscal conditions and the agency’s expectations for the coming years. Its assessment suggests that sustained improvements in public finances will require more than revenue collection measures alone, particularly if spending pressures remain elevated.
PEMEX Downgrade Highlights Energy-Sector Risks
HR Ratings lowered PEMEX’s global-scale debt rating from BBB+ to BBB, in line with its revision of the sovereign rating. The decision comes as the company seeks to increase domestic fuel production and reduce Mexico’s dependence on imported refined products, despite declining crude oil output.
The state oil company’s refining strategy has gained importance as international oil prices have climbed above US$100 per barrel. In mid-September 2026,Brent crude reached US$109.29 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate rose to US$104.26 per barrel following attacks on Saudi infrastructure, disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and reduced Russian refining capacity, reported MBN.
At the Mexico Market Briefing, José Verdugo, fuel and refining analyst for the Americas at S&P Global, said domestic refining can support energy sovereignty and improve profitability when refined-product prices rise faster than crude prices.
Mexico’s dependence on imported gasoline, diesel and jet fuel declined to 44% from 67% at the end of 2023, according to S&P Global data. Domestic fuel production reached approximately 1 million barrels per day, supported by refinery rehabilitation and the Olmeca refinery in Dos Bocas.
However, the benefits of expanded refining capacity depend on PEMEX’s ability to secure sufficient crude supplies. Declining production could limit the company’s flexibility to supply domestic refineries while also taking advantage of favorable international prices through crude exports.
Production Declines Complicate PEMEX’s Strategy
PEMEX’s operating figures show improvements in refining alongside continued pressure on crude extraction. In 2Q2026, liquid hydrocarbon extraction averaged 1.6 million barrels per day, while total hydrocarbon production reached 2.44 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 4.6% year over year.
Crude processing increased 2.9% to 1 million barrels per day, and refined-product output rose 3.4% to 1.03 million barrels per day. Diesel production increased 19.3%, contributing to the improvement in refining performance.
Nevertheless, crude production fell to 1.33 million barrels per day in August, down 2.7% from August 2025 and the lowest monthly level in PEMEX’s statistical records dating to 1990.
Crude exports also declined, falling from approximately 450,000 barrels per day in July to 275,737 barrels per day in August. Export revenue dropped from US$1.05 billion to US$626.9 million over the same period.
Exploration and production expert Alma Porres attributed some of the downward pressure to natural declines in mature fields, including Quesqui and Ixachi. She said future production from deepwater and shallow-water projects, including Trion and Zama, will be important to meeting domestic refining requirements and export commitments.
Limited inventories add another operational constraint. Fuel stocks cover fewer than 10 days of gasoline and diesel demand and approximately three days of jet fuel consumption, according to the source data.

articles.title: Gold Price Forecast — XAU/USD ($4,187.70) Gains as Neutral Warsh Weakens the Dollar — $4,331 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Gold Price Forecast — XAU/USD ($4,187.70) Gains as Neutral Warsh Weakens the Dollar — $4,331 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Spot gold rose 0.43% to $4,187.70, reaching a $4,199.50 high after the dollar index fell 0.7% to 101.80.
- Global gold ETF holdings reached a record 4,256 tonnes after a record $31 billion in third-quarter inflows.
- Gold remains below its 100-day average at $4,242, 50-day at $4,331 and 200-day at $4,522.
Spot gold is bid at $4,187.70 an ounce at 10:39 a.m. ET, up $17.90, or 0.43%, on the day. The ask is $4,189.70. Friday’s range has run from $4,146.60 to $4,199.50, and the high came within 50 cents of the $4,200 handle before sellers pushed back. December COMEX futures trade at $4,206.90, up $36.80, or 0.88%. That leaves the usual contango premium of $19 over spot.
This is the second straight daily gain. Spot gold closed Thursday at $4,175.10, up 1.79% on the day, after trading from $4,096.80 to $4,175.80. That rebound came after Wednesday’s 1.51% drop to $4,101.70, when the September CPI report pushed spot to an intraday low of $4,073.80. In 48 hours gold has gained $114 from that low, or 2.8%.
The wider picture is more mixed. Gold is down 0.4% for the week as of the London morning. It is down 2.22% over the past month and down 3.68% over 12 months. Year to date, December futures are down 4.38%, and over six months the loss is 13.05%. The metal sits 25.2% below its intraday all-time high of $5,595.47, set on January 29, 2026. The LBMA afternoon benchmark peaked at $5,405.00 the same day.
The SPDR Gold Shares ETF (GLD) is at $383.58, up 0.23%. It has traded between $381.07 and $384.06 today, against a 52-week range of $360.12 to $509.70. Its net assets are $141.7 billion, the largest gold ETF by a wide margin. GLD is down 3.21% year to date and down 3.25% over a year.
In India, 24-carat gold on the MCX rose ₹793 to ₹148,282 per 10 grams, from ₹147,489 at the prior close. Physical demand in major consumer markets is following the dollar price higher.
Silver is at $57.86 to $57.92, up 0.7% to 0.84%, after a 3% gain on Thursday. The gold-to-silver ratio is 72.32, down from 72.64 on Thursday. Silver is down 18.54% year to date, much worse than gold. Platinum rose 0.7% to $1,636.98 and palladium 0.5% to $1,132.09. All three are still on track for weekly losses.
The setup is clear. Gold is pushing against the top of a two-week range just below $4,200, supported by a weaker dollar and lower Treasury yields. The open question is whether it can break that range or will fall back toward $4,100 again. The next sections lay out the levels and drivers.
Neutral Warsh, Weaker Dollar: The Overnight Catalyst
The move overnight came from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. In a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Warsh said conditions since the September meeting had “broadly conformed to our expectations.” On the October decision, he said: “I don’t prejudge meetings.”
For gold, that was enough. Markets were braced for a hawkish signal after September’s hot CPI and PPI reports. Warsh did not give one. The dollar index fell 0.7%, dropping to its lowest level in almost two weeks. It slid from close to an 18-month high near 103 to test 101.80. The dollar is now on track for its first weekly decline in five weeks.
Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar makes it cheaper for buyers using euros, yen, rupees and yuan. Before Warsh spoke, gold had dipped to the $4,150 area in Asian trading. Buyers stepped in there and lifted spot to $4,178.50 by 06:57 UTC. By the London morning it was at $4,176.92 and futures were at $4,198.10.
The bond market moved in the same direction. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to a three-week low below 5.10% on Thursday and is at 5.07% today. Gold pays no interest. Every basis point off long-term yields lowers the cost of holding it.
Fed pricing also shifted. Before the CPI report, markets put October hike odds at 22%. After CPI, they rose to 29%. After PPI and Warsh’s comments, an October hike is close to fully priced out, with odds in the high-20s. December remains open: markets were pricing an 85% chance of a hike by December earlier in the week, and the hot inflation data keeps that risk alive.
Other Fed officials have signaled the same patience. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed President John Williams and Governor Christopher Waller have all pointed toward an October hold. Waller noted that rate increases do not need to come at back-to-back meetings. Warsh’s appearance came just before the pre-meeting blackout period, so no more Fed guidance is expected before October 27–28.
Warsh also called the AI investment boom “probably the most important thing that’s happening in the global economy on the upside.” He has linked part of the rise in long-term yields to large technology firms competing for capital. That matters for gold. If AI-related borrowing keeps pushing yields up, it keeps the opportunity cost of holding gold high. If AI credit stress pushes investors into Treasuries, as it did Thursday, yields fall and gold benefits.
The Warsh effect is real but short-term. It lifted gold to the top of its range. Breaking out of that range needs more than a quiet Fed chair.
The Inflation Paradox: 6.3% PPI and 3.7% CPI Without a Breakout
On paper, this week’s inflation data should have sent gold higher. The September producer price index rose 1.3% for the month, more than double the 0.6% forecast. It was the largest monthly jump since March 2022. Year over year, PPI reached 6.3%, against a 5.3% forecast. Core PPI rose to 5.0%, above the 4.4% expected. Goods prices climbed 2.6% in the month, and services rose 0.8%.
Consumer prices were also hot. September CPI rose 0.6% for the month and 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% forecast. Core CPI increased 0.3%, versus a 0.2% forecast, for an annual core rate of 2.6%. Energy prices rose 5.2% in a month and gasoline jumped 9.1%. September retail sales rose 0.8%, showing that consumer spending is holding up even with higher prices.
The paradox is that gold fell on the CPI report. On Wednesday, spot dropped 1.51% to $4,101.70 and touched $4,073.80. The reason is the Fed. Hot inflation raises the odds of more rate hikes, and higher rates raise real yields, the inflation-adjusted return on bonds. Real yields are gold’s main short-term headwind. For a day, the rate risk mattered more to gold than the inflation itself.
PPI on Thursday had the opposite effect. Gold rose 1.79%, even though the producer data was worse. Treasuries rallied, the 10-year yield dropped 10 basis points, and money moved into safe-haven assets as concerns over AI-related debt spread. CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds were yielding 15.78% on more than $50 billion of debt. That pushed investors toward government bonds and gold at the same time.
The inflation data matters over the medium term. A 6.3% PPI print points to more pressure on consumer prices in coming months. Gold’s long-term case rests on protecting purchasing power when inflation stays above central bank targets. Real yields near current levels are a headwind today, but sustained inflation tends to win out over time.
The key number to watch is the real yield, not the headline yield. With a 10-year Treasury at 5.07% and CPI at 3.7%, the real yield based on current inflation is 1.37%. If inflation keeps rising while the Fed holds, real yields compress and gold benefits. If the Fed hikes in December while inflation stabilizes, real yields rise and gold stays stuck.
The data does not settle the question. It supports both sides of the trade. The outcome depends on how the Fed responds at its next two meetings.
Record 4,256 Tonnes in ETFs: The Demand That Price Hasn’t Caught
The strongest support for gold this month is in the fund flow data. Global gold ETFs took in $10 billion in September, bringing third-quarter inflows to a record $31 billion. Holdings rose 67 tonnes in September to a record 4,256 tonnes. In the third quarter alone, holdings grew by 211 tonnes.
That buying happened while prices fell. Total ETF assets under management dropped 7% in September to $574 billion because the gold price declined. But holdings in tonnes increased. Investors added more metal even as the dollar value of their positions shrank. This is buying on weakness, not chasing a rally.
European-listed funds led the way. They took in $3.6 billion in September and a record $14 billion in the third quarter. UK funds were the largest contributor in September, adding $2.2 billion. German and French funds also had solid inflows. Swiss-listed funds recorded inflows even though their holdings dropped 1 tonne, a result of how currency-hedged products work.
Holdings at 4,256 tonnes with gold 25.2% below its January record creates a clear gap between demand and price. In past cycles, record ETF holdings came with record prices. This time, the price is being held down by real yields while physical demand keeps growing. That gap tends to close one of two ways: either prices rise, or ETF buyers start to sell. So far there is no sign of selling.
The second quarter was different. ETFs saw 44.8 tonnes of outflows as gold fell from its January high toward $4,000 by the end of June. The shift from second-quarter outflows to record third-quarter inflows shows investors stepped back in once prices stabilized in the $4,000 to $4,300 range.
GLD is the bellwether. It holds $141.7 billion in net assets. Its 52-week range runs from $360.12 to $509.70, and at $383.58 it sits 6.5% above its low and 24.7% below its high. Trading in GLD is light today, at 962,985 shares by 9:55 a.m. against a 9.28 million daily average. Investors are not rushing in after the Warsh-driven move.
Global gold trading volumes averaged $423 billion per day in September, down 2% from August. Liquidity is stable. The market can take large flows without disorder.
For the forecast, ETF demand acts as a floor. A record 4,256 tonnes held through a 25% drawdown from the peak shows that these buyers have long-term conviction. Dips toward

articles.title: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all - CNBC
articles.summary: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Traders are betting overwhelmingly that the Federal Reserve won’t raise interest rates when it meets later this month. But that judgment rests in part on assumptions about how the Fed communicates that may no longer hold under its new chairman. Kevin Warsh has left room to maneuver toward a hike, should he choose to use it.
To be clear, Warsh said outright at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok Friday morning that he wasn’t signaling a decision one way or the other. His remarks nonetheless reinforced a judgment in the markets that the Fed would pause its rate increases, with the futures market assigning a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning. That judgment follows remarks by other Fed speakers, including the chair’s traditional top lieutenants, who indicated they were comfortable holding.
There are good reasons for investors to expect the Fed to wait. But there is also a case in the inflation data that Warsh could invoke to push the Federal Open Market Committee toward an increase on Oct. 28. Investors are overlooking that case based on longstanding past experience with the Fed.
But the chairman has repeatedly rejected the convention of telling markets what he plans to do before the committee meets. That raises the possibility that investors are dangerously complacent about the probability of a rate hike in October.
That complacency rests on a few bases. One is that the chairman’s top lieutenants speak for him, or at least wouldn’t contradict him in public. That was true in the past, but may not be so anymore.
In recent weeks, both Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams gave remarks that indicated they see little urgency in raising interest rates. The markets quickly repriced in favor of a hold in October.
Warsh, Jefferson and Williams make up an informal decision-making team atop the Fed known as the troika. Warsh could arguably coordinate with the troika even if he doesn’t believe in communicating his own views. But outsiders can’t be certain that traditional conventions surrounding the public statements of the New York Fed president and the Fed vice chair have survived the leadership transition.
Another assumption is that Warsh broadly accepts the FOMC’s view of the economy. “The world has broadly conformed to our expectations,” Warsh said in Bangkok of the economy since September.
That can be read as saying that relatively hot inflation readings from the consumer and producer price indexes in recent days don’t disconfirm the view expressed in the Fed’s most recent Summary of Economic Projections released at the conclusion of the September meeting. At the time, the median Fed official believed there would be one more rate hike in 2026 — which left room to pause in October and raise again in December.
But Warsh went out of his way at the September press conference to disclaim the SEP. “Those aren’t my forecasts,” he told a reporter.
Warsh set out his own idiosyncratic reading of the economy in detail at a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of August. It described the economy as growing strongly, with inflation a greater worry than the jobs market. Warsh’s strongly hawkish views then set up the FOMC to unanimously raise interest rates in September. That hawkish position relied heavily on what he sees as loose credit conditions.
The Chicago Fed’s National Financial Conditions Index has risen about 0.05 points since Jackson Hole but remains negative, indicating financial conditions have tightened but remain loose overall.
Does Warsh believe the market has done his work for him? Is having “removed a dose of accommodation,” as he put it Thursday, enough? We can infer these answers, but we won’t really know them until the FOMC press conference.
Then there is the inflation data. The consumer price index rose 3.7% for the year through September, while the producer price index gained 6.3%. The new data implies that the next reading of the Fed’s preferred inflation reading, core personal consumption expenditures, will come in at 3.1% year over year. Headline PCE, which will be affected by energy prices, would be higher.
Warsh has gone out of his way to say that figures at that level are a problem. After economists questioned whether Warsh might tolerate inflation above 2%, he was unequivocal in Jackson Hole: “There should be no misunderstanding,” Warsh said. The Fed’s 2% PCE goal “is a firm, fixed target.”
Warsh is visibly learning on the job. He may well be coming to understand that the Fed chairman can’t operate alone and must rely on the staff and the rest of the FOMC to help him do his job. Likewise, he may discover that markets don’t issue a clear signal independently of the Fed.
Raising rates while the markets strongly expect otherwise is a recipe for volatility. That factor has prompted interventions by officials like Jefferson and Williams in the past. A surprise decision after they were seen to guide the market could dent their credibility and make the Fed’s decisions even harder to predict.
But how Warsh will settle these matters isn’t clear yet. Warsh could go into the October meeting primed to muscle up wavering committee members based on booming demand for AI spending and warm readings in the inflation data. Or he could sit back and tack toward the middle of the committee once he assesses its views.
Warsh still has the potential to surprise us, and it’s risky to assume otherwise.

Warsh gave no forward guidance, while CPI/PPI and strong retail sales are being increasingly ignored by markets as they price an 85% October hold. That mismatch favors a pullback in front-end yields as the market “waits for data” rather than hikes immediately. Buy U.S. 2-year Treasury futures (or 2Y Treasury notes) for a yield drop into the October meeting.
Key Risk: A fresh inflation/retail upside shock that forces the market to price an October hike back above 50%.
If October is a hold but December is still ~89% likely, the path stays restrictive. Banks and other rate-sensitive cyclicals can underperform when the market shifts from “immediate hikes” to “higher-for-longer,” especially if growth stays resilient but inflation remains sticky. Sell SPDR Financial Select Sector ETF (XLF).
Key Risk: A clear growth slowdown that triggers aggressive rate-cut pricing, reversing the “higher-for-longer” narrative and lifting XLF.
- Markets assign an 85.1% chance of the Fed holding rates in October.
- Warsh declines to signal decisions, saying he does not prejudge meetings.
- - UBS expects additional quarter-point rate increases in December and March 2027.
Expectations that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady at its October meeting surged on Friday, even as persistent inflation and strong economic data continued to complicate the outlook for monetary policy.
CME FedWatch data showed an 85.1% probability of the Fed leaving rates unchanged at its next meeting. That was up from around 72% a day earlier and close to an even split about a month ago.
The shift in expectations comes as investors weigh fresh inflation data against the possibility of further monetary tightening. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, meanwhile, declined to indicate which way policymakers were leaning ahead of the upcoming decision.
The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points last month, taking its benchmark rate to a range of 3.75%-4.00%. The September move was its first rate increase in three years.
What did Warsh say?
Speaking at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday, Warsh maintained his stance of avoiding advance signals about the Fed's interest-rate decisions.
"I don't prejudge meetings," Warsh said during a discussion with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. "I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
However, he reiterated the central bank's commitment to bringing inflation under control, referring to last month's rate increase as a move toward tighter monetary policy.
"We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago."
Warsh's comments leave the October decision open, with policymakers continuing to assess incoming data as they balance inflation risks against broader economic conditions.
Inflation data complicates outlook
The Fed faces a challenging environment as price pressures remain elevated, partly because of persistently high energy costs.
Wednesday's consumer price index report showed headline inflation at 3.7% annually, while core inflation reached 2.6%. Both readings were slightly above expectations, initially raising the likelihood of another rate increase in October before those odds eased on Thursday.
The producer price index added to concerns about persistent inflation. Wholesale prices rose 1.3% in September and increased 6.3% from a year earlier, marking the largest annual increase since December 2022.
Retail sales also came in stronger than expected, advancing 0.8% against economists' consensus forecast of 0.3%.
The combination of higher producer prices and resilient consumer spending has reinforced concerns that inflation could remain difficult to contain. However, the latest figures have not prevented markets from increasingly pricing in an October pause.
December hike likely
While expectations for an October rate increase have declined, markets continue to anticipate further tightening before the end of the year.
CME FedWatch data indicated an approximately 88.9% probability of a rate increase at the Fed's December 9 meeting, up from 83% a week earlier.
UBS Global Wealth Management has also revised its forecast, expecting the Fed to extend its tightening cycle into 2027.
In a research note led by economist Andrew Dubinsky, UBS projected a quarter-point rate increase in December, followed by another 25-basis-point hike in March 2027.
The bank expects policymakers to pause after the March increase to assess the cumulative impact of higher interest rates.

articles.title: Nifty, Sensex investors alert! US bond yields remain above 5% - 5 ways this could impact your investments, portfolio - Livemint
articles.summary: Nifty, Sensex investors alert! US bond yields remain above 5% - 5 ways this could impact your investments, portfolio  Livemint
articles.full_text:
US Bond Yield Rise: The sharp reversal in US Treasury yields has drawn attention to the outlook for global financial markets, with implications for capital flows, currencies, borrowing costs and equity valuations.
The US 10-year Treasury yield retreated from a peak of 5.33% following Wednesday's inflation data to 5.086% by Thursday's close, holding near that level on Friday. The 10-basis-point decline on Thursday marked its biggest single-day fall since August 2025, despite September consumer inflation accelerating to 3.7%, producer prices rising 6.3% year on year, stronger retail sales and crude oil prices remaining above $100.
Sandip Jha, Chief Product Officer at Godrej Wealth, cautioned that the decline may not signal a sustained turnaround in the bond market.
“The decline in US 10-year yields looks more like a tactical correction than a change in the underlying trend. While yields have eased amid risk-off flows and a flight to safe-haven assets, the underlying macro backdrop remains far from supportive of a sustained bond rally. With inflationary pressures expected to remain sticky and economic activity remaining resilient, the fundamental case for a sustained rally in Treasuries remains weak. Unless the macro data begin to soften meaningfully, yields could reverse course and move higher again,” Jha said.
The US 10-year Treasury yield had climbed from 4.76% at the end of August 2026 to 5.33% on Wednesday, reaching a multi-decade high.
The increase comes amid elevated crude oil prices, resilient US economic activity, widening fiscal deficits and growing investor demands for higher compensation for holding long-term government debt. These factors have reinforced expectations of interest rates remaining elevated for longer.
For Indian investors, the development matters because US Treasury yields serve as a global benchmark for borrowing costs and influence how international investors allocate capital across markets.
Here are five ways rising US yields could affect investments and what investors should consider doing, according to a report by IndusInd Bank.
Higher US Treasury yields can make American fixed-income investments more attractive relative to emerging-market assets. As the return available on US government debt increases, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) may become more selective about investing in Indian equities, particularly when the additional returns do not adequately compensate for currency and market risks.
Such a shift could put pressure on Indian stock prices and contribute to volatility, especially if foreign investors continue to withdraw money from domestic markets.
The IndusInd Bank report noted that rising US yields can affect the relative attractiveness of Indian assets and influence international capital flows.
Movements in US Treasury yields can influence domestic bond-market sentiment and Indian government security (G-sec) yields. Higher global borrowing costs may push domestic yields upwards, increasing the cost of raising money for governments and companies.
The IndusInd Bank report showed that India's 10-year benchmark government bond yield rose to 7.18% on September 30, 2026, from 6.95% at the end of August. It attributed the increase to rising global yields, elevated crude oil prices, domestic inflation concerns and tighter banking-system liquidity.
For existing bondholders, rising yields can mean falling market prices for bonds, particularly those with longer maturities. However, higher yields can also improve the returns available to investors entering the market at the new levels.
Higher US yields can strengthen the dollar by improving the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated investments. A stronger dollar could put pressure on the Indian rupee, particularly when foreign capital flows are volatile.
A weaker rupee can increase the domestic cost of imported goods, including crude oil. This may add to imported inflation and complicate the policy outlook for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
Currency movements can also affect companies differently. Businesses dependent on imported raw materials may face higher costs, while exporters earning revenues in dollars could benefit from favourable currency translation, depending on their cost structures and hedging arrangements.
Higher global interest rates influence overseas borrowing costs for companies. If elevated yields persist, businesses that depend heavily on external financing could face more expensive debt, potentially affecting profitability and investment plans.
Higher interest rates can also reduce the present value of future corporate earnings, putting pressure on equity valuations. This can be particularly relevant for companies whose valuations depend heavily on profits expected several years into the future.
The report identified elevated fiscal deficits and Treasury issuance as factors that could keep US yields high, reinforcing the possibility of a prolonged higher-interest-rate environment.
Rising yields are part of a broader global picture involving inflation, geopolitical uncertainty, energy prices and uneven economic growth. These factors can influence investor sentiment and trigger sharp market movements even when a company's long-term business outlook remains intact.
IndusInd Bank's report highlighted India's resilient domestic fundamentals but cautioned that global developments can affect markets in the short term.
For investors, the key is not to predict the exact peak in US yields but to understand how prolonged high rates could affect their holdings. A disciplined approach, periodic portfolio reviews and diversification can help manage risk without abandoning long-term investment objectives.

articles.title: Kevin Warsh offers no clues on Fed’s next rate decision - Mettis Global
articles.summary: Kevin Warsh offers no clues on Fed’s next rate decision  Mettis Global
articles.full_text:
MG News | October 16, 2026 at 04:24 PM GMT+05:00
October 16, 2026 (MLN): The US Federal Reserve is not showing whether it will raise interest rates again at its October 27-28 meeting, even as September inflation came in hotter than expected, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at the IMF meetings in Bangkok on Friday, in a conversation with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.
Kevin Warsh neither endorsed nor rejected recent remarks from
fellow Fed officials that the central bank is in no hurry to tighten further. 
He said he does not prejudge meetings and will not say now
what the Fed might do at its remaining meetings this year, calling it a “new
chapter” for the central bank. 
He has brought a more limited communication style to the Fed
and wants markets to respond to the economy itself rather than to official
signals. Georgieva joked that he had just disappointed half the audience or
more.
In September, the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to a
range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase in three years. The move came as the
US faces rising energy prices and higher costs linked to an AI-investment boom.
Speculation about another hike grew this week after a firm
inflation report showed US consumer prices up 3.7% year-on-year in September,
compared with a 3.4% gain in August.
Kevin Warsh described artificial intelligence as the most
consequential change to the global economy in his lifetime. He said the surge
in AI spending is lifting aggregate demand and pushing up prices in the near
term, and that the road ahead may be bumpy. 
Over the longer run, he said, the technology would act as a
positive supply shock, expanding the economy’s capacity to produce goods and
services without necessarily raising prices. 
He said the investment surge “isn’t by accident” and that
the US’s economic momentum is not found everywhere in the world. 
Several East Asian economies, including South Korea and
Taiwan, are also gaining from rising exports of chips and computing equipment.
Kevin Warsh spoke as global economic pain mounts from higher
borrowing costs and energy prices due to the Iran war. Oil has risen from about
$70 per barrel before the war to about $105 now. 
Inflation and heavy borrowing by AI companies have pushed
investors to demand higher yields on government bonds, particularly from
heavily indebted countries. The IMF expects the global economy to grow 3.1% in
2026, down from 3.5% last year.
Kevin Warsh said inflation is a common challenge across countries,
with governments responding using their own domestic tools, resulting in a
“synchronous tightening in monetary policy”. 
He called this a positive development. He also said he was
pleasantly surprised by how well many countries have weathered recent
geopolitical uncertainty, and that resilience was showing up almost everywhere,
more than he would have predicted five or six months ago.

articles.full_text:
Three things landed within two days: a hot inflation report, a Bitcoin dip below $80K before bouncing to $82K, and a Fed chair who refused to say what comes next.
Bitcoin Crypto News today links all three to one date, October 27–28, when the Fed meets to decide on rates. What Warsh left unsaid is where the story starts.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF and World Bank event in Bangkok on October 16. He did not reveal the next move and said he does not prejudge meetings. His main points as per official press release:
Inflation: the Federal Reserve stays committed to bringing it down, and it remains a major challenge.
Last move: he defended September’s 25 bp hike, the first since 2023, per the Fed’s press conference. It lifted the target range to 3.75%–4%.
Growth: strong investment is lifting the US economy.
Global picture: the world economy is more resilient than expected.
AI: he expects a big productivity gain, but its near-term effect on jobs is unclear.
The US PPI data for September came in far above forecasts. Producer prices rose 1.3% in the month, against about 0.5% expected, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics:
PPI, monthly: up 1.3%
PPI, yearly: 6.3%
Producer gasoline prices: up 20.3%
Core PPI (no food, energy or trade services): up 0.5%
A hot CPI report, showing 3.7% yearly inflation, had landed a day earlier.
Fuel costs drove much of the jump, but core producer prices also rose 0.5%. That is why a Fed rate hike cannot be ruled out, even with the chairman keeping quiet.
Traders read the silence as a pause. Polymarket prediction page on the interest rate decision shows:
No change: 87%, with about $13.05M traded
25 bps increase: 14%, with about $9.94M traded
A Fed rate hike is still possible, but its odds have been falling. The FOMC meeting in October runs on the 27th and 28th.
Bitcoin price today stands at $82,086.52, up 1.62% in 24 hours, per CoinMarketCap. The chart shows the dip first: BTC slid to just under $80K, then jumped past $82K and has held a tight range since.

These are one analyst’s levels, not forecasts. This article is not financial advice, and BTC can move sharply in either direction.
For crypto news today, the chain is simple: hot prices raise hike odds, and a calm Federal Reserve lowers them. The October 27–28 meeting settles it.

articles.title: [SMM Iron Ore Weekly Brief] Iron Ore’s Decline Slows as Hot Metal Steadies and Port Stocks Build - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: [SMM Iron Ore Weekly Brief] Iron Ore’s Decline Slows as Hot Metal Steadies and Port Stocks Build  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
In the first full trading week after the holiday, iron ore extended its decline, but the fall was markedly smaller than in the week before the break. The SGX main contract eased from $91.24/mt on October 9 to $90.45/mt on October 15, down $0.79 or 0.87%; the DCE main contract I2701 fell from 682.5 yuan/mt to 671.5 yuan/mt, down 1.61%; and the MMI 61% iron ore port spot index slipped from 664 yuan/wmt to 654 yuan/wmt, down 1.51%. Against a 2.35% drop in the SGX contract the previous period, the loss of downward momentum this week is clear.
The week was steady first and weaker later. The futures board was close to flat on October 12, then closed lower for four consecutive sessions, leaving I2701 at 671.5 yuan/mt on October 15, a cumulative 31 yuan/mt below the last pre-holiday session on September 30.
Onshore and offshore strength diverged this week. The yuan central parity firmed 77 basis points over the week to 6.7253, so on a yuan-converted basis the SGX contract fell only 6.8 yuan/mt while the DCE fell 11 yuan over the same stretch, widening the onshore-offshore spread from minus 11.7 yuan to minus 15.9 yuan and deepening the onshore discount. That is the mirror image of the last pre-holiday session, when the offshore market was pricing in the demand vacuum of the break while the onshore board was lifted by position cutting and short covering. With the post-holiday repositioning complete, the board is again reflecting China’s own inventory and demand pressure.
II. Supply: a third straight weekly fall in arrivals, ports still building, and freight pulling cost support away
SMM shipping data put global iron ore shipments at 34.14 million mt in the week to October 9, down 1.80 million mt week on week, while arrivals in China came to 27.91 million mt, down 1.18 million mt. That is a third consecutive weekly decline, a cumulative 3.41 million mt below the 31.32 million mt of the week to September 18. Volumes destined for China fell to 19.43 million mt, down 3.49 million mt from 22.92 million mt in the week to September 25.
Arrivals are contracting, yet ports are still building. Imported ore inventories across the 35 ports stood at 148.30 million mt on October 16, up 2.85 million mt from the last pre-holiday reading on September 25; SMM’s 10-port inventories were 105.14 million mt on October 15, up 2.12 million mt from before the break, with fines and lump accounting for most of the build. Port outbound volume of imported ore over the same period was 3.19 million mt, below the 3.24 million mt of the week to September 25. This build has not been pushed up by arrivals; outbound shipment simply has not kept pace, which makes it demand showing through in the supply numbers.
The change most worth recording on the supply side this week is freight. Australia-to-China freight fell from $14.39/mt on October 9 to $11.60/mt on October 15, down 19.4% over the week, while Brazil-to-China freight eased from $33.68/mt to $31.39/mt, down 6.8% on the week and a cumulative 27.1% below the $43.06/mt of September 24. Last week’s commentary set out a conditional view: if Brazil-to-China freight held at the level then prevailing, low-grade capacity facing the same margin pressure might follow with cuts of its own. That condition has not held this week. Freight has turned down first, and the external premise behind CSN Mineração’s freight-driven production cut has changed. For iron ore prices, lower freight pulls landed costs down directly, and cost support beneath the market loosens with it.
III. Demand: hot metal steadies while maintenance losses keep widening, though more slowly
The holiday-period drop has already been realised. Average daily hot metal output across 242 steel mills was 2.3532 million mt in the period to October 7, down 35,000 mt from 2.3882 million mt on September 30, and 2.3520 million mt in the period to October 14, a further decline of just 1,200 mt, leaving it 36,200 mt below the pre-holiday level. The blast furnace operating rate was 87.03% and capacity utilisation 86.81%, down 1.54 and 1.34 percentage points respectively from before the break. After six consecutive periods of decline from 2.4080 million mt in the period to September 2, hot metal has essentially stopped falling this week.
The drag has not lifted. Hot metal lost to blast furnace maintenance came to 1.9011 million mt in the period to October 16, up 78,600 mt week on week and a fourth consecutive period of expansion from 1.5288 million mt in the period to September 18, a cumulative increase of 372,300 mt. The increments themselves are converging, however, running at 101,100, 113,900, 78,700 and 78,600 mt across the four periods, with the last two slowing noticeably. A peak in the pace of maintenance expansion typically comes before hot metal turns back up.
Mill margins have repaired in a real way. The second round of coke price cuts took effect at midnight on October 12, with wet-quenched coke down 100 yuan/mt and dry-quenched coke down 110 yuan/mt, taking the national average for quasi-grade-one dry-quenched metallurgical coke from 2,310 yuan/mt to 2,200 yuan/mt. After two rounds, the spot margin on BF rebar recovered from minus 179.79 yuan/mt before the holiday to minus 74.33 yuan/mt on October 15, regaining 105.46 yuan in three weeks. Margin repair gives hot metal the conditions to stabilise, but it has not yet turned into incremental iron ore buying; mills are still taking rigid-demand volumes and show little appetite for active restocking.
IV. Marginal disturbances
A third round of coke price cuts is still being contested. Coke producers fell back into losses after the second round landed and are more inclined to curb output, while mills have already repaired margins somewhat, leaving them with less leverage to press prices than in the first two rounds. Market sentiment is driven by the combination of high inventories and expectations that hot metal has bottomed, and whichever side delivers a clear signal first is likely to decide the direction iron ore takes next week. Annual long-term contract negotiations are also worth watching; SMM iron ore commentary flagged them as a point of focus for the futures board twice this week.
The average margin on imported iron ore narrowed over the week from 15.37 yuan/mt to 9.60 yuan/mt, dragged down by falling port spot prices.
V. Outlook and what to watch
The SGX main contract is likely to trade in an $88-93/mt range next week. Hot metal is close to its floor and maintenance losses are growing more slowly, which limits how much further demand can fall; but port inventories are high in absolute terms and outbound shipment has yet to pick up, so there is just as little room above. The direction favours range-bound trading at low levels. Whether the centre of gravity shifts lower again rests on two trackable data points: whether arrivals in China extend their decline in the next period, and whether 10-port inventories post their first drawdown of this cycle.
From a fundamentals standpoint, the cost side is what needs watching more closely. Freight has fallen by more than a quarter in three weeks. If that trend continues, cost support beneath iron ore will weaken further, and the case for overseas production cuts driven by freight pressure will weaken with it. At the macro level, no new information emerged this week. This chain can be verified within the fourth quarter.

Speaking at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on 16 October, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh refused to signal whether the Fed will raise interest rates again at its October 27–28 meeting, keeping markets uncertain after September’s rate hike.
Meanwhile, Warsh also warned that artificial intelligence could transform the global economy, but its short-term impact will be difficult to manage.
Warsh Refuses to Signal October Fed Rate Decision
During a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Warsh said the Fed would decide its next move based on the economic situation at each meeting.
“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”
He also made clear that the Fed would not offer advance signals about its rate decisions.
“It’s a new chapter at the Fed [and] we’re not in that business anymore.”
September Rate Hike Was Necessary To Keep Inflation in Focus
Further commenting on the Fed’s 25-basis-point rate hike in September, which raised the target range to 3.75%–4%, Warsh said policymakers needed to reduce monetary support to bring inflation under control.
Despite Kevin Warsh offering no hints about the Fed’s next move, CME FedWatch data showed traders pricing in an 87.3% chance that the Fed will hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.
Warsh Warns AI Growth Could Be “Very Bumpy”
Beyond interest rates, Warsh described artificial intelligence as “probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime.”
He said the technology could make economies more productive and wealthier, but warned that the shift would not be smooth.
“I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose.”
He said AI could make economies more productive and wealthier, but warned that the transition would be “very bumpy.”
Its near-term effect on jobs remains uncertain, while rising investment in AI infrastructure could also create price pressures.
