articles.title: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn’t - Real Investment Advice
articles.summary: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn’t  Real Investment Advice
articles.full_text:
The economy is running bad inflation, and the bad kind is the temporary kind, which is precisely why the bond market refuses to panic.
Most of the argument about inflation right now is a fight between people using the same word for two completely different things. One side sees a 3.7% headline print and starts sketching a repeat of 1979. The other sees core running more than a point below it and declares the problem solved. Both are reading the same release. The distinction that matters is not how big the number is, but whether anybody’s income is financing it. That is the line between “good” inflation and bad inflation, and almost nobody draws it.
Good Inflation, Bad Inflation, And The Difference Nobody Makes
There is a general framework to inflation, and it is older than any of us. Prices can rise because buyers are bidding for scarce goods with money they’ve actually earned. Or prices can rise because the cost of producing something has jumped for reasons unrelated to demand. An oil embargo will do it, as we saw in the 1970s. So does a shuttered Strait of Hormuz, a new tariff schedule, or a pandemic that takes half the world’s shipping capacity offline for eighteen months.
This is an important point for the “debasement” crowd, whose narrative overlooks the underlying fundamentals.
“The following economic illustration is taught in every ‘Econ 101’ class. Unsurprisingly, inflation is the consequence if supply is restricted and demand increases via monetary interventions.”
However, there is a very important distinction to be made about inflation. The first type is the “good” kind of inflation, and it is genuinely good. Demand pushes prices up; firms book wider margins; tight labor markets funnel those margins into paychecks, and the higher paychecks fund the higher prices. The loop closes and becomes self-reinforcing because every leg of it is paid for by real output.
The second kind, the “bad” kind of inflation, closes nothing. A tariff is a tax, just like an oil shock is a tax. Somebody’s cost went up, and the money has to come out of a budget that did not grow. Every dollar of that price increase is a dollar not spent somewhere else. Bad inflation doesn’t create the income that pays for it, so it destroys the demand that supports it. Such is the mechanism behind the oldest saying in commodities: “high prices cure high prices.”
Think of it this way. A group of people drives the same way to work every day. Half get a raise, the other half doesn’t. The city decides to put a toll booth on the road they drive to work; each year, that toll rises. Both groups have an increasing number draining their bank accounts each month. However, only one group has sufficient compensation to continue using the toll road. The group without the compensation raise is eventually forced to stop using the toll road; traffic falls, and the operator cuts the toll to win them back.
What The September Print Actually Says
Let’s review the recent August data to see what the message, versus the narrative, actually is. The headline CPI came in at 3.7% year over year in September. Core came in at 2.6%, a tick higher than August. Read that pair again, because it is the whole argument. The gap between them widened from nine-tenths of a point to one and a tenth, meaning the headline accelerated roughly three times faster than the core.
That gap suggests a very different narrative than what the media suggests. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month alone and 34.2% over the year, and the BLS attributes over half the entire monthly increase in the all-items index to that one category. Energy overall is up 20.4%. Meanwhile, core goods, where a genuine demand boom would show up first and loudest, rose 0.7% over twelve months, sitting exactly where it was in August. Shelter ticked up to 3.2%
Now the part I owe you, because I set a test in advance. Core ticked up, shelter ticked up, and services’ less energy reached 3.1%, which would eventually prove me wrong. One month of tenths is noise rather than a trend. It is also the first month this year that those three moved the wrong way together, and core goods holding flat at 0.7% is why I am not moving yet, because that is where a demand boom announces itself first, and it has not.
Headline CPI pulled further away from core in September. The shaded area is the spread, and the spread is energy. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, September 2026.
I’ve been making this argument since June, when I wrote about why the May 4.2% headline was an oil story rather than a demand story. To wit:
“A 4.2% headline that is three-fifths gasoline is not the same animal as a 4.2% headline driven by wages, rents, and services broadening.”
Four months later, the composition has not changed. What has changed is that the evidence against the demand-pull story got considerably stronger.
Labor Just Set A 79-Year Low
The most important evidence comes from the labor market. If this were the “good” kind of inflation, workers would be capturing some of it. They are not.
Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the twelve months through September, more than double the August decline. Nominal wages rose 0.1% on the month against a 0.6% CPI print, so purchasing power went backward at the fastest pace of the year. Run the same calculation off average hourly earnings and CPI, and you land in the same place. Real wage growth is near -0.7%, down from over 1.5% as recently as last spring.
In April 2026, real wage growth crossed below zero and hit its weakest reading in September. The gold bars represent the months when wages grew faster than prices. The red bars are months when they didn’t. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, August 2026.
Then there is the one number that everyone simply overlooked. In the second quarter, labor’s share of nonfarm business output fell to 52.8%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics flagged that as the lowest level in a series that begins in the first quarter of 1947. Read that again. There have been 79 years of data, 2 dozen business cycles, 4 major wars, the Volcker shock, the China trade shock, and the pandemic. Despite all that, in what is supposed to be an economic boom, we just set a record low.
Here is what it looks like graphically. This is not what an inflationary boom looks like.
Labor’s share of output has been falling for a quarter century and just made a series low. Good inflation requires this line to rise. Source: BLS, Productivity and Costs, Q2 2026.
Stop and notice that in the chart above, this is not a 2026 event. The erosion in labor runs back to the early 2000s, long before “artificial intelligence” or “surging debt.” The last two years have simply accelerated the numbers. With respect to the inflation question, the timing matters most. A price level that is rising while labor’s slice of output hits an all-time low is the textbook signature of cost pass-through rather than demand-pull. In this environment, corporations are fixated on protecting profit margins, while workers are absorbing the difference.
The economic activity surveys tell the same story if you take the time to read past the headlines. The ISM services printed 54.9 in September, with new orders easing to 59.8. That reads like a demand boom until you see prices paid at 74.0, the highest since July 2022, while the employment index has not exceeded 50.1 in three months. Steady orders, hot input costs, flat payrolls. When respondents were asked what was driving those costs, fuel came up about twice as often as anything else.
Where The Inflation Bulls Have A Point
As always, we need to examine both sides of every argument, as the inflation bulls do have a valid point.
The strongest one is the AI buildout. Memory is genuinely scarce; its scarcity is genuinely caused by capital spending, and the producer price index for storage devices has climbed 23% since the end of 2024, while import prices for computers and parts are up 37%. J.P. Morgan’s research team puts the memory shock at 0.2% to 0.4% on core inflation. That is capex-driven price pressure; it is real, and it did not come from an embargo. However, that scarcity will eventually reverse. As with oil prices, high prices eventually curtail demand.
The second argument is that tariffs are a policy choice, not a weather event. That is a true statement, and a tariff regime that stays in place for years produces a price level that stays elevated for years. Calling that “transitory” is a semantic trick. I can’t argue with that. A permanent tax produces a permanent price. However, the current tariffs were not enacted by Congressional legislation, which would make them more permanent. In this case, they were enacted through executive order, which means the next Administration can repeal them quickly.
The third is that energy is not reliably mean-reverting on any schedule you can trade. Geopolitics doesn’t run on a calendar. However, high oil prices, as shown in the chart below, reliably mean-revert over time.
Those are all sound and valid arguments, but there is a problem with all three, though. Every one of them describes a SUPPLY constraint. A memory shortage is, by definition, a shortage. Call the tariff what it is: a tax. And the Middle East risk is a supply risk. None of them creates the income that pays the higher price. All three fail the same test: gasoline fails, and a more flattering story doesn’t change what the bill does to a household budget.
Why Bad Inflation Cures Itself
“Inflation is inflation. My grocery bill doesn’t care about the taxonomy.”
That is a fair statement. The pain from inflation is the same either way, and when you are staring at the number on the gas pump, the squeeze on household budgets happens regardless. Just because it happens to be the academically preferable kind, the household budget just doesn’t care. However, the taxonomy isn’t about how it feels, but how it ends, and bad inflation ends in a way the good kind never does.

articles.title: PBOC Deputy Governor Tao Ling: Three Major Measures to Smooth the International Circulation of the RMB - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: PBOC Deputy Governor Tao Ling: Three Major Measures to Smooth the International Circulation of the RMB  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
People's Bank of China (PBOC) Deputy Governor Tao Ling said on October 16 at the Global Wealth Management Forum - 2026 Shanghai Suhewan Conference that the RMB has yet to form a smooth international circulation—from being obtainable to being convenient to use to being held long-term. The PBOC will further optimize its measures to build an integrated chain of receiving RMB, using RMB, investing in RMB, and hedging RMB risks.
In her keynote speech, she disclosed the latest progress in RMB internationalization: on an all-inclusive basis, the RMB is now the world's third-largest payment currency; it ranks fifth in global foreign exchange trading and is the fastest-growing among major currencies; and over the past five years, the RMB has consistently ranked among the top three in global trade finance, with its share rising from around 2% to approximately 7%.
Tao Ling noted that the RMB becoming an international currency will provide a reliable new option for global trade and investment and financing activities. China's political, economic, and social stability over the long term, its position as the world's second-largest economy, its status as a major trading partner for more than 160 countries and regions, and the basic stability of the RMB exchange rate at a reasonably balanced level have all created favorable conditions for RMB internationalization.
Latest Data on International Use of the RMB
In the payments arena, a multi-channel, wide-coverage RMB cross-border payment and clearing network is taking shape. The Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), domestic and overseas fast payment systems, and QR code interoperability are all advancing steadily, while the digital RMB has also made positive progress.
In investment and financing, the willingness of overseas entities to raise RMB financing has clearly increased. Overseas entities can invest in onshore RMB assets through Bond Connect, Stock Connect, and qualified investor access mechanisms. RMB government bonds and central bank bills are now issued on a regular basis offshore, with outstanding dim sum bonds and panda bonds currently exceeding 2 trillion yuan (approximately $299 billion).
In foreign exchange trading, the range of participants in China's onshore interbank FX market continues to expand, with overseas central banks and monetary authorities, international financial organizations, sovereign wealth funds, and RMB clearing banks all eligible to participate.
In reserve currency terms, according to data released by the International Monetary Fund, as of the end of Q2 2026, both the scale and share of RMB foreign exchange reserves had risen, ranking seventh among major reserve currencies. The RMB's weight in the Special Drawing Rights (SDR) currency basket stands at 12.28%, behind only the US dollar and the euro.
As of the end of June 2026, a total of 1,200 overseas institutions had entered China's onshore interbank bond market, with overseas entities holding 3.2 trillion yuan (approximately $479 billion) in onshore bonds. The scale of RMB government bonds in the offshore market is also growing, and their application scenarios as eligible collateral continue to expand.
Three Major Measures to Build an Integrated Chain
In her speech, Tao Ling elaborated on three key policy measures to smooth the international circulation of the RMB.
The first measure is to provide RMB liquidity to the offshore market. She said that whether the offshore market has sufficient RMB is a prerequisite for overseas entities to obtain and use the currency. There are three main channels for supplying RMB liquidity: trade, direct investment, and financing. Since 2022, the PBOC, together with relevant departments, has improved a multi-tiered offshore RMB liquidity supply mechanism.
Going forward, the PBOC will continue to support financial institutions in conducting RMB overseas lending and cross-border trade finance, improve interbank cross-border RMB financing policies, encourage more overseas institutions to participate in the issuance and trading of panda bonds, and support Hong Kong in developing its RMB dim sum bond market. Building on the already-launched offshore RMB bond repo and cross-border repo businesses, the PBOC will continue to promote product innovation and mechanism improvement in the repo and derivatives markets. At the same time, it will support clearing banks in better fulfilling their role as liquidity providers in the offshore market, leverage currency swap mechanisms, and establish normalized swap fund usage arrangements with more eligible countries and regions.
The second measure is to broaden channels for RMB asset allocation. Tao Ling pointed out that once overseas entities obtain RMB liquidity, the question becomes how to move from being willing to hold it to actually holding onto it—rather than treating the RMB merely as a payment instrument and quickly converting it into other currencies after transactions. This requires investable RMB assets and market hedging tools that allow RMB funds to settle and stay.
To this end, the PBOC will support more types of overseas investors in participating in China's financial markets through appropriate means, investing in Chinese onshore stocks, equity, bonds, gold derivatives, and commodity futures. It will develop the RMB and foreign exchange markets, enrich trading products, and advance FX derivatives trading. It will increase the supply of RMB assets in the offshore market and promote RMB bonds as globally recognized eligible collateral. It will also strengthen the interconnection of domestic and overseas financial market trading platforms and financial infrastructure.
The third measure is to raise the level of capital account liberalization. Tao Ling particularly emphasized that capital account liberalization and capital account convertibility are not entirely the same thing. If a transaction uses only RMB, it does not involve currency conversion—only the cross-border movement of currency. Therefore, measuring the level of capital account liberalization requires considering not only currency convertibility but also the cross-border movement of currency. It requires considering not only foreign currencies but also the domestic currency. If currency conversion is restricted and cross-border movement is restricted, the willingness of various entities to obtain and hold RMB may diminish.
She said the PBOC will follow the requirements of the 15th Five-Year Plan and, together with the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) and other relevant departments, steadily enhance the convenience of cross-border fund conversion and cross-border fund movement, improve financial market opening channels, integrate and optimize institutional rules, support the development of the Shanghai International Financial Center, and consolidate and elevate the status of the Hong Kong International Financial Center.
The Diversification Trend of the International Monetary System
In her speech, Tao Ling reviewed the evolution of the international monetary system. She said that over hundreds of years, the international monetary system has been in constant evolution, and the dominant international currency has the attributes of a global public good. Changes in the dominant international currency reflect profound shifts in the global landscape. After World War II, an international monetary system centered on the US dollar, supplemented by other currencies, was formed.
She believes the current international monetary system is undergoing changes and may develop a more diversified configuration in the future. This will help push sovereign currency-issuing countries to strengthen policy discipline and enhance the resilience of the international monetary system.
On risk prevention, Tao Ling said that in advancing capital account liberalization, China will adhere to coordinating development and security, improve macroprudential management of cross-border capital flows, strengthen the risk prevention system commensurate with capital account liberalization, and foster a stable and sound monetary and financial environment.
She concluded by saying that advancing RMB internationalization is a task of great historical significance and contemporary value that must be pursued actively, prudently, step by step, and with sustained effort. She expressed hope for continued communication and cooperation with all parties to expand the high-level opening-up of China's financial sector and inject new positive energy into global economic and financial stability.

articles.title: Ailing Shilling forces BoU into emergency policy tightening amid $200m capital flight - Daily Monitor
articles.summary: Ailing Shilling forces BoU into emergency policy tightening amid $200m capital flight  Daily Monitor
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has returned to direct intervention in the foreign exchange market for the first time since June 2022, selling approximately $30 million (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday in an aggressive bid to arrest the local currency's slide past the psychological Shs4,000 threshold against the US dollar.
The direct market sale capped a dramatic week in which the central bank was forced to convene an emergency Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting and deliver its largest benchmark interest rate increase in 15 years.
In his weekly market assessment, Mr. Stephen Kaboyo, Partner at Alpha Capital and forex market analyst, noted that the local unit experienced significant volatility following BoU’s multi-pronged approach.
"Uganda Shilling experienced major shifts after the BoU stepped in with a hike in the benchmark rate following an emergency Monetary Policy meeting. In a multi-pronged approach, the Central Bank, in a surprise move, also intervened in the market, an action last seen in June 2022 by selling about 30 million dollars (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday. The move triggered a strong rebound, driving the shilling back below the 4000 threshold. However, in subsequent market sessions, the currency surrendered its short-lived gains," Mr. Kaboyo said.
Looking ahead, Mr. Kaboyo warned that market fundamentals remain fragile. "In the coming days, the outlook indicates that underlying pressures remain intact. The shilling will continue facing persistent downward market forces that will keep it on the back foot, with the primary driver being the substantial outstanding exposure of portfolio investors to the local bond market. The unpredictable nature of these flows will keep the unit on the edge," he added.
The central bank's intervention briefly halted eight consecutive sessions of losses after the currency hit a record low of Shs4,143 per dollar—its weakest level since 1993, making it the worst-performing currency among 144 tracked globally by Bloomberg this month. Data from LSEG showed the shilling temporarily gaining over 2 percent on the day following the action.
In an official statement detailing the outcomes of the special MPC meeting held on October 14, 2026, BoU Governor Dr. Michael Atingi-Ego announced a dramatic 225-basis-point increase in the Central Bank Rate (CBR), lifting it from 9.75 percent to 12.0 percent. The hike represents the largest monthly increase since October 2011 and elevates the benchmark rate to its highest level since December 2016, ending a two-year period of unchanged monetary policy. Additionally, the central bank raised the Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) for commercial banks from 11.0 percent to 13.5 percent, effective September 24.
The central bank linked the drastic tightening to heightened Middle East geopolitical conflicts, surging global energy prices, and tighter international financial conditions. These external headwinds expanded Uganda's current account deficit by $1.4 billion (Shs5.6 trillion) to a total of $4.6 billion (Shs18.4 trillion), while headline inflation accelerated to 4.6 percent in September up from 4.1 percent in August.
Adding to the liquidity strain, estimates from Citigroup reveal that over $200 million (Shs799.8 billion) exited Uganda's domestic market in just two weeks as offshore investors reallocated capital from local government bonds into higher-yielding US dollar assets.
Introduced in July 2011 at 13 percent under BoU's Inflation Targeting Lite framework, the CBR serves as a key signal for the cost of money and aims to anchor core inflation around 5 percent.
The policy rate reached a historic peak of 23 percent in November 2011 when inflation approached 30 percent, before gradually easing to 9.5 percent by October 2017. During the COVID-19 pandemic in June 2021, the rate hit an all-time low of 6.5 percent to stimulate economic activity. Prior to the latest decision, the rate was last raised during an emergency meeting in July 2022 to 8.5 percent and had remained steady at 9.75 percent since October 2024.
Financial experts and economists remain divided on whether monetary tightening is the effective remedy for current market conditions.
Mr. Uthman Mayanja, Country Senior Partner at PwC Uganda, explained that the central bank's primary objective is mitigating imported inflation pressures.
"The Bank of Uganda's decision is about controlling inflation. As the shilling weakens, imports such as fuel and machinery become more expensive. Eventually, this drives prices for consumer goods higher. The typical response is to raise interest rates to make saving more attractive and borrowing more expensive, thereby easing pressure on prices. In turn, higher interest rates strengthen local and international demand for Ugandan treasury bills and bonds, which should reduce pressure on the Shilling. In short, the Bank is tightening money supply today to contain inflation risks from a weaker shilling, while also making shilling-denominated investments more attractive," Mr. Mayanja noted.
Conversely, Dr. Fred Muhumuza, a senior economist at Makerere University, argued that hiking interest rates is an inadequate solution for external supply-side shocks.
"The central bank is trying to also tell people to think twice before you borrow," Dr. Muhumuza stated, pointing out that "BoU is emphasising the message of risk aversion, but to even tell them that this is not a risk, it is a reality…that is the space we are in." He maintained that raising domestic interest rates cannot resolve imported fuel price inflation or structural foreign exchange shortages.
Adding to these concerns, Dr. Susan Kavuma warned that commercial banks will rapidly transmit the higher central bank rate to end-user borrowing costs, severely dampening private sector credit growth. She highlighted that Uganda’s average lending rate of 17.3 percent recorded in July was already higher than neighboring regional peers like Kenya.
Similarly, Ms. Jane Nalunga, Country Director at SEATINI Uganda, cautioned that the ultimate economic burden will fall on vulnerable households and small businesses.
"BoU has raised the CBR by 225 basis points to respond to the record depreciation of the shilling, worsening BoP amid the mounting inflation pressure. It's important to note that this is a remarkable increase marking the end of the 2 years of unchanged rates," Ms. Nalunga said. "While the increase in the CBR intends to curb inflationary pressures and exchange rate depreciation, it comes at a cost."

articles.title: Chart of the day: 10-year Treasury yields hit reverse this week but the real test is still ahead - investingLive
articles.summary: Chart of the day: 10-year Treasury yields hit reverse this week but the real test is still ahead  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- A sharp reversal from 5.30% has put the 5.00% mark back in focus for the bond market
Seeing as to how the bond market is faring to end the week, you probably wouldn't have guessed that we actually got hotter-than-expected inflation data from both the US CPI and PPI reports in the past few days. In fact, you might even think it was the opposite. Yet, here we are.
10-year Treasury yields are down to 5.09%, poised for back-to-back weekly declines for the first time since June. That is certainly keeping things interesting with yields tumbling back to draw in the 5.00% mark again as broader market sentiment turns more cautious.
The rejection this week at 5.30% following the US CPI report stands out rather clearly, with yields failing to sustain a break higher before retreating sharply. And that now puts the spotlight back on the 5.00% level, which had previously played the role in keeping yields from breaking out back in September.
As such, it would require a firm daily close below 5.00% to deliver a stronger signal that the recent upward momentum is starting to unravel.
After which, that could open up a move towards 4.70%, where the 100-day moving average (red line) is also sticking nearby at 4.73%. Further below, the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 4.50% could come into consideration.
But for now, it's baby steps first. I wouldn't be too quick to call an end to the broader uptrend just yet.
10-year yields are still comfortably holding above the key 5.00% threshold in the past few sessions. And any semblance of a rebound back towards 5.20% or even 5.30% again would put the recent rejection back to the test.
And from a fundamental standpoint, nothing much has really changed. Inflation pressures are still holding up and the same structural factors underpinning yields since last month are also still very much in place. Heavy Treasury issuance and concerns about the long-term trajectory of US debt are key reasons why investors are demanding more compensation to hold longer-dated government bonds.
But at least for the time being, all eyes are turning back to the 5.00% mark as the line in the sand. Hold above and we're still talking about the upward pressure in yields being sustained for the most part. But break below, and this could turn the sharp pullback this week into something more meaningful perhaps.

articles.title: Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia - Business Standard
articles.summary: Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia  Business Standard
articles.full_text:
Home / Markets / News / Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia
Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia
Indonesian stocks suffered a massive 11 per cent decline on Friday after MSCI threatened its "emerging market status", which could prompt massive foreign selloff from the Southeast Asian economy.
MSCI’s proposed downgrade of Indonesia is less about immediate passive outflows and more about the long-term cost of losing benchmark inclusion, according to analysts. Indonesian stocks suffered a massive 11 per cent decline on Friday after MSCI threatened its "emerging market status", which could prompt massive foreign sell-off from the Southeast Asian economy. According to a Reuters report, Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite plunged as much as 11.4 per cent to its lowest point since early November 2020, clocking its worst one-day drop since January 1998. Earlier in the day, the benchmark opened 8 per cent lower, which triggered a 30-minute trading halt. MSCI reported that market participants had raised significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behaviour. The index aggregator is considering moving Indonesia from Emerging Market to Standalone status, with feedback until April 30, 2027 and a decision by June 30, 2027.
What does it mean for Indonesia?
Indonesia's weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets index fell from 1.16 per cent at the end of 2025 to 0.43 per cent by September 30, and its constituents fell from 18 to 9, as MSCI froze additions and deleted names flagged under Jakarta's own concentrated-holding framework, Harshal Dasani, business head at INVasset PMS, said. At 0.43 per cent, he said, that forced passive selling runs to a few billion dollars, which is less than the market lost in Friday's session. For the year, the index is down 39 per cent, making it one of the worst-performing emerging markets this year.
Justin Khoo of VT Markets said that forced selling by index-tracking funds, potentially accelerating foreign outflows, weakening the rupiah, and tightening domestic financial conditions are the immediate concerns for the market. "An 11% plunge alone is unlikely to destabilize Indonesia's financial system. However, with the country's stock market already down nearly 40% this year, sustained foreign capital outflows could weaken market liquidity, discourage investment and further erode investor confidence," he added. Standalone status, according to Dasani, is the index equivalent of delisting from global portfolios. This would make foreign ownership a discretionary hedge-fund decision rather than an allocation, and the cost of equity rises for years. He observed that Argentina went standalone in 2021 over capital controls and is still there.
Limited global spillover
Despite being Southeast Asia's largest economy, Indonesia is a small part of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, suggesting limited direct global spillover. Other ASEAN markets may benefit from portfolio reallocations, although broader regional sentiment remains vulnerable, he noted. articles.title: BAE Systems cyberattack disrupts US federal court operations - BleepingComputer
articles.summary: BAE Systems cyberattack disrupts US federal court operations  BleepingComputerCyber Incident Halts Bankruptcy Notices Nationwide  WSJUS federal bankruptcy court operations disrupted by cybersecurity incident  ReutersCyber Incident at BAE Systems Disrupts US Federal Bankruptcy Noticing  Infosecurity MagazineAttack on BAE-managed system disrupts US bankruptcy courts  The Register
articles.full_text:
The Administrative Office of the US Courts (AOUSC) says a cyberattack on government contractor BAE Systems has taken down the notice system used by federal bankruptcy courts.
In a Thursday press release, the Administrative Office of the US Courts said the BAE Systems cyberattack also halted the production and distribution of bankruptcy notices.
"The Administrative Office of the US Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems. BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations," AOUSC said.
"As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the Judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service."
BAE Systems is Europe's largest defense contractor, designing and manufacturing military technology for the UK and US defense departments, and a major provider of enterprise IT, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity services to military, intelligence, and civilian government agencies worldwide.
"We are aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it. We are coordinating closely with AOUSC on the response," a BAE Systems spokesperson told BleepingComputer.
An AOUSC spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer contacted them earlier today for more details on the attack.
The US Federal Judiciary, the independent judicial branch of the US federal government, also said last year that it was strengthening cybersecurity defenses after a cyberattack impacted its electronic case management systems.
The federal Judiciary added that while most documents in the system are public, it now protects certain sealed filings containing sensitive information with stricter access controls designed to block attackers.
"The federal Judiciary is taking additional steps to strengthen protections for sensitive case documents in response to recent escalated cyberattacks of a sophisticated and persistent nature on its case management system," it said.
While the agency stopped short of confirming a breach of confidential documents, a Politico report said at the time that hackers had breached CM/ECF electronic case management systems and the PACER federal court document management platform, gaining access to sensitive data (including the identities of confidential informants).

articles.title: FX Daily: Inflation vs. AI overbuild story dominates - ing think
articles.summary: FX Daily: Inflation vs. AI overbuild story dominates  ing think
articles.full_text:
Financial markets have calmed a little after Coreweave stock bounced on Thursday. But the debate between intensifying price pressures needing tighter monetary policy and a tech correction requiring a softer policy outlook continues. Expect more consolidation in FX markets today and more interest in local stories, such as Indonesia's equity travails
USD: What does the flatter yield curve mean?
The sell-off on Coreweave assets saw a modest reversal yesterday after Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, said that Coreweave's financial strength was improving and its cost of capital was declining. Perhaps those comments should not be surprising from a major shareholder in Coreweave; let's see how long this bounce in Coreweave assets lasts. The big takeaway this week has been the recovery of the long-end of the US Treasury market, even as inflation data continues to come in hot. Here it seems that investors are starting to find value in long-dated Treasuries and are viewing those as a middling hedge against a correction in the AI trade. Were the tech sell-off to gain momentum, that Treasury buying would move to the shorter end of the curve.
While fears of an AI correction may be growing, inflation data continues to come in hot. Yesterday it was US September PPI data blowing away consensus. And today, import prices should come in near 8% year-on-year, the highest since summer 2022. Inflation data is keeping short-dated interest rates supported and has delivered a near 20bp flattening in the 2-10 year Treasury curve this week.
What does that mean for FX? Typically, an environment where the Fed is applying the brakes while growth prospects are being revised down is good for the dollar against activity and emerging market currencies. It is only when short end rates break lower that the dollar is ready to drop. And we are not there yet.
Barring another big leg down in AI stocks and risk assets in general, expect the dollar to consolidate near recent highs. We would continue to expect some defensive outperformance of the Swiss franc in this environment. DXY will probably struggle to get above the 102.40/50 area now, while support is 101.75/80.
Chris Turner
EUR: Inflation to be confirmed at 3.8% today
Today's eurozone data should see September CPI confirmed at 3.8% – well above the European Central Bank's 2% target. Markets are still reeling from the hawkish set of inflation forecasts delivered at the ECB September press conference, a key driver of the near 75bp of further tightening expected from the ECB. Our team looks for just one more hike, however, and developments in French bond markets will have a big say in whether the ECB needs to tighten much more from there.
EUR/USD has received a lift from this week's unease in US AI stocks and may be entering a decent consolidative phase now. This could be worth a move all the way to 1.1340/50. But do not expect EUR/USD to be the big outperformer on a further US equity correction. We think a lower USD/CHF would take the lead there.
Chris Turner
CEE: Wage embers and price sparks
The CEE week ends with mostly second-tier data. Hungary releases August wage figures this morning, one of the central bank’s remaining domestic obstacles to achieving stable inflation. We forecast wage growth of 7.1%, still well above CEE peers, while the agreed minimum wage increase raises the risk of renewed wage pressures next year.
Later, the Czech Republic publishes September producer prices. Alongside agricultural prices, these suggest inflationary pressures are broadening beyond fuel costs, posing an upside risk to the CPI outlook, as discussed in our CEE report earlier this week. Turkey will also release September inflation expectations, the final relevant data point before next week’s central bank meeting. We expect the Central Bank of Turkey to resume its easing cycle, which was paused after the US-Iran conflict began, by cutting the policy rate from 37.0% to 36.0%.
CEE fixed income saw a strong rally yesterday, tracking core markets despite negative global sentiment; Hungary and Romania have outperformed the rest of the region over the past two days. We maintain the view that the koruna and zloty yield curves cannot decouple from the global narrative, and that higher energy prices will keep rate hikes priced in for longer. The Hungarian curve will face a test next Monday or Tuesday with the release of the draft budget for next year – an event drawing significant market attention, though expectations may be overly optimistic. FX, on the other hand, remains more or less stable, and we continue to hold our bearish views for the CEE region in general.
Frantisek Taborsky
IDR: MSCI downgrade warning sinks local assets
In a statement that will have been a difficult read for Indonesian authorities, MSCI said overnight that it was launching a consultation to reclassify MSCI Indonesia indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status. Merely dropping Indonesia to Frontier Markets would not properly recognise the depth of the market problems, says MSCI. These problems are opaque shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behaviour, according to MSCI.
Local equity indices fell 10-11% on the announcement and an already weak rupiah gapped above the 18000 threshold. Expect more FX intervention from Bank Indonesia to protect this year's high at 18200 – but clearly pressure for a weaker rupiah is building. Please see ING's Deepali Bhargava's latest comments on USD/IDR here.
Indonesia's problems serve as a reminder that EMFX will increasingly be driven by local stories over the coming quarters. How the AI trade fares will dominate Korea and Taiwan, Brazilian assets could be re-rated further on a Bolsonaro presidency, and Hungary's euro ambitions will have a major say on local asset markets. Please see our latest thinking on this topic in October's edition of FX Talking.
Chris Turner

articles.summary: Euro-Dollar Bounces Back, But Upside Limited Warns KBC  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Image © Adobe Images
A drop in US bond yields has lifted the single currency off its lows, and analysts at a Belgian bank see limited room for further gains while French risks linger.
The euro has recovered above 1.12 against the dollar as US Treasury yields fell, though analysts at KBC Bank see the rebound running short of fuel.
US yields drive the pair: higher US yields pull capital into dollar assets, and their fall since Wednesday's inflation surprise removes the force that took the euro to a 17-month low of 1.1113.
"The sharper US yield drop weighed on the dollar. EUR/USD recovered to north of 1.12 with minor follow-up gains this morning. We see little further upside potential for the common currency with the French theme slumbering in the background," says KBC Bank's morning note.
The ten-year Treasury yield has eased to around 5.09% from 5.33% after the CPI release, as haven demand from a sell-off in technology stocks flowed into US bonds.
The Euro to Dollar rate trades at 1.1234 today, 0.5% below its 21-day moving average at 1.1293:
Above: EUR/USD at daily intervals with the 21-day moving average and RSI.
UniCredit's FX strategist Roberto Mialich says the euro has room to breathe if US yields retreat towards 5.00%, with French public finances the barrier to anything more.
"Re-approaching or even exceeding 1.14 has probably become a difficult task at this point," he says.
The euro's own rate support also looks stretched, with markets pricing three more European Central Bank hikes against Commonwealth Bank of Australia's call for one final move in December.
"Despite its latest consolidation, the EUR should remain vulnerable to any potential return of sovereign credit risks," says Credit Agricole in its weekly FX outlook.
The Fed Offers No Push
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gave no guidance on the 28 October policy meeting at an IMF event on Friday, and markets now see an 85% chance of no change.
"We're not in that business anymore," Warsh said of forward guidance.
Credit Agricole's analysts argue the dollar's rate advantage has stopped growing, and its positioning model is long EUR/USD with a target of 1.1651.
"We doubt that the USD would benefit significantly from further improvement of its relative rate advantage over the rest of G10," says Credit Agricole.
The bank's fundamental call is more cautious, with EUR/USD forecast at 1.13 in three months.
The Levels
KBC sees sterling extending gains against the euro, with a weekly close below 0.8455 in EUR/GBP an important technical signal, equivalent to GBP/EUR above 1.1827.
UOB's technical analysts expect EUR/USD to range-trade between 1.1160 and 1.1280 over the coming one to three weeks.
The 1.1280 ceiling sits just below the 21-day average at 1.1293, so the bounce has nearly closed the gap PSL's modelling flagged at the lows.
A daily close above 1.1293 would test KBC's call; until then, the range floor at 1.1160 is the next stop.

articles.title: Felix Nikolas Prehn on mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury yield - investingLive
articles.summary: Felix Nikolas Prehn on mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury yield  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- The average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.40 per cent in the week of 8 October, Freddie Mac data show, up from 6.76 per cent on 10 September. Over the same stretch, the 10-year Treasury yield climbed too.
Felix Nikolas Prehn is an economist and former investment banker whose research examines money, asset prices and US households from 2000 to 2026. A buyer who opens a mortgage quote is looking at the last link in a chain that starts in the bond market.
The starting point for a mortgage rate
A St. Louis Fed explainer on mortgage rates names the 10-year Treasury note as the benchmark for the 30-year mortgage. Treasury securities count as very low risk because the US government backs them, so investors use their yields as the yardstick for other long-term investments.
The choice of a 10-year note for a 30-year loan comes down to how long people keep their mortgages. Many are written for 30 years, but most are paid off, refinanced or ended by the sale of the home well before then. The average life of a mortgage is much closer to 10 years.
Some banks bundle thousands of mortgages into securities and sell them to investors, who receive the principal and interest homeowners pay. Those investors compare the return on mortgage-backed securities with the return on the 10-year note. The two respond to the same signals, such as data on inflation and economic growth, and their yields often move in the same direction.
The securities are riskier than Treasuries, so investors demand a higher yield for taking that risk. The explainer calls the market value of that extra risk, plus the added costs of a mortgage (origination expenses, servicing fees and lender profit), the mortgage spread. The mortgage rate is roughly the Treasury yield plus that spread.
Movement of the two lines
Freddie Mac's weekly survey records the average rate lenders quoted on 30-year fixed loans. The Treasury Department publishes the 10-year yield each business day. Treasury data put the 10-year yield at 4.95 per cent on 10 September and 5.22 per cent on 8 October, so both lines rose over the four weeks.
Between those dates the survey logged 6.95 per cent, 7.03 per cent and 7.28 per cent in the weeks of 17 September, 24 September and 1 October. The mortgage rate did not jump in one step. It climbed week by week.
Five years earlier, the survey for 7 October 2021, showed an average 30-year rate of 2.99 per cent, and the 10-year yield that day was 1.58 per cent.
For the week of 8 October 2026, the same two readings were 7.40 per cent and 5.22 per cent.
Those are single dated readings, not a full history. The survey is an average of quotes and reflects what lenders offered that week, so an individual borrower's quote, or a rate locked earlier or later, can differ from the published figure.
The change for a buyer
A buyer who shopped for a typical 30-year loan in October 2021 faced a survey average of 2.99 per cent. A buyer who closes now meets a survey average near 7.40 per cent for the same 30 years.
A fixed-rate loan keeps the rate it was signed at for the whole term, so the higher rate reaches only the people who sign now. Owners with a 2021 loan keep paying the old rate.
The loan amount does not have to change for the monthly bill to change. Because mortgage and Treasury yields often move together, a buyer who shops in September and closes in October can see a different quote on the same house.
The same shift appears from another side for anyone saving a deposit rather than already holding a mortgage. The savings goal is attached to a loan whose rate has moved. The monthly payment depends on the mortgage rate in force at the point of signing, not only on the price of the house.
Prehn's paper on housing
The paper does not analyse how lenders price mortgages, but it examines the part of the chain that runs from interest rates to housing. Its text, available on Zenodo as a preprint since 25 September 2026, free to read and reuse with credit, describes a discount-rate channel: when the expected path for interest rates falls, long-lived assets such as housing become worth more today.
A second channel runs through credit. The paper states higher asset prices raise the borrowing capacity of people who already own assets, which finances further purchases.
Rents are where that shows up for people who do not own. The paper states housing costs feed into rents slowly, so owners have already gained by the time renters see the change.
Housing is also where the paper locates the bottom half's debt. It states that 68 per cent of that group's assets are a home or consumer durables, and that the group owes $3.2 trillion in mortgages.
About Felix Nikolas Prehn
Felix Nikolas Prehn, also known as Nikolas Prehn, is an economist and former investment banker, born in Germany. He is a tech founder: he co-founded TradeVision.io (Acetrader Inc), founded Winston Daily and The Prehn Institute, and publishes weekly on YouTube. He is also a painter and sculptor and a public advocate for animal rescue.
About The Prehn Institute
The Prehn Institute is an independent research institution founded by Felix Nikolas Prehn. He is a tech founder: he co-founded TradeVision.io (Acetrader Inc), founded Winston Daily and The Prehn Institute, and publishes weekly on YouTube. It publishes research on the financial markets and provides instruction in professional market practice.

articles.title: US Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offers no signal on October interest rate decision - CNBC TV18
articles.summary: US Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offers no signal on October interest rate decision  CNBC TV18
articles.full_text:
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the central bank's next move ahead of the October rate decision, stating he does not believe in pre-judging Fed meetings while addressing global economic conditions and AI during an IMF event.
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the country's central bank's next move that would be taken later this month.
He was speaking during a Fireside Chat with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok on Friday October 16.
Also Read: Hassett says Fed can curb inflation without hurting US economy
"I don't believe in pre-judging Fed meetings....""At the Fed, we made clear that we would deliver price stability"Kevin Warsh
Also Read: US inflation rises to 3.7% as gasoline prices surge, putting Fed rate outlook in focus
His comments came days before policymakers decide whether to raise interest rates again. He spoke as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings.
Warsh said the world had behaved as the Fed expected since its September meeting. "Since the September FOMC meeting, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," he said.
He added that rising prices were a global issue, not just a problem for the United States. Warsh said that most countries had tightened monetary policy around the same time, meaning no country could avoid the effects.
Describing an "investment surge" as the most important upside development in the global economy, crediting good policies, he said that "Right now, we have structural growth, an investment surge."
Warsh on Artificial Intelligence
Warsh warned that artificial intelligence (AI) would reshape demand first. "AI is going to hit the demand side of the economy before the supply shock," he said.
He expected the technology to make the economy more productive and create more wealth, but said the path would be bumpy and the near-term impact on jobs remained uncertain.
The US Fed will hold a field hearing on AI in the San Francisco Bay Area, a month later on November 16.
Warsh's Comments Build On Last Month's Fed Rate Hike
The US Federal Reserve had last month raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% which marked its first increase since 2023.
Two weeks ago, senior officials who advised Warsh signalled the bank was in no hurry to raise rates again, and bets on an October rise tumbled according to a CNBC report.
September inflation data, however, came in firmer than expected. Core consumer prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.33%, the second straight firm monthly reading.
The Fed's communication blackout began on Friday, and its next meeting runs on October 27 and 28, less than a week before the the country's midterm elections.

articles.title: Fed Chairman: We will ensure price stability. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Fed Chairman: We will ensure price stability.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - Kevin Warsh offered no comments on monetary policy or forecasts for the US economy, except to reiterate that the Federal Reserve will bring about price stability.
On the morning of October 16th, local time, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok, Thailand , all attention was focused on the conversation between Kevin Warsh, Chairman of the US Federal Reserve (Fed), and Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Global financial circles awaited a clear message about the direction of capital flows ahead of the Fed's executive meeting on October 27-28. However, the response was a decisive stance from the head of the US central bank. According to Reuters, Mr. Warsh stated that he would not make any pre-determined decisions for the upcoming meeting, while remaining silent on the possibility of further interest rate increases or a pause, as generally expected by investors.
"We have made it very clear that we will ensure price stability, and about a month ago we partially scaled back our easing," the Fed chairman said. "I am not predicting the outcome of the Fed meetings. I don't believe in making statements right now about what I can do at the remaining meetings this year," he emphasized.
Investors have scaled back their bets on the possibility of an interest rate hike at the US central bank's policy meeting on October 27-28.
You may also like
This probability, which had hovered around 27% before Mr. Warsh's statement, fell below 15% after his comments.
Stocks continued to rise while the dollar edged lower; S&P 500 index futures erased earlier losses of up to 0.6% to turn around and gain 0.2%.
"It's clear he won't be offering anything that the market can pick up on and consider hawkish – a term referring to a stance advocating for monetary tightening/raising interest rates to curb inflation," Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a report to clients.
The Fed raised interest rates by 0.25 percentage points in September, the first increase since 2023. This decision was supported by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also believe another increase is likely this year. In recent weeks, several key officials have reiterated that further rate hikes may be needed, but stressed they still have time to gather economic data before taking further action. Mr. Warsh once again expressed optimism about artificial intelligence (AI), calling it the most important invention of the global economy. But he also cautioned that AI may be driving demand in the short term.
The Fed chairman said that, as a central bank regulator, he views this new technology seriously, but also "with prudence and responsibility."
"Clearly, it's impacting the demand side of the economy before it impacts the supply side. If you're running a central bank, your job is to try to ensure price stability and full employment, so you have to see this as a shock," Warsh said.
You may also like
The Fed chairman argued that while this is a positive supply shock in the medium term, it is currently driving up aggregate demand and its impact on employment remains unclear. Some of Warsh's colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the wave of investment fueling AI infrastructure could cause the economy to overheat.
According to the plan shared by Mr. Warsh at the event, the Fed will hold a thematic hearing on artificial intelligence in San Francisco on November 16th. Specialized working groups are also working diligently to prepare new analytical facilities to best serve the Federal Open Market Committee's policy-making meetings.
Following Mr. Warsh's remarks, all eyes in the international business world are now focused on the Fed's agenda at the end of October, where decisions on the cost of capital will be determined based on finalized data at the last minute.

These changes create opportunities for suppliers that can qualify ultra-thin foil and serve battery and electronics manufacturers reliably.
KEY MARKET TAKEAWAYS

INDUSTRY SHIFTS & MARKET DYNAMICS
Electric vehicle and energy storage expansion is increasing demand for battery-grade copper foil, particularly for anode current collectors. Global lithium-ion battery copper foil shipments reached 1.302 million tonnes in 2025, increasing 41.7% from 2024, while China supplied 82.9% of the total.
The 6-micron grade remained the mainstream product, accounting for more than 70% of shipments, while 5-micron and 4.5-micron grades together reached a 24% share. These developments highlight the growing importance of thinner foil as battery manufacturers pursue higher energy density and lower copper consumption per cell.
However, volatile copper prices, high production costs for ultra-thin grades, and trade measures can complicate purchasing decisions. The United States introduced a 50% Section 232 tariff on semi-finished copper products and copper-intensive derivatives effective August 1, 2025.
Meanwhile, China's dominant position in battery-grade foil shipments is encouraging buyers to evaluate alternative supply sources. Consequently, manufacturers with qualified thin-foil production, consistent quality, and diversified supply networks may find opportunities as battery and PCB capacity expands across major markets.

articles.full_text:
The Pound-Euro could strengthen if Andrew Bailey reinforces November hike expectations, while lingering French debt concerns may keep the Euro vulnerable.
The Pound to Euro (GBP/EUR) exchange rate traded sideways on Thursday, with the single currency able to stem its recent selloff, amid a correction in the US Dollar (USD).
At the time of writing, the GBP/EUR exchange rate was trading at around €1.1817. Virtually unchanged from the start of Thursday's session.
DAILY RECAP:
The Euro (EUR) stabilised on Thursday as a pullback in the US Dollar (USD) offered the single currency some temporary relief from concerns over France's ongoing debt crisis.
USD exchange rates slid through the start of the European session amid an ongoing correction following Wednesday's stronger-than-expected US inflation figures, with the US currency getting caught up in the wider selloff in AI tech stocks.
However, the Euro's upside potential was limited as France's fiscal challenges remained a key source of concern for EUR investors, with markets extremely doubtful the government will succeed in pushing its 2027 budget through parliament amid considerable opposition to the proposed spending cuts.
While stuck in a narrow range against the Euro, the Pound (GBP) pushed higher against most of its other peers on Thursday, following the publication of the UK's latest GDP data.
August's month-on-month growth figures saw the UK record a modest 0.1% expansion, down from 0.4% in July, but beating forecasts for a 0.1% contraction.
The surprising resilience of the UK economy was encouraging for GBP investors, as it raised the odds of the Bank of England (BoE) delivering an interest rate hike at its November policy meeting to over 90%, while also relieving some of the pressure on Chancellor John Healey as he prepares to deliver his Autumn budget later in the month.
Near-Term GBP/EUR Forecast: Hawkish BoE Bailey Remarks to Strengthen Sterling?
Turning to the end of the week, markets will look to a speech by BoE Governor Andrew Bailey for fresh impetus in the Pound Euro exchange rate.
Sterling sentiment may strengthen if Bailey is more explicit in signalling that the bank is about to enter a new tightening cycle, particularly if his comments boost bets for further hikes past next month.
Meanwhile, the Eurozone's finalised CPI figures for September are expected to confirm that inflation in the bloc accelerated to a dizzying 3.8%, but they may have little impact on the Euro as the European Central Bank (ECB) remains cautious regarding further tightening.

articles.title: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening - CNBC
articles.summary: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening  CNBC
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a “synchronous tightening” by central banks around the world.
“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. “It’s a new chapter at the Fed [and] we’re not in that business anymore,” he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
“Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh’s comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October,” Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. “We continue to expect a second and final hike in December.”
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was “a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world,” which means “there’s no free riders.”
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world’s GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF’s warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won’t work as something that needs to be taken “with a grain of salt.”
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be “very bumpy,” and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
“I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose,” Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and “say this was hugely consequential.”
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

Open Free Demat Account
Mumbai, 16 October 2026: US equities closed higher on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields and easing pressure on heavily indebted artificial intelligence infrastructure companies helped major indices recover from steep early-session losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to close at 52,177.69, the S&P 500 added 25.12 points, or 0.33%, to end at 7,744.06, and the Nasdaq Composite edged up 20.16 points, or 0.08%, to settle at 26,713.03.
Broader market performance reflected a pronounced rotation out of semiconductor and AI-linked shares into defensive sectors including healthcare, consumer staples and financials, with movements across bond and commodity markets also shaping the session’s direction.
Dow Jones Gains 556 Points as Rate Fears Ease, Defensive Rotation Lifts Blue Chips
The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened at 51,858.06 and closed at 52,177.69, gaining 556.21 points or 1.08%. The index touched an intraday high of 52,250.18 and a low of 51,681.37. Movements in key constituents drove the index’s advance, with Nike (NKE) rising 1.11% and Coca-Cola (KO) adding 2.27%, while Chevron (CVX) climbed 3.12% and Walmart (WMT) gained 2.22%. Home Depot (HD) surged 3.39% and McDonald’s (MCD) advanced 2.61%.
On the losing side, Nvidia (NVDA) fell 2.94%, Caterpillar (CAT) dropped 2.17%, and Amazon (AMZN) declined 2.25%. The session followed a global sell-off in semiconductor shares that sent South Korea’s Kospi index down more than 7% overnight, before US equities recovered as bond yields retreated and defensive names attracted buying interest.
S&P 500 Rises 0.33% as Falling Yields Support Broader Market Gains Today
The S&P 500 opened at 7,687.31 and ended at 7,744.06, gaining 25.12 points or 0.33%. During the session, the index reached 7,754.15 at its high and 7,669.66 at its low. Movements across healthcare, consumer staples and energy sectors influenced the broader benchmark, while individual constituents including Accenture (ACN) which rose 5.96%, and Marathon Petroleum (MPC) which gained 4.77%, recorded notable changes.
Phillips 66 (PSX) advanced 4.65%, while Corning (GLW) declined 6.38% and Oracle (ORCL) dropped 5.48%. The index’s closing performance came as hotter-than-expected wholesale inflation data was offset by a safe-haven flow into Treasuries that pushed the 10-year yield down to 5.086%, its lowest level since September 22.
Nasdaq Gains 0.08% as Technology Shares Rebound, Driving Stronger Closing Market Gains
The Nasdaq Composite opened at 26,380.77 and closed at 26,713.03, marking a gain of 20.16 points or 0.08%. Its intraday high stood at 26,754.02, while the low was 26,308.85.
Technology and growth-oriented shares including Adobe (ADBE) which rose 3.56%, and Intuit (INTU) which gained 2.71%, contributed positively to the index’s daily performance, while Broadcom (AVGO) fell 4.35%, Micron (MU) dropped 4.79%, and Arm Holdings (ARM) declined 6.48%. Netflix (NFLX) added 2.68% and PepsiCo (PEP) advanced 3.73%.
The technology-heavy benchmark responded to a sharp retreat in Treasury yields and easing concerns over AI-related debt financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang expressed optimism about data centre operator CoreWeave’s prospects, helping the stock reverse a 15% rout from the previous session and close 5.94% higher.

Russell 2000 Gains 1.4% as Smaller Stocks Advance Amid Falling Treasury Yields
The Russell 2000 opened at 2,730.45 and closed at 2,767.27, gaining 37.74 points or 1.4%. It recorded an intraday high of 2,768.02 and a low of 2,725.06. Movements among smaller-cap companies contributed to the benchmark’s performance as declining Treasury yields and a rotation away from large-cap technology shares influenced broader trading.
Notable gainers within the index included Haemonetics (HAE), which rose 17.46%, Veradermics (MANE), which advanced 14.13%, and Erasca (ERAS), which gained 9.49%. On the losing side, Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) fell 13.58%, MaxLinear (MXL) dropped 12.72%, and Hut 8 (HUT) declined 10.87%.
S&P 100 Moves 0.14% as Large-Cap Shares Track Yields and Defensive Rotation
The S&P 100 opened at 3,849.76 and finished at 3,855.14, recording a gain of 5.38 points or 0.14%. The index traded between 3,855.14 and its intraday low during the session. Movements in major large-cap constituents, including Apple (AAPL), which rose 1.11%, and IBM (IBM), which gained 2.77%, contributed to its daily performance as markets responded to the drop in long-dated Treasury yields and a shift toward value-oriented sectors. Salesforce (CRM) added 1.44% and Verizon (VZ) advanced 1.27%. Conversely, Microsoft (MSFT) fell 1.35%, and Intel (INTC) dropped 5.34%.
Dow Composite, Transport and Utility Indices Reflect Broad Market Recovery Trend
The Dow Jones Composite Average opened at 16,212.65 and closed at 16,320.20, gaining 169.34 points or 1.05%, after moving between a high of 16,327.99 and a low of 16,171.06. The Dow Jones Transportation Average ended at 20,106.68, compared with an opening level of 19,835.45, representing a 1.40% move. The Dow Jones Utility Average closed at 1,107.66, changing 0.08% from its opening level of 1,108.17, having traded between 1,105.97 and 1,116.88 during the session. Movements in relevant constituents reflected the broad recovery in equity markets as bond yields declined and investors rotated into sectors beyond technology.
Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Falls 0.88% as Chip Stocks Extend Global Sell-Off
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) opened at 11,280.89 and closed at 11,581.22, losing 103.17 points or 0.88%. Its intraday high was 11,620.14, while the low was 11,171.53. Semiconductor-related constituents, including Intel (INTC), which fell 5.34%, Micron (MU), which dropped 4.79%, and Broadcom (AVGO), which declined 4.35%, contributed to the sector benchmark’s daily performance amid a global chip rout that saw South Korea’s Kospi index plunge more than 7% overnight. The SOX index recorded its eighth consecutive session of declines, the longest such streak since October 2008.

NYSE Composite Changes 0.84% as Broader Shares Track Yields and Sector Rotation
The NYSE Composite Index opened at 23,941.05 and closed at 24,066.65, recording a gain of 201.22 points or 0.84%. The index traded between 24,085.19 and 23,874.01 during the session. Movements across industrial, healthcare and consumer-oriented segments contributed to its performance as declining Treasury yields and a pronounced rotation away from technology shares shaped broader US equity trading.
The advance followed the previous session’s decline and reflected the recovery in market breadth that saw more than half of S&P 500 constituents trading above their 200-day moving averages, an improvement from less than 40% at the end of September.
S&P MidCap 400 and SmallCap 600 Move 1.03% as Yield Decline Shapes Trading
The S&P MidCap 400 opened at 3,610.15 and closed at 3,648.40, moving 37.15 points or 1.03%, with an intraday range of 3,649.43 to 3,593.55. The S&P SmallCap 600 opened at 1,647.75 and ended at 1,668.92, gaining 21.92 points or 1.33%, after trading between 1,669.45 and 1,646.76. The two benchmarks reflected movements among mid- and small-cap shares as the sharp decline in Treasury yields and a broad rotation into defensive sectors affected the wider market, with homebuilder stocks rallying notably as Lennar gained over 5%.
Producer Prices Surge 6.3% and AI Debt Fears Drive the Session’s Market Direction
The principal market catalyst was the release of September’s Producer Price Index, which rose 1.3% month-on-month and 6.3% year-on-year, marking the largest annual advance since December 2022 and exceeding expectations of 5.5%. Core PPI, excluding food and energy, rose 5.0% year-on-year, also surpassing forecasts of 4.4%. Treasury yields fell sharply despite the hotter inflation reading, with the 10-year yield declining 10.2 basis points to 5.086% and the 30-year yield dropping to 5.43%, as a global sell-off in semiconductor shares drove safe-haven flows into government bonds.
Concerns over the financing models employed to fund the AI infrastructure buildout also shaped the session. The stock reversed an early decline of more than 9% to close 5.94% higher after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated that CoreWeave’s cost of capital was decreasing and expressed optimism about the company’s prospects.

The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) changed 2.43% to 16.46, compared with its previous close of 16.87. The index, which measures expected volatility in the S&P 500 over the coming 30 days, had earlier touched a two-week high of 17.56 before retreating as equities recovered from session lows.
Its movement during the session coincided with the sharp decline in Treasury yields and the rebound in AI-related shares from early losses, which reduced demand for downside protection. articles.title: Fed’s Mary Daly: Rates may rise, but not in a hurry - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Fed’s Mary Daly: Rates may rise, but not in a hurry  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON - The US Federal Reserve (Fed) may need to raise short-term interest rates again to bring persistently high inflation under control.
However, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Mary C. Daly stressed that there was no immediate need to make such a decision at the monetary policy meeting on 27-28 October 2026.
In an exclusive interview with Reuters on Wednesday (14 October), Daly said a further interest rate increase was more likely to be necessary than not.
Nevertheless, the timing of any move remained under consideration by policymakers, according to Reuters.
Daly said the Fed still had time to assess economic developments and did not need to rush into a decision based on limited data.
Several other Fed officials have also indicated in recent weeks that the central bank was unlikely to raise interest rates in October. The Fed's benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%-4%.
Meanwhile, long-term borrowing costs remain relatively high.
Mortgage rates, for example, have reached around 7.5%, weighing on demand in several sectors of the economy.
Daly said financial market participants understood how the Fed responds to developments in inflation.
This was reflected in changing investor expectations following the release of the latest data, which showed rising price pressures in the United States.
US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% year on year in September, exceeding economists' forecasts.
The figure remains above the Fed's 2% inflation target, which is measured using a different, although related, indicator to the Consumer Price Index.
The data release initially prompted market participants to increase their bets on a possible interest rate increase in October.
However, those expectations eased after investors examined the individual components of inflation more closely.
Daly explained that rising petrol prices were one of the main drivers of the overall increase in inflation. Meanwhile, core inflation continued to show persistent price pressures but had not experienced a sharp acceleration.
Nevertheless, she acknowledged that the latest data had increased inflation risks.
She said these risks needed to be taken into account but should not automatically be treated as a certainty requiring the central bank to act immediately.
Daly believes policy decisions should be based on all available information, particularly when there is still time for further assessment.
Changes in market expectations indicate that the possibility of another interest rate increase remains open.
Based on financial market pricing, investors estimate there is around a 40% chance that the Fed will raise interest rates again at its next meeting.
That figure increased following the inflation report but no longer makes a rate increase the most likely scenario.
Daly stressed that stability in the labour market gave the Fed room to remain focused on price stability.
However, the central bank needs to balance inflation risks against broader economic developments.
She also emphasised the importance of clear policy communication with the public. According to Daly, the Fed has a responsibility to explain its policy objectives, be accountable for its decisions and communicate how it assesses economic risks.
With inflation still elevated, the direction of Fed policy over the coming months will depend heavily on incoming economic data.
Although another interest rate increase remains possible, Daly's remarks suggest that the central bank wants to retain flexibility before deciding on the timing and scale of its next adjustment. (DK/LM)
