Summary
- PBOC CNY reference rate setting for the trading session ahead.
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.
---
The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.
Summary:
- The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.
- China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours.
- The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number.
- If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks.
- A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains.
- For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August.
- In September the PBOC strengthened the fixing for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2023, and the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023.
- The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore, with Goldman Sachs expecting Beijing to remain comfortable with sustained but gradual appreciation.
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.
Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.
That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.
September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.
The timing has been linked to diplomacy.
The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

articles.title: Frank Elderson: Ensuring resilience in the face of uncertainty
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
Ensuring resilience in the face of uncertainty
Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the ECB-Bank of England Conference on supervising climate risk in a non-linear world
Frankfurt am Main, 14 October 2026
It is a pleasure to open this joint ECB-Bank of England conference.
Bringing together experts across disciplines from 18 countries and three continents to discuss how we can ensure resilience in an increasingly non-linear world, this event could hardly be more timely.
For much of modern finance, risk management has rested on a simple but consequential assumption: with enough data, sufficient information about borrower behaviour, robust models and a solid understanding of historical patterns, banks can estimate the losses they may face with a reasonable degree of precision.
These estimates inform how banks price risk, set aside provisions for expected losses and determine how much capital they need to absorb any large, unexpected losses. This approach works well when the underlying relationships are broadly stable and has long served as a useful basis for managing financial risks. And of course, today’s modelling is already supplemented by additional layers of risk management, including model overlays, stress testing, underwriting, risk appetite setting and other processes.
But the world facing us today is becoming more complex, more interconnected and more uncertain almost by the day.
Think about geopolitical fragmentation, demographic change, artificial intelligence and quantum computing and, of course, the central theme of this conference: the risks from the ongoing climate and nature (C&N) crises.
These macro trends differ in many respects.
They differ in origin.
They differ in scope.
They differ in speed.
Yet they all share a common denominator: they arise in complex and highly interconnected systems, which often exhibit non-linear behaviour. This means that small changes can spread and trigger disproportionately large effects. These macro trends can amplify shocks through feedback loops. They can lead to abrupt transitions through tipping points. Events that were considered remote tail risks yesterday are moving closer to tomorrow’s baseline.
Addressing non-linearities is undoubtedly challenging but still manageable as long as we remain in the realm of what is measurable. However, an even bigger challenge arises when we enter a world characterised by what Frank Knight termed uncertainty, as distinct from risk, or what John Kay and Mervyn King later popularised as radical uncertainty.[1] The underlying idea is the same: a form of uncertainty in which future events, their probabilities and even the relevant outcomes cannot be measured with any meaningful degree of confidence.
Today I would like to use a simple framework to explore this challenge. The distinction between what we know, what we know we don’t know, and what we don’t even know we don’t know. Or put differently: known knowns, known unknowns and unknown unknowns.
The world we know: the known knowns of C&N risks
Let me begin with what we already know about C&N risks.
Over the past decade, banks and supervisors have made substantial progress in identifying, quantifying and managing C&N risks.[2]
Together, we have built the foundational architecture needed to capture the known knowns of C&N risks in risk management, stress testing and scenario analysis.[3]
Today, we not only see and feel the effects of rising temperatures; increasingly, we can measure them. Thanks to better tools, better data and better modelling, we are increasingly able to quantify the direct damage caused to the economy by C&N risks.[4] Just think about the heavy toll this summers’ extreme weather took on economic activity, labour productivity[5] and supply chains.[6]
Importantly, we also increasingly understand the transmission channels to the financial risk categories facing banks.
For example, with better climate hazard and geo-location data, banks can better model the financial impacts of droughts and flooding on traditional financial risk metrics such as loss given default (LGD).
We know banks’ initial estimate of the impact of different transition scenarios on their capital position.
And we also know that since 2022 the average share of interest income earned from carbon-intensive sectors by significant supervised banks has remained consistently above 70%.
We know the average energy performance of the properties they finance. We know what share of exposures they have in areas vulnerable to physical risk and what proportion of those exposures, in turn, has deteriorating credit quality. While many of these impacts still rely on estimates, banks have made significant strides in recent years, thanks also to the availability of public data sources, which cover an increasing number of physical risk hazards.[7]
But as important as this progress is, it only tells part of the story.[8]
We know that many of the C&N risks that matter most are, by their very nature, forward-looking. And we know that because these risks are very different from past events, they are not fully understood and remain difficult to quantify.
The progress made so far therefore provides a springboard for a more difficult, but necessary conversation: a conversation about some of the fundamental challenges of these risks and uncertainty, a conversation not only about what we know, but also about what we know we do not yet know.
What remains uncertain: the known unknowns of C&N risks
And that brings me to the second category in our framework: the known unknowns.
These are risks that we know exist, but whose timing, magnitude or probabilities remain uncertain.
This is not a new challenge. Economic forecasting operates in a similar environment. The economy, like the climate, is a complex adaptive system. We cannot forecast it with precision, but we can explore plausible scenarios and assess our resilience against them.
C&N risks provide several examples:
We know that tipping points exist but we do not know exactly when they will be reached. Worryingly, scientists have identified several components of the Earth system for which the tipping point may already be approaching, including the dieback of the Amazon rainforest and the collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
We also know that compound events can amplify impact. We do not know precisely how such interactions will unfold. A severe drought will likely occur alongside a heatwave. Water scarcity could coincide with a major agricultural disruption. Physical damage could occur simultaneously with pressures on energy systems.[9]
And we know that nature degradation can affect economic activity through complex and interconnected channels. We know that humanity is living well beyond most of its planetary boundaries.[10] In fact, seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. What remains uncertain is how these forces may interact, amplify each other and ultimately propagate through the economy and the financial system.
In all these examples we run into a fundamental problem: the future impacts of climate change and nature degradation are, by definition, not reflected in the historical data used in traditional risk analysis.
Using scenario analysis to address known unknowns
When dealing with uncertainty, scenario analysis is an indispensable tool. Scenarios are best understood not as forecasts, but rather as structured explorations of plausible futures. Their purpose is not to tell us what will happen, but to help us think more systematically about what could happen. They allow us to identify vulnerabilities, test assumptions and investigate transmission channels that may otherwise remain hidden.
Encouragingly, climate scenario analysis has advanced considerably in recent years. The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios have become the global reference point for assessing how climate change may affect economies and financial systems over both short and long horizons. These scenarios have evolved to encompass a wider range of risks while also providing financial projections. By offering a publicly accessible set of scenarios, they have significantly improved the capacity of the central banking community to quantify climate risks in a consistent, transparent and comparable manner across jurisdictions.
But scenarios are a starting point, not an endpoint. When facing uncertainty, we need to avoid a scenario “tunnel vision’’ where risk identification and capital planning becomes anchored to a narrow set of scenario narratives. With heightened uncertainty, the objective of scenarios should not only be to explore baseline pathways, but also to investigate how vulnerabilities might be exposed under extreme yet plausible conditions.
And we know that the current climate scenarios have their limitations.
As Simon Sharpe has observed, scientists are trained not to overstate risks, while risk managers are trained not to underestimate them. This distinction also matters for climate models designed by scientists. These models capture what can be quantified robustly, but not necessarily everything scientists know is likely to occur.
Take thawing permafrost, for example. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) concludes with high confidence that further warming will cause further thaw, thus releasing more carbon. Yet most global climate models do not represent this feedback directly. The separate adjustment used in the latest assessment still excludes abrupt thaw and interactions with Arctic wildfires. Research suggests that nature’s own emissions from thawing permafrost or wildfires could add as much as 0.6°C in an adverse scenario.[11] Similar limitations apply to additional emissions from warming wetlands and freshwater systems. articles.title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
articles.summary: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offenderUS lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.
It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.
A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.
If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.
The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.
Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.
Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.
The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.
Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.
That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.
After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.
In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.
Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.
The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.
“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.
Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”
Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.
